item.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
item.description: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year. On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit) , 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life. On 31 May, the comet was languishing at magnitude +17.39 (the higher the magnitude, the fainter an object is), but within less than 14 hours it had dramatically brightened to magnitude +11.05, bringing it into range for observation with small amateur telescopes. By June 2, 220P was up to magnitude +8.23 and was technically visible for a short while in 10x50 binoculars from a dark site, prompting amateur astronomers and astrophotographers to chase down this rare event. By perihelion, the comet had faded back to magnitude +12, but more was to come. A second outburst began at the end of July, brightening from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 by 6 August. Telling the tale of a dirty snowball Comets are often referred to as dirty snowballs, and beneath their dusty crust are ices made from various volatiles, including water, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Solar heating, even at the distance of Mars, can cause these ices to rapidly sublimate into gases, and the pressure of the escaping gas rips the surface apart, spewing huge amounts of dust in to space. Models based on observations of 220P’s outburst indicate that it spewed out between tens of billions and hundreds of billions of pounds’ worth of cometary dust that filled the comet’s coma, the diffuse 'atmosphere' that clings to the comet’s solid nucleus. The dust particles, which are just millionths of a meter across, expanded outwards from the comet at about 1,280 feet (390 meters) per second, scattering sunlight and causing the coma to substantially brighten. "We have concluded that the comet detached localized parts of its crust, creating a dust-rich envelope that increased [the comet’s brightness by] 250 times in half a day," Josep M. Trigo-Rodríguez, of the Institut de Ciències de l’Espai and the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia in Spain, said in a statement . item.content:encoded: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year. On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit) , 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life. On 31 May, the comet was languishing at magnitude +17.39 (the higher the magnitude, the fainter an object is), but within less than 14 hours it had dramatically brightened to magnitude +11.05, bringing it into range for observation with small amateur telescopes. By June 2, 220P was up to magnitude +8.23 and was technically visible for a short while in 10x50 binoculars from a dark site, prompting amateur astronomers and astrophotographers to chase down this rare event. By perihelion, the comet had faded back to magnitude +12, but more was to come. A second outburst began at the end of July, brightening from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 by 6 August. Telling the tale of a dirty snowball Comets are often referred to as dirty snowballs, and beneath their dusty crust are ices made from various volatiles, including water, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Solar heating, even at the distance of Mars, can cause these ices to rapidly sublimate into gases, and the pressure of the escaping gas rips the surface apart, spewing huge amounts of dust in to space. Models based on observations of 220P’s outburst indicate that it spewed out between tens of billions and hundreds of billions of pounds’ worth of cometary dust that filled the comet’s coma, the diffuse 'atmosphere' that clings to the comet’s solid nucleus. The dust particles, which are just millionths of a meter across, expanded outwards from the comet at about 1,280 feet (390 meters) per second, scattering sunlight and causing the coma to substantially brighten. "We have concluded that the comet detached localized parts of its crust, creating a dust-rich envelope that increased [the comet’s brightness by] 250 times in half a day," Josep M. Trigo-Rodríguez, of the Institut de Ciències de l’Espai and the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia in Spain, said in a statement . Comet 220P/McNaught imaged from an observatory in Spain on 7 August following its second outburst. (Image credit: Peter Carson.) While this is the first time that 220P has been seen to outburst, over the years we have witnessed other comets spectacularly brighten out of nowhere. A recent and well-known example is comet 17P/Holmes , which brightened a million-fold in the fall of 2007 as it rose from magnitude +17 to magnitude +2.8, becoming a welcome naked-eye sight in the constellation of Perseus for many people as they made the evening commute home. The short 5.5-year orbit of 220P marks it out as a Jupiter -family comet. "Jupiter-family comets are extremely interesting objects to study because they originate primarily from the Kuiper Belt and the Scattered Disk region, later migrating inward until Jupiter captures them into short-period orbits," said Trigo-Rodríguez. Studying outbursts such as the two experienced by 220P provides vital clues as to the bulk characteristics of Jupiter-family comets, giving us insight into objects that originated from beyond the orbit of Neptune . An illustration of a comet approaching Earth. (Image credit: Robert Lea) Of particular interest to Trigo-Rodríguez is what we should do were one of these objects ever to be found on a collision course with Earth . "Particularly we are interested in the tensile strength and nature of comets in the framework of our studies on impact hazards," said Trigo-Rodríguez. "Some comets seem determined to demonstrate that they are fragile enough and perhaps give us the chance to invoke disruptive approaches that might be substantially different from the ones already tested or proposed for asteroids." For now, 220P is heading back out to its furthest point from the sun, which is just inside the orbit of Jupiter at a distance of 4.68 astronomical units or 435 million miles (700 million kilometers). Having passed as close to Earth as it is going to get this time around on 12 October at a distance of 1.04 astronomical units or 97 million miles (156 million kilometres), the comet is currently magnitude +13 and fading. All eyes will be on 220P during its next time around the sun in late 2031. The findings were published on Nov.3 in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society .

item.title: Darey Art Alade, Tola Odunsi, Uti Nwachukwu & More Step Out for DStv ExpectMoreNaija Launch
item.description: On Wednesday, 4 November some of your favourite entertainment and lifestyle personalities converged at The Royal Box, Victoria Island, as MultiChoice Nigeria, a CANAL+ company, unveiled its new DStv and GOtv package line-up under the ‘Expect More’ campaign. The evening blended performances with a first-hand look at the new packages, had personalities including media executive Obi Asika , filmmaker Tola Odunsi , actors William Benson and Enado Odigie, entertainment power couple Darey and Deola Art-Alade , costume designer Yolanda Okereke, BBNaija stars Temi Nkem, Kola Omotosho and Imisi Ayanwale , and media personalities Uti Nwachukwu, Chuey Chu and Hero Daniels in attendance. Co-hosting the evening were media personality and actress Folu Storms and Deji Osikoya, who kept the energy high throughout, guiding guests through the night’s programme and the interactive spaces inspired by each package. Media Personalities Folu Storms And Deji Osikoya On The Red Carpet At The #ExpectMoreNaija Event Welcoming guests, MultiChoice Nigeria CEO Kemi Omotosho described the launch as the start of a new era for subscribers, with packages shaped by what Nigerians have asked for: more value, more choice and more content that speaks to them “We are in a new era of entertainment, and it is made for our customers,” she said. “From the 5th of November, we’re going to be doing three big things: giving you more choice and a clear, easy line-up, so you can choose what you want.” The Loud Urban Choir Performing at the #ExpectMoreNaija Event The night also featured a moving performance from spoken word artist Ibquake , while The Loud Urban Choir had the room singing along to a medley of some of Nigeria’s biggest songs. So, what’s new? Under the new structure, DStv packages now comprise Starter, Select, Sports and Premium, while GOtv customers can choose from Easy, Starter, Select and Sports. Starter (₦6,000) now includes two brand-new channels, SuperSport KICKOFF and Africa Magic+, bringing football and homegrown drama to more Nigerian homes. For the die-hard football fans, Sports (₦21,000) covers every Premier League and Champions League match, plus WWE and UFC. For more details, head over to www.dstv.com and www.gotvafrica.com , and join the conversation with #ExpectMoreOnDStv and #ExpectMoreNaija. item.title: How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause
item.description: Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people's lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities. Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people's impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences. A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity. Read full article Comments

item.title: Record-breaking Andy Robertson is Scotland’s finest captain
item.description: As he passes Kenny Dalglish’s appearance total, it is important to remember that it is the left-back’s journey that sets him apart Andy Robertson may not be Scotland’s greatest player, but he is indisputably their finest captain. It counts as sacrilege, even to generations who have watched Kenny Dalglish only on YouTube, to reputationally place Robertson above the Liverpool hero on the basis of a cap haul that will reach 103 in St Gallen on Monday. Dalglish’s international career ended at 102 and the curious events that meant he missed the 1986 World Cup. There is no requirement to compare a left-back in 2026 to a forward from decades earlier. Dalglish and Robertson are men in different positions in essentially a different sport. Instead, Robertson’s march to the top of the cap pile gives cause to laud his contribution. Continue reading...

item.title: Ramla Ali Wins IBF and WBO Titles to Become Somalia’s First Boxing World Champion
item.description: Unified world champion Ramla Ali poses in the ring with her WBO and IBF super-bantamweight belts and her coaching team in Arlington, Texas. Photo Credit: Yahya Ali/Instagram British-Somali boxer and fashion model Ramla Ali is officially a unified world champion! On 8 November 2026 at the College Park Center in Arlington, Texas, the 37-year-old athlete captured the vacant IBF and WBO super-bantamweight world titles after securing a split-decision victory over American contender Mikiah Kreps . During the ten-round bout, Ali dropped Kreps with a sharp right hand in the third round—the sole knockdown of the night—before two judges scored the contest 97–92 and 96–93 in her favour, against one scorecard of 98–91 for Kreps. With this triumph, Ali became Somalia’s first-ever professional boxing world champion and a unified titleholder in one unforgettable night. Born in Mogadishu, Somalia, she fled the civil war as a child with her family and grew up in East London, initially taking up boxing in secret as a teenager before turning it into a life-changing calling. Ramla Ali makes her ring walk behind the Somali and British flags ahead of her super-bantamweight world title fight in Arlington, Texas. Photo Credit: Yahya Ali/Instagram Her remarkable journey from refugee to Olympic athlete and champion is also the subject of the biographical feature film In the Shadows. Directed by Anthony Wonke , the film premiered at the 70th BFI London Film Festival on 9 October 2026 before opening in UK and Irish cinemas on 30 October—just over a week before she lifted her world title belts in Texas. BAFTA-winning Top Boy actress Jasmine Jobson stars as Ali alongside Peaky Blinders actor Finn Cole as her husband and former coach, Richard Moore , with both Ali and Moore serving as executive producers on the project. This championship milestone builds on a string of barrier-breaking firsts across sports, cinema, and fashion. Long before her title win in Arlington, Ali made history as the first Muslim woman to win an English amateur boxing title, the first boxer to win an international gold medal while representing Somalia, and the first boxer to represent Somalia on the Olympic stage when she competed in the women’s featherweight division at the Tokyo 2020 Summer Olympics. Ramla Ali celebrates in the ring as the referee raises her hand following her split-decision victory over Mikiah Kreps on 8 November 2026. Photo Credit: Yahya Ali/Instagram Away from the ring, she has carved out an equally notable space in global luxury fashion. Ali has graced the covers of British Vogue, Elle UK, Harper’s Bazaar Arabia, and Grazia UK, served as a brand ambassador for Cartier and Dior, and made history as the first boxer to wear custom ring attire created by major fashion houses—including bespoke fight kits designed by Dior, Off-White, Versace, Alexander McQueen, and Burberry featuring the panther emblem from Somalia’s coat of arms. Now holding both the IBF and WBO super-bantamweight belt

item.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
item.description: null Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off. Long-distance view of Ship's historic landing on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) SpaceX has caught Super Heavy on three test flights to date. But it had never caught a Ship before; indeed, it had never even tried before Saturday. It's tougher and riskier to catch Ship; the upper stage flies much higher and faster than Super Heavy, so its return trip is much more more involved. Saturday was therefore a very big day for the company. "That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes." The F light 15 mission plan gave us a sneak peek at the future: The double catch will be standard on operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will enable rapid inspection, refurbishment and reflight of the megarocket, according to SpaceX. And the company is indeed planning on rapid reflight. Elon Musk has said that SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship launches per year by 2030, which works out to more than one liftoff every hour on average. Why such a mind-boggling cadence? Because SpaceX plans to build megaconstellations far larger than anything circling Earth today. For example, it wants its next-gen Starlink V3 broadband network to consist of 100,000 satellites . And its planned Starmind AI data-center constellation will be 10 times bigger than that, featuring one million spacecraft , if all goes to plan. For perspective: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network in low Earth orbit (LEO), by far the largest constellation ever assembled, is about 11,000 strong at the moment. A look at the 33 Raptor engines of Starship's Super Heavy booster during the vehicle's Flight 15 test launch on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Josh Dinner, Space.com/Future) Rocket recovery is only part of the reuse equation, of course; there's also refurbishment and reflight. And that gets us back to the "work left to do" discussion, for SpaceX has yet to demonstrate rapid reflight with either Super Heavy or Ship. item.dc:creator: Mike Wall
item.content:encoded: null Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off. Long-distance view of Ship's historic landing on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) SpaceX has caught Super Heavy on three test flights to date. But it had never caught a Ship before; indeed, it had never even tried before Saturday. It's tougher and riskier to catch Ship; the upper stage flies much higher and faster than Super Heavy, so its return trip is much more more involved. Saturday was therefore a very big day for the company. "That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes." The F light 15 mission plan gave us a sneak peek at the future: The double catch will be standard on operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will enable rapid inspection, refurbishment and reflight of the megarocket, according to SpaceX. And the company is indeed planning on rapid reflight. Elon Musk has said that SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship launches per year by 2030, which works out to more than one liftoff every hour on average. Why such a mind-boggling cadence? Because SpaceX plans to build megaconstellations far larger than anything circling Earth today. For example, it wants its next-gen Starlink V3 broadband network to consist of 100,000 satellites . And its planned Starmind AI data-center constellation will be 10 times bigger than that, featuring one million spacecraft , if all goes to plan. For perspective: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network in low Earth orbit (LEO), by far the largest constellation ever assembled, is about 11,000 strong at the moment. A look at the 33 Raptor engines of Starship's Super Heavy booster during the vehicle's Flight 15 test launch on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Josh Dinner, Space.com/Future) Rocket recovery is only part of the reuse equation, of course; there's also refurbishment and reflight. And that gets us back to the "work left to do" discussion, for SpaceX has yet to demonstrate rapid reflight with either Super Heavy or Ship. The company has reflown Super Heavy vehicles on two separate occasions. Booster 14 initially launched on Flight 7 in January 2025, then lifted off again on Flight 9 in May of that year. Booster 15 flew on Flight 8 and Flight 11 , which lifted off in March 2025 and October 2025, respectively. Several months separated each of these Super Heavy reflights. And SpaceX has yet to reuse a Ship, as it had not caught one during a mission until Saturday. That could change soon: Before Flight 15 lifted off, Musk said that the company wants to reuse both of its Starship stages. That option may still be on the table for Flight 15's Ship. And we should expect full reuse to be a priority on Starship test flights over the longer haul, with SpaceX working toward shorter and shorter turnaround times — perhaps until an hourly cadence is in sight, if that goal is indeed achievable. Over the next few years, most Starship launches will likely be devoted to building out the Starlink V3 and Starmind megaconstellations. But the rocket will also carry people to deep space, if all goes to plan, which will require the checking of another set of boxes. NASA selected Ship to be the first crewed lunar lander for its Artemis program , which aims to establish a base near the lunar south pole by 2032 or so. Current plans call for Ship to land astronauts in that locale for the first time on the Artemis IV mission, which is targeted to fly in 2028. SpaceX needs to install a crew cabin and life-support system in Ship to make that happen. The company is working on that now and has made considerable progress, according to NASA. Last month, an agency presentation reported that SpaceX is on target to finish building "Cabin 1," a full-scale ground prototype of Ship's crew cabin, by the end of the year. There's another hurdle to clear, however. On all deep-space missions, Ship will need to fill up its fuel tanks after launch, at a "depot" that SpaceX will set up in Earth orbit. (Launching Ship with full tanks is not an option, as it would be incredibly heavy in that case.) The depot will be filled by "tanker" variants of Ship. It's unclear how many tanker visits will be required for each Ship deep-space mission; outside experts have floated numbers as high as 22, while Musk has cited six to eight as a probable range. Whatever the actual number, Ship will need to demonstrate proficiency with off-Earth refueling, something it has yet to do. And there's more to it than just a simple rendezvous: Ship's engines run on liquid oxygen and liquid methane, so the propellants must be kept extremely cold throughout the process. We're likely to see the first refueling test relatively soon, as time is of the essence for SpaceX. If the company can't get Ship ready for the Artemis IV moon landing in 2028, NASA may go with another private lander — Blue Origin's Blue Moon , which the agency also contracted for Artemis missions. All of this is to say that, while Flight 15 was a big success for Starship and SpaceX, there's a lot of work left to do — and a lot for space fans to watch for over the coming weeks and months.

item.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
item.description: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness. Continue reading...

item.title: LEO gets a birthday bash, 75 years after clocking in
item.description: Business computing turns 75 this month, and Cambridge's Centre for Computing History is throwing a party for LEO, the machine that helped start it all. The LEO@75 event takes place on Saturday, November 28, from 10am to 5pm, with film screenings, historical displays, and hands-on activities for children. The Register has written about the Centre for Computing History a few times. It's an interactive computer museum just off Coldhams Lane in Cambridge, and back in 2018 it won National Lottery funding to help it "preserve, archive and digitise a range of LEO Computers artefacts, documents and personal memories." Admission supports the museum charity, with student and concession tickets at £10 and family tickets starting at £15. As well as stuff for the grown-ups, including a film screening, it will include events for smaller children (5-7) and a Python coding event for older (12-16) kids. Regular readers might recall our story about the Lyons Electronic Office back in 2021, celebrating its 70th anniversary. The Reg also published an obituary for Mary Coombs, the first female commercial programmer the following year. Coombs started programming LEO in 1952. Both stories offer more on the machine and the people behind it. LEO was an early computer, but from three-quarters of a century away, it's easy to miss just how early. Its design was based on Cambridge University's EDSAC, developed by a team led by the late, great Sir Maurice Wilkes. The Reg mentioned EDSAC in our obituary for Wilkes, and went into more detail for his centenary in 2013 . It also crops up in our Geek's Guide to Cambridge . The design of EDSAC was directly inspired by John von Neumann's famous, and incomplete, "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" – which The Reg talked about in 2011 . The draft report was circulated in 1945, based on the proposal for EDVAC, four years before the hardware was delivered. That was also the year John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert completed its predecessor, ENIAC. In its original form, ENIAC was programmed by setting switches and reconnecting cables; EDVAC, by contrast, was designed to store its instructions in memory. The report set out what's now called the "von Neumann architecture." Wilkes and Douglas Hartree drew on those ideas in developing EDSAC, LEO's immediate forerunner and one of the world's earliest practical stored-program computers. The first working electronic stored-program machine was the Manchester "Baby," the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, which ran its first program in 1948 . EDSAC ran its first program in May 1949 – a few months before the delivery of BINAC, Eckert and Mauchly's first stored-program machine. LEO ran its first commercial application in 1951. That was also the year the US Census Bureau took delivery of Eckert and Mauchly's UNIVAC I . ®

item.title: Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’
item.description: The former England centre-back answers your questions on Diego Maradona, Bobby Robson and on staying in strange places “Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap. It turns out dozens of Guardian readers want to pick the brains of a much-loved centre-back who was feted en route to a World Cup semi-final and tormented four years previously by the mercurial genius of Diego Maradona. Did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”? Butcher found himself in the post-match doping-control room alongside his nemesis at the Azteca in 1986. “I tapped my head, then my hand, and then he tapped his head,” Butcher says. “He didn’t admit to it because, if he had, I’d have been right across that room.” Continue reading...

item.title: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership
item.description: Clubs with wealthy proprietors can maintain a loss-making operation but things can be more complex when the supporters carry the can When you walk up from Haydons Road railway station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium. AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter – but that makes running a loss‑making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board, which runs AFC Wimbledon, for seven years. “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.” Continue reading...

item.title: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
item.description: Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true The resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry. Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet. Continue reading...

item.title: SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch
item.description: STARBASE, Texas —The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position. Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms. Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket. Read full article Comments

item.title: This Week In Space podcast: Episode 236 — Alienspotting
item.description: null On Episode 236 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. When we think of extraterrestrials, our minds generally go from the latex-suited bipedal aliens seen in Star Trek and Star Wars to more exotic critters in sci-fi movies. Scientists think in terms of carbon-based microbial life and other lower life forms. But some researchers, such as Tikhonov from Washington University, suggest that life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. He further suggests a new definition of life: something that takes in and transforms energy and replicates. His ideas radically expand our notions of alien life and how it might be recognized. item.title: 'Alien: Fireteam Elite 2' is a good old-fashioned bug hunt, ironically plagued by bugs
item.description: The first Aliens: Fireteam Elite was among my favorite Alien video games , and there were a lot of reasons to be excited for a sequel. At Summer Game Fest 2026 , we learned of many smart changes and improvements to the formula, and I was eager to go bug-hunting again. A new campaign, fully reworked classes, and four-player co-op. What could go wrong? Months later, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2's debut has been difficult, mostly due to glaring tech issues. Despite this, it's still a welcome jolt of action for a franchise that's been focusing on making the Xenomorphs scary again in recent years. Alien: Romulus (2024) and Alien: Earth (2025) have reestablished the acid-blooded Xenomorphs as bona fide horror icons, while games like Aliens: Dark Descent bet on tense real-time tactics and squad management; Rogue Incursion spooked VR and non-VR players alike; and we even have Isolation 2 's pure survival horror to look forward to. Rough edges aside, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is a necessary return to mindless shooting and treating the Xenos as a relentless horde, dropping the stalking and slasher-inspired murders in favor of sci-fi shootouts and macho one-liners. It's far from a novel idea — even the original game is only five years old — but a classic for a reason. Another glorious day in the Corps (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) Believe it or not, another colony has fallen prey to the Xenomorphs in Fireteam Elite 2. The familiar setup takes a new team of Colonial Marines to a mining facility on LV-558, where contact has been lost with the first wave of Marines that went in to deal with the threat. This isn't first contact; the Marines are more than used to bug hunts by now, which means there's less exposition to cut through before getting to the Xeno-blasting chaos. The writing certainly won't stun the Academy (and there's definitely too much of it in between missions), but the agility here is appreciated. We've fought these aliens many, many times before. Fireteam Elite 2 is smart enough to sidestep fake tension and just hit the ground running. (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) All the design changes and upgrades reinforce the intent to make the ultimate Aliens action game. Classes have more defined roles and access to better, more destructive sci-fi weapons, and the upgrade to four-player fireteams is welcome when aliens and hostile synths won't stop pouring in. Tired of replaying campaign missions on higher difficulties and with modifiers? Prepare for the worst in this shooter's version of the classic horde mode. At its best, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 understands why James Cameron's masterpiece still holds up. During the biggest Xenomorph onslaughts — when the bullets are flying and acid is spraying — the game's shortcomings and jankier elements fade away. Game over, man (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) There are still some scares hiding in here, though, ready to make complacent players jump out of their seats. Special Xenomorphs
item.dc:creator: Fran Ruiz
item.content:encoded: The first Aliens: Fireteam Elite was among my favorite Alien video games , and there were a lot of reasons to be excited for a sequel. At Summer Game Fest 2026 , we learned of many smart changes and improvements to the formula, and I was eager to go bug-hunting again. A new campaign, fully reworked classes, and four-player co-op. What could go wrong? Months later, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2's debut has been difficult, mostly due to glaring tech issues. Despite this, it's still a welcome jolt of action for a franchise that's been focusing on making the Xenomorphs scary again in recent years. Alien: Romulus (2024) and Alien: Earth (2025) have reestablished the acid-blooded Xenomorphs as bona fide horror icons, while games like Aliens: Dark Descent bet on tense real-time tactics and squad management; Rogue Incursion spooked VR and non-VR players alike; and we even have Isolation 2 's pure survival horror to look forward to. Rough edges aside, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is a necessary return to mindless shooting and treating the Xenos as a relentless horde, dropping the stalking and slasher-inspired murders in favor of sci-fi shootouts and macho one-liners. It's far from a novel idea — even the original game is only five years old — but a classic for a reason. Another glorious day in the Corps (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) Believe it or not, another colony has fallen prey to the Xenomorphs in Fireteam Elite 2. The familiar setup takes a new team of Colonial Marines to a mining facility on LV-558, where contact has been lost with the first wave of Marines that went in to deal with the threat. This isn't first contact; the Marines are more than used to bug hunts by now, which means there's less exposition to cut through before getting to the Xeno-blasting chaos. The writing certainly won't stun the Academy (and there's definitely too much of it in between missions), but the agility here is appreciated. We've fought these aliens many, many times before. Fireteam Elite 2 is smart enough to sidestep fake tension and just hit the ground running. (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) All the design changes and upgrades reinforce the intent to make the ultimate Aliens action game. Classes have more defined roles and access to better, more destructive sci-fi weapons, and the upgrade to four-player fireteams is welcome when aliens and hostile synths won't stop pouring in. Tired of replaying campaign missions on higher difficulties and with modifiers? Prepare for the worst in this shooter's version of the classic horde mode. At its best, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 understands why James Cameron's masterpiece still holds up. During the biggest Xenomorph onslaughts — when the bullets are flying and acid is spraying — the game's shortcomings and jankier elements fade away. Game over, man (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) There are still some scares hiding in here, though, ready to make complacent players jump out of their seats. Special Xenomorphs have tricks to pounce on distracted players, throwing chaos into the middle of their carefully coordinated rain of fire. Others have the ability to spit from afar, breaking tight defenses that count on the Xenos' predictable tactics from other games and the movies. It's been 40 years since Aliens first graced the big screen , but Fireteam Elite 2 manages to refresh that mix of horror and action well enough, despite sharing much of its bones with the original game. But the disturbing lack of polish threatens to undo Cold Iron Studios' best ideas. Those ideas include more varied enemies, which can disrupt almost any tried-and-tested team composition, and even a late-game class that rewards an extensive knowledge of the game by letting veterans pick weapons from all over the roster to create a custom loadout. (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) These playful creative swings somewhat offset the frustration caused by glitched objectives, enemy AI that often goes off the rails, and performance issues that have often given me flashbacks to its predecessor's worst moments on PS4. Sometimes, you can just tell when six extra months would've done a game a lot of good, and it's obvious that Fireteam Elite 2 will be in a much better place by spring. That said, its loose and confident approach to design is rare to see when dealing with games that adapt well-established IPs like Alien. Recent Star Wars games have achieved just that , and even if Fireteam Elite 2 misses some of its shots and has faced more initial trouble than the USCM's first incursion on LV-426, it's safe to say its heart and mind are in the right place. No one can take that away from the devs. Show me another modern Alien video game that allows you to zap Xenomorphs to death with a big cannon or to hold them off with combat drones. We've seen developers win uphill battles before, and we know for a fact the huge Alien fandom is as enduring as the deadly extraterrestrials, so Daybreak and Cold Iron have a chance to turn things around and solidify Fireteam Elite 2 as the iterative but satisfying sequel it actually is. Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is available now for PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC. A Nintendo Switch 2 version is coming in 2027.

item.title: Microsoft confirms all services are restored after global outage
item.description: Microsoft has said that all services have been fully restored after a global outage which affected the NHS, police, schools and other services across the UK.

item.title: Why did Starship Flight 15 booster abort 'chopsticks' landing catch? SpaceX still investigating (video)
item.description:
Tariq is the Editor-in-Chief of Space.com based out of our New York City office and joined the team in 2001, first as an intern and staff writer, and later as an editor. He covers human spaceflight, exploration and space science, as well as skywatching and entertainment. He became Space.com's Managing Editor in 2009 and Editor-in-Chief in 2019. In October 2022, Tariq received the Harry Kolcum Award for excellence in space reporting from the National Space Club Florida Committee. In June 2025, the National Space Society awarded him the Space Pioneer Award for Excellence in Mass Media at the International Space Development Conference in Orlando, Florida.

Hailing from Stockton, California (where he attended the same high school as NASA astronaut Jose Hernandez), Tariq studied print journalism and astronomy at the University of Southern California in Los Angeles, earning a bachelor's degree in journalism in 1999 along with a minor in astronomy. He then served as a staff reporter for The Los Angeles Times covering education and city beats in La Habra and Fullerton in Orange County for the Our Times sections.

In 2000, Tariq became the city reporter for the Huntington Beach Independent, a weekly publication of the Los Angeles Times, covering local politics and events, crime, business and environmental issues. He left the Los Angeles Times in 2001 to study science journalism at New York University, where he earned a master's degree in 2002 from NYU's Science and Environmental Reporting Program (now the Science, Health and Environmental Reporting Program) under the direction of space reporter William Burrows.

Tariq first joined Space.com as an intern in September 2001 while also serving as a research assistant for nutrition writer Gary Taubes and writing freelance projects, where his work appeared in The Scientist and Laboratory Equipment Magazine. He became a full-time reporter covering spaceflight in 2004, with this first launch being NASA's STS-114 Return to Flight mission in July 2005.

Tariq is also an Eagle Scout (yes, he has the Space Exploration merit badge) and went to Space Camp four times as a kid and a fifth time as an adult. When not writing about space, you can find Tariq watching the latest Star Trek TV series, sci-fi movies and reading about hippos, his favorite animal. You can find Tariq at Space.com and as the co-host to the This Week In Space podcast with space historian Rod Pyle on the TWiT network. To see his latest project, you can follow Tariq on Twitter @tariqjmalik.

Update for 3:40 p.m. ET on Nov. 14: SpaceX's Kate Tice provided more information about the booster abort at about 3:30 p.m. EST (1830 GMT) on Nov. 14, during the company's Flight 15 webcast. "Early indications are that the booster ended its boostback [burn] early due to a low fuel mass alarm," she said. "The team is still investigating the root cause on that." SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13), triggering an automatic abort that destroyed the booster. The giant Starship rocket , a massive two-stage vehicle that's the largest launcher on Earth, soared into orbit from SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas on Friday on the company's ambitious Flight 15 test flight. The goal: To land both the Super Heavy first stage and the Ship upper stage, for the first full Starship recovery — and the first complete recovery of an orbital launch system in history. The Super Heavy stage, called Booster 22, came back to Earth mere minutes after liftoff as planned. Instead of returning to its launch tower to be caught mid-air by the tower's metal "chopstick" arms , however, the rocket veered offshore and detonated its flight termination system. SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot initially said that a guidance issue appeared to be the cause. The Super Heavy first-stage booster of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 rocket explodes during splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico after launching its Ship upper stage to orbit from Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Josh Dinner, Space.com/Future) Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon . Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g. View Deal "We were initially 'go' for a catch," Huot said during live commentary on Friday, about seven hours into the mission. "But in the later stages of the coast, the booster aborted itself for a GNC issue that it detected, and that put it into its contingency landing offshore." Super Heavy exploded a few feet above the waves of the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after liftoff. GNC is short for Guidance and Navigation Control, a criticial system used by rockets to control their flight and ensure they remain on their planned course. Such a system is vital for any landing attempt by a Starship Super Heavy or Ship upper stage to ensure the vehicle returns to its landing site safely and doesn't veer off course to damage SpaceX's Starbase or surrounding populated areas. In an update during SpaceX's Flight 15 coverage on Saturday, however, Huot said that Super Heavy's GNC system actually performed well. "I did a disservice to our booster GNC guys last night," Huot said. "It was not a GNC issue that caused us not to come back. GNC triggered that abort; it was doing what it was supposed to do. Basically, [it] detected that the booster was not in the place that it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch, did an automated abort and then headed out to that offshore splashdown location." SpaceX is "still digging into the root cause on how we got there, and so, more to come on that," he added on Saturday. You can follow our Starship Flight 15 live updates for the latest on the mission. SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 Super Heavy Booster's explosive offshore landing abort in pictures. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Steve Spaleta/Space.com/Future) Super Heavy is powered by a cluster of 33 Raptor rocket engines that fire simultaneously during liftoff to send the 41-story Starship megarocket into orbit. During Friday's launch, all 33 engines fired as planned for the ascent, Huot said. One engine did drop out after stage separation, when Super Heavy dropped away from Ship and flipped over for a "boostback" burn to begin its trip back to Earth, Huot said on Friday. "We had 32 out of the 33 booster engines lit for boostback, which started sending it back here to the launch site," he added. A close look at the 33 Raptor engines firing simultaneously to launch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission into orbit. (Image credit: Josh Dinner, Space.com/Future) That firing was followed by the booster's landing burn. In SpaceX's launch video , Super Heavy can be seen activating 13 of its Raptor engines as planned, followed by the abort and the booster steering itself to a contingency landing zone in Gulf waters. "It did that hover, cut the engines off, the FTS — the flight termination system — triggered, and it splashed down in the water," Huot said on Friday. (The FTS is designed to destroy a booster in the event of an emergency.) As its name suggests, Starship Flight 15 is SpaceX's 15th test flight of the giant rocket, but it will be the first to attempt to catch a Ship upper stage with the chopsticks. SpaceX has successfully caught Super Heavy boosters on three test flights to date. Flight 15's Ship vehicle is in good health and will orbit Earth a total of 14 times before landing back at its launch pad in Starbase at around 4:20 p.m. EST (1920 GMT) today, if all goes well. item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
item.description: null On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier. The Apollo 12 moonwalkers also performed a lot of moon science. The astronauts picked up 75 pounds of moon rocks. Most of the rocks were basalts that formed from molten lava. These basalts showed the Apollo 12 landing site is more than 3 billion years old. The Apollo 12 astronauts on NASA's second crewed moon landing mission. They are (left to right) are Charles Conrad Jr., Richard F. Gordon Jr., and Alan L. Bean. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered Apollo 12 proved that the Apollo 11 moon landing was not just a one-off stunt while setting the stage for even more ambitious missions. To truly explore the moon and advance our understanding of how our solar system formed, the follow-on Apollo flights needed to be able to land where the geologists had identified as areas of interest. Apollo 12, with its touchdown in proximity to the Surveyor probe, proved this was possible. The Apollo 12 astronauts visited NASA's Surveyor 3 lander and took samples of it back to Earth. (Image credit: NASA) The launch of Apollo 12 also underscored the importance of having a well-prepared Mission Control team, an asset that would be critical to outcome of the next mission, Apollo 13. The ability to recover from a complete electrical short out with the simple call of a through of a switch "SCE to AUX" proved that knowing every detail about how the spacecraft worked was key to a successful program. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: Mauricio Pochettino asked the US to believe in his project. Did he believe in it himself?
item.description: The coach’s tenure with the USMNT brought a whiplash of highs and lows. He met some goals but also left many with the impression he never truly bought in It did not take US men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino very long to take his first big swing. He’d just taken the reins of the program after a disastrous performance at the 2024 Copa América cost his predecessor his job, with the first home World Cup in three decades looming on the horizon. The federation introduced him in New York City, on the 24th floor of a building overlooking the Hudson River. In short order, he was asked about the culture surrounding the program. In his answer, he invoked the four-time World Cup champion US women. Continue reading...

item.title: The 143 best holiday gifts in 2026 – obsessively tested by the Guardian US
item.description: Shatterproof wine glasses, Jellycat plushies, ‘yoga paws’ and more delightful gifts handpicked by our experts The best personalized gift ideas Nothing says holiday cheer quite like panic-browsing websites in pursuit of the perfect gift , toggling between 47 open tabs, eyes straining against your screen’s harsh blue light. But finding an item that elicits a squeal of delight from its recipient is one of the best parts of this time of year, when you have a little help. So we’ve curated 143 presents to reclaim holiday shopping as a joyous activity. Our seasoned writers and shopping experts got into the holiday spirit early, vetting gifts across kitchen, home, tech and 10 more categories. For months, we cooked, ate, traveled, hiked, ran, showered and slept with test products by our side. And we roped in our mothers, cats, dogs and the kids in our lives to make sure these gifts really work for the people (and pets!) they are meant for. Continue reading...

item.title: Mark Your Calendars! Lagos International Theatre Festival Returns to MUSON Centre This November
item.description: The Lagos International Theatre Festival ( LITF ) returns for its 2026 edition on November 14–15 at the MUSON Centre, Lagos, bringing together an exciting programme of theatre from Nigeria and around the world. The festival, which attracts more than 25,000 attendees across its programme days, has become one of the most anticipated events on Lagos’s cultural calendar. This year’s festival is themed “The Masks We Wear”, anchored by the statement “The Stage Is Everywhere.” The theme explores the different roles and identities people assume in everyday life, while inviting audiences to consider how theatre extends beyond the traditional stage. LITF 2026 brings an international dimension to Lagos, featuring artists and productions from Kenya, Canada and Brazil alongside a diverse Nigerian programme. An international highlight is LeRa Entertainments’ Under The Mango Tree from Canada, produced by Lennette Randall , with productions from Norway, Kenya and Brazil adding further cultural and theatrical perspectives. The Nigerian programme features productions from Lagos, Abuja, Enugu and Abeokuta, including Monkey Laundry , directed by Olarotimi Fakunle ; tHERapy , directed by Tosin Adeyemi ; What You Have Become , directed by Lanre Adediwura; and Behind Closed Doors , directed by Bolanle Austen-Peters. The festival will also spotlight emerging theatre makers through productions from Atlantic Hall, Evergreen College and Children’s International School, alongside professional and independent productions. The festival experience begins ahead of the main weekend with a series of events across Lagos. On November 9, Theatre Meets Food, hosted by Hilda Baci, will bring together artists, partners, cultural leaders and members of Lagos’s creative community for an evening of food, theatre and conversation. This will be followed by Embassy Nights on November 10 and 11, celebrating international cultural exchange among diplomatic representatives, artists and creative industry leaders. The programme culminates in an Opening Night Gala on November 13, ahead of the main festival weekend at MUSON Centre on November 14 and 15. LITF 2026 is supported by the Lagos State Government, LekOil, Pillar Oil, Afrexim and Amstel , alongside its growing network of international and cultural partners. Founder of LITF, Bolanle Austen-Peters , said: “The Masks We Wear is a theme that speaks to all of us. We all play different roles in our lives, and theatre allows us to examine those roles, question them, and perhaps see ourselves differently. This year, we are also reminding audiences that theatre is not confined to a theatre building. The stage is everywhere.” Festival Director, Vanessa Jev , said the diversity of voices at this year’s festival was particularly exciting, with Nigerian artists joining performers from Kenya, Canada and Brazil to create opportunities for audiences to experience different cultures and perspectives. Founded by Bolanle Austen-Peters, LITF celebrates theatre

item.title: Raphinha sees red as Brazil stunned by Japan while Argentina’s post-Messi era starts with defeat
item.description: Brazil loss in Singapore marred by unruly end to friendly Argentina beaten 2-1 by Uruguay in Buenos Aires Raphinha was sent off as Brazil crashed to a 3-2 defeat by Japan in their international friendly in Singapore. The Barcelona captain had been substituted after 71 minutes, but was shown a red card after protesting against Tatsuhiro Sakamoto’s stoppage-time winner on the touchline. The Brazil head coach, Carlo Ancelotti, was also sent off in a fractious ending to the match. Japan went 2-0 up inside 20 minutes through Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura. Vinícius Júnior reduced the deficit in the 33rd minute and scored again to drag them level on 75 minutes, before Sakamoto’s controversial late winner. Continue reading...

item.title: Her Enterprise, Africa’s Advantage: HerSphere Global Summit 2026 Convenes Africa’s Foremost Women Leaders in Lagos
item.description: Africa’s economic story is increasingly being written by women. Across the continent, women own and operate a remarkable share of small and growing enterprises, sustain household and community economies, and drive innovation in sectors from finance and technology to the creative industries. Yet the gap between participation and power remains wide. Too many women-led businesses stay small, under-capitalised and absent from the rooms where markets, policy and capital are shaped. On Tuesday, 17 November 2026, the HerSphere Global Summit 2026 will gather a distinguished assembly of leaders at the Wole Soyinka Centre, Lagos, Nigeria, to confront that gap directly. Proceedings begin promptly at 9:00 a.m. A Theme That Demands Action This year’s theme, “ Her Enterprise, Africa Advantage: Moving Women-Led Businesses Beyond Participation to Economic Power,” reflects a deliberate shift in the conversation. The question is no longer whether women belong in Africa’s economy — that has long been settled. The question is how women-led enterprises can scale, command capital, influence policy and build institutions that endure. The summit is designed to move beyond inspiration to strategy: how women founders access growth finance, how they enter regional and global value chains, how public institutions and private capital can work together to back them, and how today’s enterprises become tomorrow’s market leaders. item.title: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever (video)
item.description: null SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. Starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission plan called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket . That didn't happen; Starship's Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship succeeded in its attempt, notching a huge milestone for SpaceX and its dream of full rocket reuse. "That was the missing link," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast today, his voice thick with emotion. "That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes." SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Space.com) The Ship catch occurred today at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT; 3:20 p.m. local Texas time), roughly 22.5 hours after Flight 15 lifted off. Many SpaceX employees went outside to watch the vehicle, known as Ship 42, descend through the clouds toward its Starbase launch tower, which the company calls "Mechazilla." And they got quite a show: Ship 42 nestled gently into Mechazilla's waiting arms, while "Baby Come Back" played over SpaceX's landing webcast. "This is so incredible to see," SpaceX's Jessie Anderson said during the livestream. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes." Why was this such a big deal? SpaceX had already caught Super Heavy — on three previous Starship test flights, in fact. But it had never tried before with Ship. The upper stage is a tougher target, for it flies higher, farther and faster than the booster. Indeed, on Flight 15, Ship 42 came all the way back down from orbit. Ship 42 comes in for its landing on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) While the double-catch attempt, and the chopsticks success with Ship, were Flight 15's main headlines, the mission had other objectives as well. One was getting Ship to orbit, which had happened on just one previous Starship launch — Flight 14 , which lifted off on Sept. 28. Ship deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 broadband satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO) on Flight 14, and it did so again on Flight 15. These 52 spacecraft are the first members of a constellation that will eventually consist of 100,000 satellites , if all goes according to SpaceX's plan. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Space.com) The Ship catch occurred today at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT; 3:20 p.m. local Texas time), roughly 22.5 hours after Flight 15 lifted off. Many SpaceX employees went outside to watch the vehicle, known as Ship 42, descend through the clouds toward its Starbase launch tower, which the company calls "Mechazilla." "This is so incredible to see," SpaceX's Jessie Anderson said during the livestream. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes." Why was this such a big deal? Ship 42 comes in for its landing on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) While the double-catch attempt, and the chopsticks success with Ship, were Flight 15's main headlines, the mission had other objectives as well. One was getting Ship to orbit, which had happened on just one previous Starship launch — Flight 14 , which lifted off on Sept. 28. Ship deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 broadband satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO) on Flight 14, and it did so again on Flight 15. These 52 spacecraft are the first members of a constellation that will eventually consist of 100,000 satellites , if all goes according to SpaceX's plan. Some of those Starlink satellites took video and images of Ship 42's heat shield to check its health for today's landing attempt. Those images, combined with ground-based cameras, found Ship 42 to be in good shape and ready for its big moment. SpaceX plans to use Starship to build an even bigger network in LEO than the Starlink V3 system — Starmind, an AI data-center constellation that will harbor a million spacecraft , according to Elon Musk . (For context: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network employs about 11,000 satellites at the moment.) Assembling these megaconstellations will require an incredible launch cadence. The double chopstick catch is key to that vision, SpaceX says, for it will enable quicker inspection, refurbishment and reflight of Starship. So the company will doubtless try the maneuver again soon — probably on the next Starship flight, which won't be too far down the road. It was updated again at 4:45 p.m. ET on Nov. 14 with news of successful Ship catch.

item.title: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
item.description: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice. The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars. The missing ice Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets. Read full article Comments

item.title: Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business
item.description: More than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape , one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine , but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall. Temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production. As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management. Read full article Comments
item.dc:creator: Hannah V. Herrero, Erin L. Bunting, Jane Southworth, Jason K. Blackburn, and Stephanie Insalaco-Wyner, The Conversation

item.title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
item.description: null Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029. Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth . The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years , when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse. Jupiter, Mars and Regulus will appear close together on the night of Nov. 15-16. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva.) Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus , which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun . A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant , formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams. How to measure distances in the night sky using your outstretched hand. (Image credit: Created in Canva Pro) Mars, meanwhile, appears as a reddish, ochre disk complete with dark surface features, where basaltic rock has been scoured clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface, according to NASA . Interested in seeing and capturing the planets for yourself? Then be sure to read our guide on everything you need to observe and photograph the planets of the solar system, along with our picks of the top telescopes , cameras and lenses for exploring the night sky in 2026. Editor's Note: If you would like to share your photos of Mars and Jupiter with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

item.title: Microsoft's school email bill gives rivals something to smile about
item.description: The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces. The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news. As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like . Or, for that matter, other US tech giants . Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners. The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks. A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill. Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud." A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't." The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly." Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted. Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty. Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners. The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks. Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud." A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't." The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly." Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted. Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty. Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register : "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure. "Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy." Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service. But the Windows behemoth has given educational institutions a fresh reason to investigate – and its rivals a particularly convenient opening pitch. ®

item.title: Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum
item.description: Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say. A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters. Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms. "Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said. "I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable. "So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently." McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not. "If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added. "And we know your algorithm would." Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too. Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal. She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly. There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs. "So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content." Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories.
