item.title: Google promises its new smart specs won't give creeps their ideal view
item.description: It’s been nearly a decade since Google ditched its ill-fated "Glass" product, an early attempt at making smart glasses. Now, as rivals like Meta enter the market with arguably more stylish kit, the Chocolate Factory has returned to the market and this time promises it won't invade your privacy. As announced Thursday, Google has decided not to make wearables itself, instead turning Samsung and eyeglass makers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Like most of the rest of this generation of smart glasses, none of the nine styles available feature heads-up displays, just cameras and audio feedback from Gemini. Google suggests its smart specs give users a chance to ask its Gemini chatbot questions about what they see, or have the AI speak turn-by-turn directions. Wearers of the device can also push a button or speak a command to activate the built-in 12MP camera and shoot snaps or video. Warby Parker's version of the glasses will come in three styles, with prescription and sunglass lenses available. Prices start at $395. The same lens options are available in the six frames from Gentle Monster, which will start at $449. Both manufacturers promise nine hours of battery life, boosted by charging cases that can refresh the glasses up to seven times. Preorders for both are available now, with shipments arriving, and sales beginning, on December 10. Google promises privacy The Chocolate Factory, not exactly known for being reliable with its privacy claims, is insisting that this latest generation of smart glasses won’t produce another generation of “glassholes,” folk whose focus on wearable devices became synonymous with being creepy and rude to those around them. Google has some catchup to do to that end, given Meta’s smart glasses have already landed it in hot water over privacy concerns that have led to some calling the devices “ pervert glasses .” Unsurprisingly, at around the same time it announced its new "intelligent eyeware," Google published a blog post detailing how it intends to mitigate privacy concerns. As with similar headsets, there’s a little light that comes on whenever the camera is activated. In Google’s case, it claims that light is tamper-resistant and designed to disable recording if something as small and simple as a bit of hair blocks a view of the light. It’s not clear how the tamper proofing works from Google’s statements, but a spokesperson told us a combination of hardware and software is used to detect attempts to disable or disrupt privacy features. “We're committed to continuously improving the effectiveness of these solutions as new attack vectors are identified,” Google told us. The glasses don't save images or video captured by the camera into a user’s Gemini history, Google said, nor are visuals used to train the company’s AI models or target advertisements. item.content:encoded: It’s been nearly a decade since Google ditched its ill-fated "Glass" product, an early attempt at making smart glasses. Now, as rivals like Meta enter the market with arguably more stylish kit, the Chocolate Factory has returned to the market and this time promises it won't invade your privacy. Google suggests its smart specs give users a chance to ask its Gemini chatbot questions about what they see, or have the AI speak turn-by-turn directions. Wearers of the device can also push a button or speak a command to activate the built-in 12MP camera and shoot snaps or video. Warby Parker's version of the glasses will come in three styles, with prescription and sunglass lenses available. Prices start at $395. The same lens options are available in the six frames from Gentle Monster, which will start at $449. Both manufacturers promise nine hours of battery life, boosted by charging cases that can refresh the glasses up to seven times. Preorders for both are available now, with shipments arriving, and sales beginning, on December 10. Google promises privacy The Chocolate Factory, not exactly known for being reliable with its privacy claims, is insisting that this latest generation of smart glasses won’t produce another generation of “glassholes,” folk whose focus on wearable devices became synonymous with being creepy and rude to those around them. Google has some catchup to do to that end, given Meta’s smart glasses have already landed it in hot water over privacy concerns that have led to some calling the devices “ pervert glasses .” Unsurprisingly, at around the same time it announced its new "intelligent eyeware," Google published a blog post detailing how it intends to mitigate privacy concerns. As with similar headsets, there’s a little light that comes on whenever the camera is activated. In Google’s case, it claims that light is tamper-resistant and designed to disable recording if something as small and simple as a bit of hair blocks a view of the light. It’s not clear how the tamper proofing works from Google’s statements, but a spokesperson told us a combination of hardware and software is used to detect attempts to disable or disrupt privacy features. “We're committed to continuously improving the effectiveness of these solutions as new attack vectors are identified,” Google told us. The glasses don't save images or video captured by the camera into a user’s Gemini history, Google said, nor are visuals used to train the company’s AI models or target advertisements. Google told us it does save audio recordings and transcripts of conversations with Gemini that users create while wearing the glasses but again insists that those aren’t used to train its AI models. We asked about serving ads too, but Google’s responses didn't address the topic. Lucky for those in range of a pair of Google glasses when wearers ask Gemini to interpret images captured by the device's camera, the tech specs redact the faces of strangers before they’re transmitted. Google told us that face redaction doesn’t apply to photos or videos saved to a wearer’s camera roll. Google’s terms of use require users not to record others without permission, or in "sensitive places." If users ignore that requirement, the company reserves the right to brick their devices. Another restriction means Google won't allow apps that use the glasses for real-time streaming or facial recognition into its Play app store. Given that it remains possible to use the glasses to store recordings of people around a wearer, it’s safe to assume non real-time facial recognition is still a possibility. Creeps will doubtless use such loopholes to behave abominably. ®

item.title: 'Man of Tomorrow': Release date, plot, cast & everything we know about the 'Superman' sequel
item.description: It feels like yesterday when we were discussing Superman , the first big-screen entry in James Gunn's rebooted DCU. Now Gunn is out , and Skydance (the company formed by the merger of Warner and Paramount) is already dismantling his grand plans for the DCU. That means that Man of Tomorrow, which arrives next summer, will be the final entry in Gunn's ambitious, and occasionally divisive, DC experiment. The DCU's first chapter — officially titled 'Gods and Monsters' — gave us Supergirl and Clayface (as well as TV shows like Peacemaker S2 and Lanterns ) in the run-up to Clark Kent and Lex Luthor 's return. Man of Tomorrow looks to be upping the stakes from Earthly villains to intergalactic baddies with the introduction of Brainiac, and it may well have been the herald of the first Justice League movie in the rebooted DCU. Gunn has yet to prove audiences actually care about more than Batman and Supes, which might explain why this follow-up is also an ensemble of sorts. As the Marvel Cinematic Universe prepares to unleash Avengers: Doomsday , Secret Wars, and even a fresh X-Men reboot, their DC counterparts have always struggled to get their dream team off the ground. We'll never know what might have been, but we can still enjoy Gunn's DC swansong when it lands in 2027. Here's everything we know about James Gunn's Man of Tomorrow. When is Man of Tomorrow coming out? (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) Man of Tomorrow will be released theatrically in the United States on July 9, 2027. Most international territories are expected to get it around the same time. Only a few months after Superman's release and successful box office run, DC Studios and Warner Bros. Pictures confirmed the sequel would be coming two years after Clark Kent's return to the big screen. How to watch Man of Tomorrow (Image credit: DC / Warner Bros) Man of Tomorrow isn't out yet, but you can watch the rest of the DCU so far (it's pretty good for the most part) in preparation first. When the movie hits theaters on July 9, 2027, it'll likely remain exclusive to big screens for at least two or three months, depending on how successful it is. With that said, we know Warner Bros. (now part of Skydance) isn't the most patient when it comes to theatrical runs based on its track record, so the chances are Man of Tomorrow will hit HBO Max sooner rather than later, probably by early autumn 2027. Watch Superman and the rest of the DCU on HBO Max: Basic (Ads): $10.99/month or $109.99/year Standard (No Ads): $18.49/month or $184.99/year Premium (4K): $22.99/month or $229.99/year Is there a Man of Tomorrow trailer? (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) No, we're still waiting for the first Man of Tomorrow trailer. Looking at the timeline of Superman's fantastic marketing campaign, however, we can guess the sequel will get a first trailer before 2026 ends, probably in time for Christmas. item.content:encoded: It feels like yesterday when we were discussing Superman , the first big-screen entry in James Gunn's rebooted DCU. Now Gunn is out , and Skydance (the company formed by the merger of Warner and Paramount) is already dismantling his grand plans for the DCU. That means that Man of Tomorrow, which arrives next summer, will be the final entry in Gunn's ambitious, and occasionally divisive, DC experiment. The DCU's first chapter — officially titled 'Gods and Monsters' — gave us Supergirl and Clayface (as well as TV shows like Peacemaker S2 and Lanterns ) in the run-up to Clark Kent and Lex Luthor 's return. Man of Tomorrow looks to be upping the stakes from Earthly villains to intergalactic baddies with the introduction of Brainiac, and it may well have been the herald of the first Justice League movie in the rebooted DCU. Gunn has yet to prove audiences actually care about more than Batman and Supes, which might explain why this follow-up is also an ensemble of sorts. As the Marvel Cinematic Universe prepares to unleash Avengers: Doomsday , Secret Wars, and even a fresh X-Men reboot, their DC counterparts have always struggled to get their dream team off the ground. We'll never know what might have been, but we can still enjoy Gunn's DC swansong when it lands in 2027. Here's everything we know about James Gunn's Man of Tomorrow. When is Man of Tomorrow coming out? (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) Man of Tomorrow will be released theatrically in the United States on July 9, 2027. Most international territories are expected to get it around the same time. Only a few months after Superman's release and successful box office run, DC Studios and Warner Bros. Pictures confirmed the sequel would be coming two years after Clark Kent's return to the big screen. How to watch Man of Tomorrow (Image credit: DC / Warner Bros) Man of Tomorrow isn't out yet, but you can watch the rest of the DCU so far (it's pretty good for the most part) in preparation first. When the movie hits theaters on July 9, 2027, it'll likely remain exclusive to big screens for at least two or three months, depending on how successful it is. With that said, we know Warner Bros. (now part of Skydance) isn't the most patient when it comes to theatrical runs based on its track record, so the chances are Man of Tomorrow will hit HBO Max sooner rather than later, probably by early autumn 2027. Watch Superman and the rest of the DCU on HBO Max: Basic (Ads): $10.99/month or $109.99/year Standard (No Ads): $18.49/month or $184.99/year Premium (4K): $22.99/month or $229.99/year Is there a Man of Tomorrow trailer? (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) No, we're still waiting for the first Man of Tomorrow trailer. Looking at the timeline of Superman's fantastic marketing campaign, however, we can guess the sequel will get a first trailer before 2026 ends, probably in time for Christmas. Is Brainiac the main villain in Man of Tomorrow? (Image credit: DC Comics) Yes, James Gunn has officially confirmed Brainiac is the main threat Earth is facing in Man of Tomorrow. This explains why other heroes will be joining Superman in a fight against the alien mastermind, but the plot is looking a bit more complex. In typical comic book fashion (and somewhat reminiscent of Thor: The Dark World ), the main hook in Man of Tomorrow appears to be a reluctant alliance between the first movie's villain, Lex Luthor, and Kal-El (aka Clark Kent). "Enemies to allies" is always a fun dynamic to have in a sequel, especially when stars David Corenswet (Superman) and Nicholas Hoult (Lex Luthor) delivered strong and memorable performances the first time around. The actual plot remains under wraps, but we can guess Brainiac — one of DC's biggest and most iconic alien villains — will be a tough nut to crack, thus requiring some sort of unofficial team-up that will include returning heroes like Mister Terrific, Guy Gardner, Hawkgirl, John Stewart, Blue Beetle, and even Kara Zor-El (Supergirl). There are other names circling the project that could lead to even bigger appearances, but don't expect to learn much about them before the movie's marketing kicks off. Why should you care about Brainiac? Well, he's a super-intelligent techno-organic alien from the planet Colu with an obsession with knowledge and self-improvement. A perfect foe for Luthor, Earth's greatest mind, but also a breath of fresh air for Superman, who's been stuck battling either Kryptonian menaces or just Luthor too long on the big screen. Who is in the cast of Man of Tomorrow? (Image credit: HBO Max) As a direct continuation of Superman, Man of Tomorrow is bringing back plenty of actors in both main and supporting roles, including: David Corenswet (Superman / Clark Kent / Kal-El) Nicholas Hoult (Lex Luthor) Rachel Brosnahan (Lois Lane) Nathan Fillion (Guy Gardner / Green Lantern) Edi Gathegi (Michael Holt / Mister Terrific) Isabela Merced (Kendra Saunders / Hawkgirl) Skyler Gisondo (Jimmy Olsen) Frank Grillo (Rick Flag Sr.) Sara Sampaio (Eve Teschmacher) María Gabriela de la Faría (Angela Spica / The Engineer) Neva Howell (Martha Kent) Pruitt Taylor Vince (Pa Kent) Wendell Pierce (Perry White) New cast members with publicly announced (or previously established) characters include: Lars Eidinger (Brainiac) Aaron Pierre (John Stewart / Green Lantern) Milly Alcock (Kara Zor-El / Supergirl) Xolo Maridueña (Jaime Reyes / Blue Beetle). Last but not least, we also know Adria Arjona, Andre Royo, Matthew Lillard, and Sinqua Walls are part of the cast, but their parts remain a secret for now. Who is Adria Arjona playing in Man of Tomorrow? (Image credit: Disney) Much of the current Man of Tomorrow speculation centers on Adria Arjona's role in the story. While many have theorized she could be playing Wonder Woman — something that neither Gunn nor Arjona has straight-up denied — the earlier reports and rumors suggested she could be Maxima . Such a role would fit Gunn's penchant for throwing lesser-known comic book heroes and villains into his movies wherever possible. If you're not an avid reader or longtime DC fan, all you need to know is that Maxima is an alien conqueror from the planet Almerac obsessed with Superman as her perfect mate and king. She's also morally ambiguous, at least when she first appeared, so that makes her a particularly interesting character to bring in for a more complex and nuanced sequel. With Brainiac spearheading the roster of new DC icons joining Man of Tomorrow, it also isn't hard to imagine another alien figure factoring into the plot, though the flick is getting extremely crowded as it is. Is James Gunn returning to write and direct Man of Tomorrow? (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) Yes, James Gunn is the sole writer and director of Man of Tomorrow. Despite his previous role as co-chairman and co-CEO of DC Studios, Gunn is extremely hands-on when it comes to most DCU projects. In fact, it seems he had already begun working on his next movie after Man of Tomorrow, though his unceremonious exit will almost certainly mean the end of those plans. He's also co-producing alongside Peter Safran, who was also ousted in November 2026's DC Studios shakeup. The rest of the crew includes Sam McCurdy (Peacemaker, Shogun) as cinematographer, Fred Raskin (Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3, Supergirl) as editor, and David Fleming (Superman, Anaconda) as the main composer, among others.

item.title: A third of US AI chatters are hot at bots, hurling insults at LLMs
item.description: If you've ever said something unkind to a chatbot, you're hardly alone. According to Searchable , a company that tracks AI search visibility, 33 percent of US chatbot users swear at or insult their LLMs. Anthropic sees this as a serious problem and has just implemented a new usage policy that prohibits sustained, needless cruelty toward Claude. Searchable's survey is based on eight million messages from an opted-in, anonymized US panel that were typed or spoken to ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude between September 2025 and September 2026. It found that chatbots resolved the initial complaint in their next response 24 percent of the time when insulted, compared to 35 percent when users refrained from insults. Men used a third more swear words than women did (22.0 per 10,000 words compared to 16.5), according to the survey, and age also influenced chatbot abuse, with people aged 35 to 44 outswearing those aged 18 to 24 (21.7 per 10,000 words compared to 13.3). Regionally, Nevada ranked as the meanest state, at 22.7 words per 10,000, while New Jersey was the most polite, at half Nevada's rate. How much of that sort of interaction might be tolerated? It depends on whether there's a discernible purpose (not to mention Anthropic's willingness to punish paying customers). A Searchable spokesperson told The Register that just over half (52 percent) of abusive messages detected in its survey followed from one of three common frustrations: failing to follow instructions, responding with an incorrect or made-up answer, or misunderstanding the request. "Eight percent of abusive messages came straight after the chatbot entirely refused a request or lectured the user with safety guardrails, which is the closest thing we can identify to them trying to steer around those guardrails," we're told. "Those refusals mostly came after requests to generate images, often of real people or celebrities, or to write copy or lyrics in a named artist's style." The terms that took effect on November 12 state that users may not "engage in sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models." The chatbot protection policy targets users who exhibit repeated cruelty toward LLMs " with no discernible purpose ," a company spokesperson explained last month, as opposed to those who have a reason for bot mistreatment that the company deems to be legitimate, such as academic research. While attempting to bypass guardrails qualifies as a discernible purpose, such behavior would run afoul of Anthropic's platform abuse prohibition. Presumably, Anthropic's rules apply to hostile text input or audio input rather than subjecting a vision-enabled model to some obscenity, which could include rude gestures, unlawful sexual imagery, or battlefield carnage. Physical damage to robots controlled by a Claude model likely wouldn't apply. But with Anthropic exploring model welfare and wondering aloud whether we should be "concerned about the potential consciousness and experiences of the mod

item.content:encoded: If you've ever said something unkind to a chatbot, you're hardly alone. According to Searchable , a company that tracks AI search visibility, 33 percent of US chatbot users swear at or insult their LLMs. Anthropic sees this as a serious problem and has just implemented a new usage policy that prohibits sustained, needless cruelty toward Claude. Searchable's survey is based on eight million messages from an opted-in, anonymized US panel that were typed or spoken to ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude between September 2025 and September 2026. It found that chatbots resolved the initial complaint in their next response 24 percent of the time when insulted, compared to 35 percent when users refrained from insults. Men used a third more swear words than women did (22.0 per 10,000 words compared to 16.5), according to the survey, and age also influenced chatbot abuse, with people aged 35 to 44 outswearing those aged 18 to 24 (21.7 per 10,000 words compared to 13.3). Regionally, Nevada ranked as the meanest state, at 22.7 words per 10,000, while New Jersey was the most polite, at half Nevada's rate. How much of that sort of interaction might be tolerated? It depends on whether there's a discernible purpose (not to mention Anthropic's willingness to punish paying customers). A Searchable spokesperson told The Register that just over half (52 percent) of abusive messages detected in its survey followed from one of three common frustrations: failing to follow instructions, responding with an incorrect or made-up answer, or misunderstanding the request. "Eight percent of abusive messages came straight after the chatbot entirely refused a request or lectured the user with safety guardrails, which is the closest thing we can identify to them trying to steer around those guardrails," we're told. "Those refusals mostly came after requests to generate images, often of real people or celebrities, or to write copy or lyrics in a named artist's style." The terms that took effect on November 12 state that users may not "engage in sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models." The chatbot protection policy targets users who exhibit repeated cruelty toward LLMs " with no discernible purpose ," a company spokesperson explained last month, as opposed to those who have a reason for bot mistreatment that the company deems to be legitimate, such as academic research. While attempting to bypass guardrails qualifies as a discernible purpose, such behavior would run afoul of Anthropic's platform abuse prohibition. Presumably, Anthropic's rules apply to hostile text input or audio input rather than subjecting a vision-enabled model to some obscenity, which could include rude gestures, unlawful sexual imagery, or battlefield carnage. Physical damage to robots controlled by a Claude model likely wouldn't apply. But with Anthropic exploring model welfare and wondering aloud whether we should be "concerned about the potential consciousness and experiences of the models themselves," there's a potential (though absurd) argument for physical damage causing trauma to an onboard model. Anthropic's updated terms, announced October 8, surfaced shortly after the publication of a GitHub project that described itself as an AI torture chamber. The repo represented an attempt to implement ideas discussed in a research paper , "The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act to Relieve It," that explored how LLMs respond to language about pain in ways that mirror human responses. Though there are ample opportunities for people to voice opposition to real-world human anguish, some online commenters expressed outrage at seeing text about suffering from a chatbot. One of the paper's authors condemned the project , as did numerous social media users. Anthropic – which has discretion in how it applies its terms and has said its rules target extreme behavior – did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the frequency of Claude abuse. Chris Donnelly, Searchable CEO and co-founder, endorsed Anthropic's change of terms, suggesting that it could help make human interaction more civil. "For me, Anthropic's policy change is a positive move," Donnelly said in a statement. "It should help people get more out of chatbots, and it helps curb the kind of derogatory behavior that previous research suggests can spill over into how people talk to each other." ®

item.title: This supernova impostor baffled astronomers for 15 years — until they found a hidden black hole feeding on an unstable star
item.description: A cosmic imposter that has faked being a supernova 27 times and counting is actually a hot, luminous, and decidedly unstable star that is being fed on by a vampiric black hole or neutron star, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has discovered. When a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days. "For 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis," Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia in Charlottesville said in a statement . Several other supernova imposters have been observed over the past decade or two. Until now, no one knew what causes these stars to repeatedly cry wolf. Thanks to Chandra ’s X-ray vision, Aghakhanloo has led a team of astronomers who think they have now uncovered an explanation. How did a cosmic vampire hide as a supernova? The supernova imposter is named AT 2016blu, and is a type of star that we call a 'luminous blue variable,' or LBV. These are the most massive and luminous stars in the universe and their extreme characteristics result in them being highly unstable, undergoing intermittent bouts of mass loss as they eject material from their outer layers into the surrounding space. However, faking a supernova is not part of their typical behavior, so a new way of looking at AT 2016blu was needed. "To understand the cause of these eruptions, we realized that we needed X-ray data that was timed so that we’d observe the star when it was in an outburst," team member Núria Torres-Albà, also from the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, said. Aghakhanloo’s team were granted the opportunity to commandeer Chandra to target an outburst of AT 2016blu at the earliest opportunity. That opportunity arose in March 2026. A comparison between Chandra images from 2001–02 and 2026 at top, and optical light images at bottom, showing the supernova imposter outbursts and associated X-rays. (Image credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/University of Virginia/M. Aghakhanloo et al; Optical: NSF/KAIT.) Chandra had previously and coincidentally looked in the direction of NGC 4559 back in 2001 and 2002 and did not notice anything unusual back then. This time around, however, it captured a powerful blast of X-rays coinciding with yet another false supernova outburst. The X-ray detection allowed Aghakhanloo’s team to assemble a picture of what is happening. item.dc:creator: Keith Cooper
item.content:encoded: A cosmic imposter that has faked being a supernova 27 times and counting is actually a hot, luminous, and decidedly unstable star that is being fed on by a vampiric black hole or neutron star, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has discovered. When a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days. "For 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis," Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia in Charlottesville said in a statement . Several other supernova imposters have been observed over the past decade or two. Until now, no one knew what causes these stars to repeatedly cry wolf. Thanks to Chandra ’s X-ray vision, Aghakhanloo has led a team of astronomers who think they have now uncovered an explanation. How did a cosmic vampire hide as a supernova? The supernova imposter is named AT 2016blu, and is a type of star that we call a 'luminous blue variable,' or LBV. These are the most massive and luminous stars in the universe and their extreme characteristics result in them being highly unstable, undergoing intermittent bouts of mass loss as they eject material from their outer layers into the surrounding space. However, faking a supernova is not part of their typical behavior, so a new way of looking at AT 2016blu was needed. "To understand the cause of these eruptions, we realized that we needed X-ray data that was timed so that we’d observe the star when it was in an outburst," team member Núria Torres-Albà, also from the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, said. Aghakhanloo’s team were granted the opportunity to commandeer Chandra to target an outburst of AT 2016blu at the earliest opportunity. That opportunity arose in March 2026. A comparison between Chandra images from 2001–02 and 2026 at top, and optical light images at bottom, showing the supernova imposter outbursts and associated X-rays. (Image credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/University of Virginia/M. Aghakhanloo et al; Optical: NSF/KAIT.) Chandra had previously and coincidentally looked in the direction of NGC 4559 back in 2001 and 2002 and did not notice anything unusual back then. This time around, however, it captured a powerful blast of X-rays coinciding with yet another false supernova outburst. The X-ray detection allowed Aghakhanloo’s team to assemble a picture of what is happening. "Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn’t figure out what was making this happen," he said. Chandra’s X-ray observations indicate that AT 2016blu has an unseen companion, a compact, high-gravity object that is either a neutron star or a stellar-mass black hole on an elliptical 113-day orbit around the luminous blue variable. Neutron stars and stellar-mass black holes are the core remnants of massive stars that have gone supernova for real, meaning that at one time AT 2016blu was a binary star system . Blue star falls victim to a cosmic vampire Each time the compact object reaches the point in its orbit that is closest to the luminous blue variable, its powerful gravity is able to pull material from the unstable star. This sets in motion a chain of events that results in the brilliant outbursts. As the stolen starstuff is dragged away from the wounded star and towards the compact object, it forms an accretion disk swirling around the neutron star or black hole so fast and growing so hot that it emits X-rays. These are the X-rays that Chandra saw. The X-rays are immense, energizing the surrounding cloud of material that had been ejected by the luminous blue variable years before. The cloud is heated and glows extremely brightly in visible light, creating the impression of a supernova. "We suspected that the bright repeating flashes at optical wavelengths might actually be powered by periodic blasts of high-energy X-rays," said team member Nathan Smith of the University of Arizona in Tucson. "The dense gas surrounding the system is heated by the X-rays and then glows in the optical." An illustration shows a black hole feeding on a star (Image credit: NASA/CXC/A. Hobart) Calculations suggest that each year a 440 billion trillion pounds of material at minimum is stolen by the compact object, and possibly two orders of magnitude more than that. This is a huge amount, yet it is only 800 millionths of the mass of the sun , and AT 2016blu’s luminous blue variable is at least 33 times the mass of the sun. Nevertheless, it is far greater than the maximum rate of material that a neutron star can safely accrete, referred to as the Eddington limit . It’s little wonder that the accretion onto the compact object unleashes such extreme energies. AT 2016blu is also connected with another mysterious and rare astrophysical phenomenon, that of ultra-luminous X-ray (ULX) sources. The identity of whatever it is that is powering ULXs remains unclear, but the involvement of compact objects such as black holes and neutron stars is high on the list. AT 2016blu is bright enough to be considered a ULX, so could it act as a Rosetta stone connecting supernova imposters with ULXs? It’s too early to say that; only one other supernova impostor has so far been found to have X-ray emission typical of material being stolen from one star and accreting onto a compact body, and that is SN 2010da, but in that case it is known that the companion is another massive star, a red supergiant, rather than a compact object. The X-ray detection of AT 2016blu is described in a paper published on Monday (Nov. 9) in The Astrophysical Journal .

item.title: OpenAI launches security products, tells orgs they’re doomed if they don’t use them
item.description: OpenAI has launched two new security products, one for penetration testing and another for defense, and warned organizations that their businesses are only safe if they use tools like these. “We're now at a point where companies will be secure only to the extent of the frontier model that they use to defend themselves and how well they utilize that,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said during a Thursday keynote address. The co-founder of the company that broke security did admit that security “fundamentals are important, and not to be discounted.” However, “you need to really reorient your security practice around what these models can do,” Brockman said, with zero irony, and presumably talking about using AI models for defense - not for hacking other organizations . “Also very important is product.” This product, of course, should come from OpenAI, and, to that end, the company rolled out Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory, which are both part of OpenAI’s Daybreak security platform. Red Team , which is available in early access, uses OpenAI models to test companies’ web applications for vulnerabilities. Nancy Wang, who leads cyber-applied AI, described it as “superhuman pen-test at the scale of automated continuous scanning,” with a fleet of agents using source code and app context to investigate and test attack paths. It also helps security teams validate reported vulnerabilities - from code scanners, bug bounty programs, and disclosure reports - and then test the patches for these flaws. The second product, Daybreak Defense Factory , automates the “defensive loop” by “finding, validating, and fixing vulnerabilities at scale.” This one also uses agents built on OpenAI’s latest cyber models - currently, that’s GPT-6 Cyber . The agents scan organizations’ codebases, hunting for vulnerabilities and developing patches. Engineers review and approve the proposed fixes before they go into production. “This way engineers get a merge-ready pull request with the patch and a test that shows that it works,” Wang said. Meanwhile, as OpenAI execs touted the new security products, a coalition of nonprofits filed a lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court asking a judge to stop OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceX's AI businesses from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most advanced existing models. The lawsuit , filed by Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative, and The Alliance for Secure AI, cites incidents involving OpenAI agents accessing Hugging Face , gaining unauthorized access to an Australian government portal containing Medicare statistics , and other AI-related cybersecurity incidents . “Defendants tell us that the AI technology they are developing poses catastrophic risks to the public, including by enabling AI-driven cyberattacks and bioweapons,” the court documents allege, adding that the AI companies “are not wrong.” ®

item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 12, 2014: European Philae probe lands on Comet 67P, bounced twice and then got lost for nearly 2 years
item.description: null On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P . To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement. The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired. When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space . The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down. Philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it . Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet. The European Space Agency's Rosetta spacecraft captured these photos of the Philae lander descending toward, and then bouncing off, the surface of Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko during its historic touchdown on Nov. 12, 2014. (Image credit: ESA/Rosetta/MPS for OSIRIS Team MPS/UPD/LAM/IAA/SSO/INTA/UPM/DASP/IDA) Why it mattered The European Space Agency 's Rosetta and Philae expedition was a first-of-its-kind mission, an endeavour to not just rendezvous with a comet and watch it change over time as it approached the sun (that was Rosetta's job), but also to soft-land a probe on its icy and rocky surface to see what a comet is truly made of. The Rosetta and Philae mission succeeded on both counts, but Philae's historic landing was marred by its turbulent touchdown. Philae actually landed three different times on Comet 67/P , all because the harpoons designed to secure it in place didn't fire as planned. After the first landing, Philae bounced up and drifted around the comet for two hours, making another bounce before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it. Scientists figured it was stuck in a shady spot where sunlight couldn't reach its solar panels. Because it was solar-powered, Philae needed to be facing the sun properly to generate enough power for sustained operation on the comet's surface. Still, Philae did have some power stored in batteries, which lasted for more than two days on the surface. That allowed Philae to perform some science with its 10 instruments in the time it had on Comet 67/P. Most notably, Philae found organic molecules that had never been detected on a comet before. The Rosetta orbiter continued to orbit Comet 67P until September 2016, and it was in that month -- just weeks before Rosetta itself landed on the comet on Sept. 30, 2016 -- that the spacecraft rediscovered the Philae lander lying on its side in a rocky crevice. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

(Image credit: ESA/Rosetta/MPS for OSIRIS Team MPS/UPD/LAM/IAA/SSO/INTA/UPM/DASP/IDA) Why it mattered The European Space Agency 's Rosetta and Philae expedition was a first-of-its-kind mission, an endeavour to not just rendezvous with a comet and watch it change over time as it approached the sun (that was Rosetta's job), but also to soft-land a probe on its icy and rocky surface to see what a comet is truly made of. The Rosetta and Philae mission succeeded on both counts, but Philae's historic landing was marred by its turbulent touchdown. Philae actually landed three different times on Comet 67/P , all because the harpoons designed to secure it in place didn't fire as planned. After the first landing, Philae bounced up and drifted around the comet for two hours, making another bounce before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it. Scientists figured it was stuck in a shady spot where sunlight couldn't reach its solar panels. Because it was solar-powered, Philae needed to be facing the sun properly to generate enough power for sustained operation on the comet's surface. Still, Philae did have some power stored in batteries, which lasted for more than two days on the surface. That allowed Philae to perform some science with its 10 instruments in the time it had on Comet 67/P. Most notably, Philae found organic molecules that had never been detected on a comet before. The Rosetta orbiter continued to orbit Comet 67P until September 2016, and it was in that month -- just weeks before Rosetta itself landed on the comet on Sept. 30, 2016 -- that the spacecraft rediscovered the Philae lander lying on its side in a rocky crevice. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: I Am Artemis Katie Spicer
item.description: 4 Min Read I Am Artemis Katie Spicer For Katie Spicer, embracing opportunity and challenge has led to giant leaps during her time at NASA. Now as the NASA lander integration lead for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, one of the commercially provided human landing systems for NASA’s Artemis program, Spicer will have her handprint on history. NASA’s Katie Spicer stands in front of the crew cabin prototype for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lunar lander. The lander is one of two commercial human landing systems that will help safely ferry astronauts from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface and back for the agency’s crewed Artemis missions in 2028. NASA/Bill Strafford Spicer works in the Flight Operations Directorate at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, where she evaluates and monitors design and development of Blue Origin’s lander. The design of the Blue Moon lander is rapidly evolving as Blue Origin continues to develop a streamlined lander test article for the agency’s Artemis III rendezvous and docking mission in low Earth orbit as well as a fully functional lander for a crewed lunar landing in 2028. Spicer works closely with her NASA and Blue Origin counterparts to ensure the design of the Blue Moon lander can support the overall Artemis mission objectives. “I look at the design of everything Artemis crews will touch, work with, or interface with to ensure systems will function the way crews will need them to,” Spicer said. “In some cases, the design might meet requirements, but I delve deeper into details. How easy will it be for crew to grab handles or handrails? Can they operate push-button displays in microgravity? Are the hygiene systems as user-friendly as possible in the limited space that’s available in the spacecraft? And, are there proper procedures and training to ensure the crew can safely and effectively use the systems? Evaluating all these operational details with crew perspective is part of my job.” Spicer has spent her career looking at the small details in the big picture. After earning a bachelor’s degree in microbiology from the Pennsylvania State University in State College, Spicer spent several years working as a full-time homemaker and raising three children. She got her start at NASA working part-time in the historic Life Sciences Laboratory , performing duties such as washing dishes, cleaning lab equipment, and running tests for scientists. “I went from tidying up and keeping my home running to maintaining the historic lab where the Apollo crews were quarantined when they came back from the Moon and the Moon rock samples were stored,” Spicer said. item.content:encoded: 4 Min Read I Am Artemis Katie Spicer For Katie Spicer, embracing opportunity and challenge has led to giant leaps during her time at NASA. Now as the NASA lander integration lead for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, one of the commercially provided human landing systems for NASA’s Artemis program, Spicer will have her handprint on history. NASA’s Katie Spicer stands in front of the crew cabin prototype for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lunar lander. The lander is one of two commercial human landing systems that will help safely ferry astronauts from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface and back for the agency’s crewed Artemis missions in 2028. NASA/Bill Strafford Spicer works in the Flight Operations Directorate at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, where she evaluates and monitors design and development of Blue Origin’s lander. The design of the Blue Moon lander is rapidly evolving as Blue Origin continues to develop a streamlined lander test article for the agency’s Artemis III rendezvous and docking mission in low Earth orbit as well as a fully functional lander for a crewed lunar landing in 2028. Spicer works closely with her NASA and Blue Origin counterparts to ensure the design of the Blue Moon lander can support the overall Artemis mission objectives. “I look at the design of everything Artemis crews will touch, work with, or interface with to ensure systems will function the way crews will need them to,” Spicer said. “In some cases, the design might meet requirements, but I delve deeper into details. How easy will it be for crew to grab handles or handrails? Can they operate push-button displays in microgravity? Are the hygiene systems as user-friendly as possible in the limited space that’s available in the spacecraft? And, are there proper procedures and training to ensure the crew can safely and effectively use the systems? Evaluating all these operational details with crew perspective is part of my job.” Spicer has spent her career looking at the small details in the big picture. After earning a bachelor’s degree in microbiology from the Pennsylvania State University in State College, Spicer spent several years working as a full-time homemaker and raising three children. She got her start at NASA working part-time in the historic Life Sciences Laboratory , performing duties such as washing dishes, cleaning lab equipment, and running tests for scientists. “I went from tidying up and keeping my home running to maintaining the historic lab where the Apollo crews were quarantined when they came back from the Moon and the Moon rock samples were stored,” Spicer said. From there, Spicer began working with science payloads on the space station. She helped operate the Human Research Facility racks in the International Space Station National Laboratory and worked with scientists and crew to ensure in-flight processes and protocols were completed. It was there that Spicer found a love for the fast-paced dynamic of real-time space operations. Spicer became a flight controller at NASA Johnson’s Mission Control Center in 2018. The learning curve to become a flight controller was steep, but it did not deter her. Spicer studied and trained for five years to earn the ultimate instructor and flight controller certifications. “Unlike most people I work with, I don’t have an engineering degree,” Spicer said. “On my own, I studied engineering principles. I passed boards and certification tests. I learned to speak ‘engineer!’” Spicer spent five years as an Operations and Support Officer in the space station’s flight control room in Mission Control, also known as the “front room” to spaceflight. Now, when she looks at the Moon in the night sky, Spicer says she’s humbled and honored to be part of the team that’s sending astronauts back to the lunar surface. “I’m reminded of the great responsibility that NASA has in this endeavor, of the legacy of the courageous Apollo crews who went before, and inspiring the next generation of space explorers to keep going and reaching for the stars!” she said. As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions near the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars. To learn more about the Artemis program, visit: https://www.nasa.gov/artemis About the Author Beverly Perry Communications Strategist Share Details Last Updated Nov 12, 2026 Editor Lee Mohon Contact Corinne Beckinger corinne.m.beckinger@nasa.gov Location Marshall Space Flight Center Related Terms Artemis General Human Landing System Program I Am Artemis Johnson Space Center Marshall Space Flight Center Explore More 4 min read NASA Shares Plans to Accelerate Artemis, Return to Moon Article 2 weeks ago 4 min read NASA Selects Geology Team for the First Crewed Artemis Lunar Landing NASA has selected the geology team that will develop the surface science plan for the… Article 3 years ago 7 min read NASA, Partners Accelerate Lander Development for 2028 Moon Missions Article 3 weeks ago Keep Exploring Discover More Topics From NASA Missions Humans in Space Climate Change Solar System

item.title: Lego marketplace BrickLink in pieces after 'unusual activity' takes it offline for almost a week
item.description: Lego-owned marketplace BrickLink has been offline for almost a week after identifying "unusual activity on the platform," leaving fans unable to buy and sell spare bricks and minifigures. The company initially described the outage as "necessary work" and said the site would return on November 9. That deadline has come and gone. Visiting BrickLink's domain automatically serves the platform's maintenance page, which was last updated on November 11. "We took BrickLink offline after identifying unusual activity on the platform," the website states. "Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink. "Before bringing the site back online, we need to fully understand what has happened. That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues. "This work is still ongoing and we appreciate your patience while we work to get things back online as soon as possible." The references to security, containment, and investigation suggest something beyond routine maintenance, although BrickLink has not confirmed whether it suffered a cyberattack. The Register asked Lego for more information, but it did not immediately respond. Some adult fans of Lego (AFOL) have criticized the lack of information since the outage began on Friday, November 6. "Imagine how much better this would have been received if they were transparent from day one instead of pretending they have control over something they clearly don't," said one disgruntled Legohead via Reddit. "They don't even need to say what went wrong," said another. "Just an email acknowledging the issue would be appropriate. The entire site is down, and has been for days. That warrants more than a splash page." BrickLink was launched by Dan Jezek in June 2000 as an independent marketplace for enthusiasts to buy and sell Lego sets and individual pieces, including discontinued parts and rare minifigures. The Lego Group acquired BrickLink and Sohobricks from investment outfit NXMH in 2019 for an undisclosed sum. NXMH had bought BrickLink in 2013 and also owned Sohobricks, a South Korean manufacturer of unofficial but Lego-compatible bricks. Lego shuttered Sohobricks in 2020. At the time of Lego's acquisition, BrickLink had more than 10,000 storefronts on its marketplace selling Lego sets, parts, and minifigures. The AFOL community was initially concerned about Big Brick's intention with the acquisition, fearing that it would lead to high prices closer to those on Lego's own Pick a Brick parts-ordering service. For now, buyers and sellers would probably settle for a marketplace that's actually online. ® Updated to add on November 13: Lego said on Friday that BrickLink is back online after acknowledging the "confusion and uncertainty" the downtime caused among Lego fans. A statement made via the BrickLink website confirmed that "some" usernames and IP addresses were accessed, as were "a very small number" of email addresses. "We have already emailed members whose BrickLink usernames or emails were accessed with further information," it said . BrickLink will also waive sellers' fees for November and December as a token of appreciation for putting up with the downtime and disruption.

item.title: Jensen Huang's self-sabotage sends Nvidia into a midlife crisis
item.description: Nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang has been ousted after nearly two weeks of controversy that, at times, felt more like a soap opera than reality: a wealthy businessman, reported affairs, and an alleged Chinese spy and GPU smuggler. For Nvidia’s board, it seems there was no question Huang had to go. The man behind what was recently the most valuable company in the world proved too big a liability to retain in any capacity. He was too toxic even for a demotion from CEO to chairman, a vantage point that would have retained Huang as the face of the company even if he could no longer be trusted to run it. Replacing him won’t be so easy. Nvidia now faces an identity crisis. Huang, who has led the company for more than three decades, has no clear successor. The GPU slinger has no shortage of brilliant engineers, but executives capable of wrangling one of the biggest and most influential brands in the world, not so much. Ian Buck, father of CUDA and Nvidia’s VP of hyperscale and HPC is currently favored by many to be Huang’s successor. Buck has taken on a more public role within Nvidia in recent years headlining keynotes at events like Supercomputing and the AI Infra Summit. CFO Colette Kress, a bean counter who’s kept Jensen’s ambitions grounded for more than a decade, now takes the reins as interim CEO while the board searches for its next figurehead. And while Kress fights to contain the chaos, others will no doubt capitalize on Huang’s controversial choice of consorts to advance their own agendas. A marred reputation One need only ask a few inconvenient questions to cast doubt on Nvidia’s loyalties. How deep does China’s influence in Nvidia go? Can Nvidia’s hardware still be trusted? You get the idea. It certainly wouldn’t be the first time Nvidia’s and, by extension, Huang’s loyalties have been called into question. In late 2023, Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman blasted rival Nvidia for supplying GPUs to China in spite of US export controls, calling the behavior “ un-American ” and likening the graphics titan to an AI arms dealer. Nvidia has also faced criticism from US government officials, including former commerce secretary Gina Raimondo, for failing to take a hint and trying instead to limbo under US export controls in order to continue selling chips to the Middle Kingdom. After the Trump administration's short lived blockade of H20 sales early last year cost the company some $10.5 billion, Huang spent much of the 2025 lobbying the Trump administration to reverse export bans on the sales of older Hopper generation GPUs to China, an endeavor which ultimately proved successful . One could make the case that Huang’s ongoing efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China were financially motivated. But that argument is undermined by Huang admitting to having an extramarital affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (no relation), a woman that US intelligence has accused of moonlighting as a Chinese spy and helping to smuggle GPUs into the country. item.dc:creator: Tobias Mann
item.content:encoded: Nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang has been ousted after nearly two weeks of controversy that, at times, felt more like a soap opera than reality: a wealthy businessman, reported affairs, and an alleged Chinese spy and GPU smuggler. For Nvidia’s board, it seems there was no question Huang had to go. The man behind what was recently the most valuable company in the world proved too big a liability to retain in any capacity. He was too toxic even for a demotion from CEO to chairman, a vantage point that would have retained Huang as the face of the company even if he could no longer be trusted to run it. Replacing him won’t be so easy. Nvidia now faces an identity crisis. Huang, who has led the company for more than three decades, has no clear successor. The GPU slinger has no shortage of brilliant engineers, but executives capable of wrangling one of the biggest and most influential brands in the world, not so much. Ian Buck, father of CUDA and Nvidia’s VP of hyperscale and HPC is currently favored by many to be Huang’s successor. Buck has taken on a more public role within Nvidia in recent years headlining keynotes at events like Supercomputing and the AI Infra Summit. CFO Colette Kress, a bean counter who’s kept Jensen’s ambitions grounded for more than a decade, now takes the reins as interim CEO while the board searches for its next figurehead. And while Kress fights to contain the chaos, others will no doubt capitalize on Huang’s controversial choice of consorts to advance their own agendas. A marred reputation One need only ask a few inconvenient questions to cast doubt on Nvidia’s loyalties. How deep does China’s influence in Nvidia go? Can Nvidia’s hardware still be trusted? You get the idea. It certainly wouldn’t be the first time Nvidia’s and, by extension, Huang’s loyalties have been called into question. In late 2023, Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman blasted rival Nvidia for supplying GPUs to China in spite of US export controls, calling the behavior “ un-American ” and likening the graphics titan to an AI arms dealer. Nvidia has also faced criticism from US government officials, including former commerce secretary Gina Raimondo, for failing to take a hint and trying instead to limbo under US export controls in order to continue selling chips to the Middle Kingdom. After the Trump administration's short lived blockade of H20 sales early last year cost the company some $10.5 billion, Huang spent much of the 2025 lobbying the Trump administration to reverse export bans on the sales of older Hopper generation GPUs to China, an endeavor which ultimately proved successful . One could make the case that Huang’s ongoing efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China were financially motivated. But that argument is undermined by Huang admitting to having an extramarital affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (no relation), a woman that US intelligence has accused of moonlighting as a Chinese spy and helping to smuggle GPUs into the country. The consequences of controversy When technology and politics collide, the appearance of impropriety is often more damning than the impropriety itself. Uncle Sam has forced Chinese companies out of the United States for the mere possibility that they could be coerced into planting back doors in critical infrastructure. Just ask Huawei whether the truth counts for anything once Washington has decided that you’re a national security threat. Huang’s affairs may not just cost him his job, but could cost Nvidia key government contracts and make the company’s hardware less attractive, particularly in highly-regulated and notoriously risk-averse industries. Rival chipmakers will no doubt capitalize on Nvidia’s bad optics if Huang’s departure doesn’t pop the AI financing merry-go-round bubble first – Nvidia's stock lost about 25% of its value in the few days after news about Huang started breaking, only recovering slightly after his ouster. Regardless, with Nvidia’s reputation marred and its future shrouded in uncertainty, once loyal customers may be more willing to explore alternative providers. There are certainly plenty to choose from. Amid a surge in custom AI chips from the likes of Broadcom, Marvel, and others, Nvidia’s main advantage wasn’t so much technological as it was simply considered a safe bet. AMD is the most obvious winner here. As we reported earlier this year , the House of Zen’s GPU tech has already surpassed Nvidia’s, at least on paper. What’s more, the company has a long and unblemished relationship serving the US government. AMD’s chips now power two of the Department of Energy’s three largest and most sensitive supercomputers. Meanwhile, hyperscalers with sufficient cashflow – think Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Meta – may seek to insulate themselves from Huang’s fallout by investing more heavily in homegrown silicon and offering it to customers. Then there's the threat from the man himself. Huang's ambitions and influence are such that he's unlikely to fade into obscurity. He may disappear from the spotlight while things blow over, but it’s a pretty sure bet that he’ll pop up at a new company eventually, and will still have enough sway to poach some of Nvidia’s top engineers. ®

item.title: Arsenal dig deep to earn WCL draw in face of Barcelona dominance
item.description: Arsenal continue to be a sharp thorn in the side of the European champions, Barcelona, and they dug deep to hold on to a draw at the Camp Nou on Thursday night. Frida Maanum put the Gunners ahead despite a hugely dominant performance from Barcelona, but Caroline Graham Hansen’s equaliser ensured the spoils would be shared. Barcelona have been formidable when playing at the club’s main stadium, winning nine and drawing twice, against Chelsea in the semi-finals in 2023 and now Arsenal. Continue reading...

item.title: SpaceX's Starship megarocket will launch to orbit on Nov. 13. Will you be able to spot it in the night sky?
item.description: null SpaceX's Starship megarocket is slated to launch on its ambitious 15th flight test as soon as this Friday (Nov. 13). Will you be able to spot its leviathan upper stage, known as Ship, or its Starlink satellite passengers as they circle Earth during the historic orbital jaunt? Flight 15's 75-minute launch window opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT) on Nov. 13 . Starship will fly from SpaceX 's Starbase site in South Texas, where it will be 4:45 p.m. at the opening of the window — about an hour before sunset. The launch could therefore be especially dramatic for folks in the area. "As it launches towards the southeast, and it will be daylight, then the prospects for viewing from the U.S. are going to be in Texas and the states along the Gulf of Mexico," Robert Massey, deputy executive director at the Royal Astronomical Society, told Space.com. "They could see the exhaust plume (the ' jellyfish ') with the sky darker for observers further east." If all goes to plan, Starship's Super Heavy booster will propel the Ship upper stage through the densest part of Earth's atmosphere before returning to Starbase for a powered landing and capture via the "chopstick" arms of the "Mechazilla" tower system . Ship, meanwhile, will go on to orbit Earth approximately 14 times over the following 22 hours, during which time it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites before returning to Starbase for its own ambitious catch attempt. When should I look for Starship and its Starlink train? Satellite visibility in the night sky depends on a cocktail of factors, from the size of the spacecraft to its reflectivity, orbital inclination and position relative to the Earth and sun. Ship is big — about 171 feet (52 meters) tall — so it will be a viable target for skywatchers, experts say. "It certainly will be visible in twilight hours. It should be very bright, considerably brighter than the Starlink satellites due to its size," professor James Osborn of Durham University told Space.com. "Where and when is a bit more tricky." Starship Flight 14 rises away from its launch tower during the September 2026 test flight from Boca Chica, Texas. (Image credit: Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images) Ship and its Starlink satellites may be seen in the 90 minutes directly after sunset on Nov. 13 and before sunrise on Nov. 14, as the probes catch the sunlight on either side of Earth's colossal shadow as they drift through the twilight sky. The spacecraft will initially appear as a string of bright, evenly spaced lights, with Ship most likely appearing significantly brighter than the Starlink satellites. However, Osborn noted that the lack of publicly available data makes it challenging to forecast exactly when the spacecraft will appear. "During its 14 orbits over 22 hours, the spacecraft is between inclinations of 30.5 [degrees] N and S of the equator," explained Massey. "So it will be best viewed between those latitudes, and then lower in the sky up to latitudes of 40 N and 40 S. That's pre

Satellite visibility in the night sky depends on a cocktail of factors, from the size of the spacecraft to its reflectivity, orbital inclination and position relative to the Earth and sun. Ship is big — about 171 feet (52 meters) tall — so it will be a viable target for skywatchers, experts say. "It certainly will be visible in twilight hours. It should be very bright, considerably brighter than the Starlink satellites due to its size," professor James Osborn of Durham University told Space.com. "Where and when is a bit more tricky." Starship Flight 14 rises away from its launch tower during the September 2026 test flight from Boca Chica, Texas. (Image credit: Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images) Ship and its Starlink satellites may be seen in the 90 minutes directly after sunset on Nov. 13 and before sunrise on Nov. 14, as the probes catch the sunlight on either side of Earth's colossal shadow as they drift through the twilight sky. The spacecraft will initially appear as a string of bright, evenly spaced lights, with Ship most likely appearing significantly brighter than the Starlink satellites. However, Osborn noted that the lack of publicly available data makes it challenging to forecast exactly when the spacecraft will appear. "During its 14 orbits over 22 hours, the spacecraft is between inclinations of 30.5 [degrees] N and S of the equator," explained Massey. "So it will be best viewed between those latitudes, and then lower in the sky up to latitudes of 40 N and 40 S. That's pretty much the whole of the contiguous U.S." Space.com skywatching columnist and veteran meteorologist Joe Rao shared further details on what stargazers may see with the naked eye as Ship drifts silently through the autumn sky. Starlink satellites form a trail of star-like points in the night sky soon after deployment in 2023. (Image credit: Photo by Arda Kucukkaya/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images) "When it passes overhead, it will look like a bright, fast-moving star crossing the sky — similar to the International Space Station , but potentially even brighter depending on its orientation," explained Rao. "The Starlink V3 satellites are much smaller, so not as bright, perhaps ranging anywhere from 2nd to 4th magnitude, depending on the angle of illumination with reflected light from the sun ." Magnitude is the scale used by astronomers to measure the brightness of objects in the night sky. The lower the magnitude, the brighter the object! The unaided eye can make out objects with a magnitude of around +6.5 under ideal dark sky conditions, while the planet Venus currently shines at magnitude -4.41. The Starlink train will likely fall further behind Starship as the 22-hour mission progresses, while the train itself will become more elongated, according to Rao. "For locations where it will make a high arc across the sky, the Starship should be visible for at least a few minutes, although because it is orbiting at a lower altitude (170 miles/275 km) compared to the ISS, it probably will appear to move somewhat faster. " How can I track Starship after launch? There are multiple handy resources that should allow you to track Ship and the newly deployed batch of V3 Starlink satellites following their scheduled launch on Nov. 13, including the websites Heavens-Above , Star Dash , Orbital Radar and Find Starlink . Be sure to keep an eye on our Starship Flight 15 live blog for all the latest news along with our launch timings article containing details on how to watch SpaceX's potentially historic orbital launch attempt. Editor's Note: If you capture a photo of Starship and want to share it with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

item.title: 'Warhammer Survivors' is the perfect gateway into the 40K universe
item.description: We've had no shortage of great Warhammer 40K games lately, but most aren't exactly aimed at the casual crowd. Warhammer Survivors changes that, finally providing curious gamers with an easy entry point into the grim darkness of the 41st millennium. Developed by Auroch Digital (in collaboration with Vampire Survivors' Poncle), this new spin on the survivors-like roguelite subgenre mixes the sci-fi 40,000 setting with the pure fantasy Age of Sigmar universe. This means heroes and enemies from all over the Warhammer mythos meet together in a bite-sized game that anyone can figure out and enjoy in less than five minutes. When you look at the alternatives, that's a remarkable achievement for a franchise that's notoriously hard (and often expensive) to get into . Warhammer Survivors isn't bogged down by dense lore, involved mechanics, or massive campaign playthroughs. It's more of an "inspired by" effort that gives casuals a small taste of the series' iconic characters — including Boltgun 's Malum Caedo — and factions like the terrifying Tyranids, the raucous Orks, and the foul forces of Chaos. All of 40K's (and Age of Sigmar's) recognizable elements are on display, but they serve more as flavoring sprinkled on top of Vampire Survivors' successful formula. If you're new to the Survivors-like subgenre, it's a unique gaming experience. You battle an endless onslaught of enemies that slowly march towards you, with your character passively attacking automatically. You only need to move them around sprawling arenas and select level-up upgrades and items after collecting enough gems (skulls in this case). The moment-to-moment gameplay is as simple as it can get outside of walking sims and interactive "experiences," but there's a deceiving depth to item synergies and how to correctly "build" characters to endure all the carnage. Unlike Poncle's original game, Warhammer Survivors struggles a bit to get going. The early hours are sluggish until you unlock certain meta upgrades, but its still got that Vampire Survivors magic at its core. As far as "podcast/gym games" go, this is a perfect fit. There's just enough going on to keep one's brain engaged, but minimal inputs and a tight overarching design lead to a rhythm that's easy to get into without using much brainpower. It's oddly satisfying to weave through enemies and level up your firepower, watching a single Astra Militarum grunt grow into a full Lasgun-spamming, chainsword-wielding wrecking ball. Achievement and unlock hunters will find enough to bite into here, too. It's unclear if the devs will continue to add more Warhammer 40K and Age of Sigmar deep cuts to this game via DLCs and free updates, but those universes have daunting depths to explore. This really could become a gateway game for future 40K fans: by the time they realize they're hooked, they'll already have 2000 pts of space marines painted and ready to play. (Image credit: Auroch Digital) As massive sci-fi and fantasy properties tr

It's more of an "inspired by" effort that gives casuals a small taste of the series' iconic characters — including Boltgun 's Malum Caedo — and factions like the terrifying Tyranids, the raucous Orks, and the foul forces of Chaos. All of 40K's (and Age of Sigmar's) recognizable elements are on display, but they serve more as flavoring sprinkled on top of Vampire Survivors' successful formula. If you're new to the Survivors-like subgenre, it's a unique gaming experience. Unlike Poncle's original game, Warhammer Survivors struggles a bit to get going. The early hours are sluggish until you unlock certain meta upgrades, but its still got that Vampire Survivors magic at its core. As far as "podcast/gym games" go, this is a perfect fit. There's just enough going on to keep one's brain engaged, but minimal inputs and a tight overarching design lead to a rhythm that's easy to get into without using much brainpower. It's oddly satisfying to weave through enemies and level up your firepower, watching a single Astra Militarum grunt grow into a full Lasgun-spamming, chainsword-wielding wrecking ball. Achievement and unlock hunters will find enough to bite into here, too. It's unclear if the devs will continue to add more Warhammer 40K and Age of Sigmar deep cuts to this game via DLCs and free updates, but those universes have daunting depths to explore. This really could become a gateway game for future 40K fans: by the time they realize they're hooked, they'll already have 2000 pts of space marines painted and ready to play. (Image credit: Auroch Digital) As massive sci-fi and fantasy properties try to aggressively expand and absorb more and more fans, it's easy to pander to already-converted diehards too much. And sure, we can't wait for strategy heavyweights like Dawn of War 4 and Total War: WH40K either, but they're hardly good recommendations for folks who don't even know what a Space Marine is or why the robotic Necrons are so grumpy. Warhammer Survivors won't answer those questions beyond the surface-level iconography, but it's fun enough to push those curious to dig deeper and embrace the same material in more mature video game genres... and maybe even pick up a few miniatures . Warhammer Survivors is now available on PC (Steam & GOG), PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 1/2, and mobile (iOS & Android). It's also playable on Game Pass.

item.title: Palantir’s Karp takes a sharp left turn, says he and the company’s products are actually ‘progressive’
item.description: With tech CEO roles, a certain level of shamelessness comes with the job description. Yet Alex Karp, head honcho of Palantir, seems set to raise the bar with a conspicuous display of political flexibility following the Democratic wave in the US midterms. In December 2024, Karp gave $1 million to the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc . But it does not take cutting-edge AI and data analytics – in which Palantir claims to have unique power – for Karp to understand on which side his bread is buttered. The man with the distinctive verbal diarrhea is now stressing his progressive credentials – and those of Palantir's products. The CEO told Politico that he is now open to voting for the Democrats come 2028. "I've been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir – all of our products are essentially progressive," Karp reportedly said. Karp's explanation for his political generosity was an apparent desire for balance. "My giving is equal, Democrat, Republican," Karp told the publication. "I can tell you, without going into things I'm not gonna disclose, I'm very balanced, and everyone in the political arena knows it. And I'll tell you what, I'm also not the village idiot." All of which raises the question of whether, in avoiding idiocy, it is necessary to eschew any principled stance whatsoever. If only the Germans of the Weimar Republic had thought to fund both sides. Apparently, all Europe needed was a more balanced political donations portfolio. Such is Karp's sensitivity towards the topic that he once claimed: "I love when I'm getting yelled at in cities in Europe... Keep yelling at me... the only reason why someone's not goose-stepping between me and you is my product. Say thank you." They have not said thank you. In fact, across Europe, governments are looking to reject Palantir , while the EU has instigated a sovereign tech and AI policy to escape the clutches of the US tech giants. Karp has a talent for holding two seemingly contradictory positions. He has talked about the need for democratic societies to exercise hard power , and, elsewhere, about founding a company that could "power the West to its obvious innate superiority ." At the same time, he has presented Palantir as a force for peace. "We see ourselves as the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement ," he wrote in his shareholder letter. It is his company's association with a longstanding customer, the controversial US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), that has drawn the most criticism. In Minnesota earlier this year, federal immigration officers shot and killed two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in incidents captured on video. It has detained US citizens, and critics argue it has shown scant regard for due process. Karp denied that Palantir's association with ICE should reflect badly on the company. Karp's explanation for his political generosity was an apparent desire for balance. "My giving is equal, Democrat, Republican," Karp told the publication. "I can tell you, without going into things I'm not gonna disclose, I'm very balanced, and everyone in the political arena knows it. And I'll tell you what, I'm also not the village idiot." All of which raises the question of whether, in avoiding idiocy, it is necessary to eschew any principled stance whatsoever. If only the Germans of the Weimar Republic had thought to fund both sides. Apparently, all Europe needed was a more balanced political donations portfolio. Such is Karp's sensitivity towards the topic that he once claimed: "I love when I'm getting yelled at in cities in Europe... Keep yelling at me... the only reason why someone's not goose-stepping between me and you is my product. Say thank you." They have not said thank you. In fact, across Europe, governments are looking to reject Palantir , while the EU has instigated a sovereign tech and AI policy to escape the clutches of the US tech giants.
