DORA, introduced in January last year, is designed to strengthen cyber security in the financial sector. "Digital sovereignty is becoming a buying decision. As customers and resellers get clearer about what it means in practice, they're asking who holds the encryption keys, who can access sensitive logs and where that data is stored," said Context veep of research Joe Turner. "We're seeing a measurable shift in the EMEA channel. EU vendors gained nearly three points of sales share in two years. An organization can keep its existing identity platform and still choose a European supplier to manage its security logs. That's the kind of decision that gives European vendors an opening." The stats indicate that EU-HQd vendors comprised 92 percent of tracked sales in security awareness training, 82 percent in vulnerability management, and 52 percent for SIEM and log management. US-headquartered companies held into 74 percent of identity and access management sales and 54 percent of cloud security sales. The Reg has asked Context for UK-specific figures to see whether British customers are also voting with their wallets for European alternatives. That certainly isn’t the case for tech purchases in the British public sector, despite Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s professed desire to buy British. Data released yesterday by the Institute for Public Policy Research showed just £1 in every £6 spent by government with the biggest technology suppliers goes to Brit businesses. Still, Burnham only came to power in July so there is time yet for him to put his money where his mouth is. Sovereign AI is another area of concern for enterprise customers. Analyst Omdia said last month that despite the marketing adjective meaning "local assets," almost a third AI providers disclose no proof of sovereignty, and some "expect enterprise to pay for audits to verify their claims." Omdia also found that 80 percent of contracts say network resilience is "out of providers control or responsibility," and "US-headquartered AI providers offer better service transparency and contract terms than a majority of local sovereign AI providers, with providers in India a notable exception." Sovereign services in Omdia's classification include data residency, operational autonomy, jurisdictional sovereignty, and technological autonomy. "Local hosting is not sovereignty. Serious providers must demonstrate their credibility through transparent operations, fair contracts and proof of competence. That includes the network, because data in transit must be sovereign too," said Camille Mendler, research director for telco B2B at Omdia. Someone should tell Microsoft and Anthropic . ®

item.title: Rockstar workers vote on union recognition as GTA VI launch looms
item.description: More than 1,600 Rockstar Games employees in the UK will begin voting on union recognition on Thursday, with the ballot kicking off just a week before the long-awaited launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. The ballot, which opens on November 12 and runs until November 26, will determine whether Rockstar formally recognizes the Rockstar Game Workers Union, part of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB). Nearly all UK employees below director level are eligible to vote. If successful, the union would become the largest recognized union in the UK games industry, giving workers a collective voice. The proposed recognition agreement follows four months of negotiations between Rockstar management and employees. It would allow workers to negotiate over pay, overtime, pensions, bonuses, leave and other employment conditions, while securing consultation rights over HR policies and AI. The vote comes at a particularly busy time for Rockstar, with GTA VI finally due to arrive on November 19, more than 13 years after its predecessor. The game is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment launches in history, although the people responsible for making it have rather more immediate concerns than sales records. "I am incredibly proud of the work we've put into making this game. I'm also proud of the union we've built here. For me, those two things are connected," said Nestor Uriate, an animation programmer and Rockstar Game Workers Union representative. "We care deeply about the games we make, and we want to make sure we can continue doing that work in an environment where we're respected, have a meaningful say over our conditions and can feel secure about our futures." The vote follows a year of bad blood between Rockstar and the IWGB. The union accused the GTA developer of union busting after it fired 31 members in October 2025, claiming they had been singled out for taking part in a private Discord group. Rockstar denied the allegations, insisting the workers were dismissed for gross misconduct rather than their union activities. The dispute subsequently reached an employment tribunal, where Rockstar unsuccessfully attempted to have blacklisting allegations struck from the case . Closing submissions are expected on November 17 and 18, meaning the legal proceedings will reach their final stages just as GTA VI prepares to hit shelves. Despite the ongoing dispute, Rockstar's head of publishing, Jennifer Kolbe, recently indicated that management would respect the outcome of the recognition vote, telling Bloomberg : "We go where the team goes. So if they want a union, they will have a union." The union campaign has also attracted support from elsewhere in the games industry, including SAG-AFTRA and the Communications Workers of America (CWA), which represents workers at Blizzard. item.title: ‘Second ball’ may be a Sunday league mantra but Yates showed its top-flight relevance
item.description: Midfielder’s old-school attributes came to the fore during Nottingham Forest’s win against Manchester City Modern football is more systematised and data-driven than ever but some things never change. Winning the first ball is important but the second ball – the holy grail for Sunday league footballers – is often more so. Nottingham Forest’s 3-1 win against Manchester City last weekend featured a classic example. Forest led 2-1 inside the last 20 minutes but City, lifted by Rayan Cherki’s sweet half-volley, were pushing for an equaliser. Continue reading...

item.title: NHS England deletes ‘misleading’ claim 137 trusts benefiting from Palantir AI tools
item.description: Exclusive: The Guardian revealed 29 hospital trusts were not or hardly using the controversial patient data tech NHS England has deleted a claim from its website stating 137 hospital trusts are benefiting from Palantir’s AI health data system after the Guardian revealed 29 of them were not using all or most of the controversial technology. Health bosses had published a list of all the NHS bodies “live” with and “realising benefits” from the AI-powered federated data platform (FDP), a system set up to improve patient outcomes, boost operating theatre efficiency and speed up bed discharges. But after 29 trusts said it was either not live or they were not using any of its applications, the original list of hospitals appears to have been taken down. Continue reading...

But after 29 trusts said it was either not live or they were not using any of its applications, the original list of hospitals appears to have been taken down. Continue reading...

item.title: Orbit Global Menu: A working global menu addon for GNOME
item.description: A new extension brings a working global menu bar to the GNOME desktop, even for some apps that don’t have menu bars at all. Orbit Global Menu is a new GNOME extension that gives the GNOME desktop a feature it was intentionally designed without, and one that some users miss very badly – this vulture being one of them. It adds a working global menu bar to the GNOME top panel. We suspect this is something that will cause strongly contrasting opinions among many GNOME users: some will by puzzled why anyone would bother, while others may think "at last!" and rush to try it. There have been other attempts to do this before, and the Reg FOSS desk has tried several of them, but we never found one that worked with the majority of applications. Our fondness for this UI feature was visible in the two-part series we wrote in September on how to customize Xfce and then in part two how to get the global menu working with more apps. The problem is getting worse over time, as in recent versions (since GNOME 40 and Gtk4), the GNOME human-interface guidelines encourage smartphone-style hamburger menus, replacing the traditional horizontal menu bar. It is tricky to add global menu bar support to apps that lack a menu bar, but Orbit's developer "Unmade" found a rather labor-intensive solution. The menu bar applet contains maps of keyboard controls for 292 different apps, so it can show a menu all on its own and then send those apps simulated keystrokes to operate it. It's not the programs' full menu trees, just a subset of them, but it works. It's also not the most elegant solution, but it is a solution and it works. We tried it on Ubuntu 26.10 and every app in the full install worked to at least some extent. If you are willing and able to build and install a small additional connector, it lets the global-menu applet talk to lots more applications. The GNOME shell is unusual among open source desktop environments, to an extent that we have criticized before. GNOME Shell was designed with a distinctive look and feel of its own, unlike almost all other desktops. It has a minimalist, stripped-down layout that doesn't look or work quite like anything else, and it's intentionally not very customizable. To change how GNOME works means writing new Javascript code, then packaging it as an extension that users can install from the GNOME Extensions website. This requires both a browser extension and a "native host messaging" connector to be installed into the underlying OS – or a purpose-written app. By default, the desktop comes with neither. The end result is that GNOME lends a visual identity to the Linux desktop, one that is clear and distinct from either Windows or macOS. (Back in 2013, this vulture argued that when Microsoft threatened to sue multiple Linux vendors over infringing Windows UI patents, some 20 years ago, this UI fragmentation was just what the company wanted .) item.content:encoded: A new extension brings a working global menu bar to the GNOME desktop, even for some apps that don’t have menu bars at all. Orbit Global Menu is a new GNOME extension that gives the GNOME desktop a feature it was intentionally designed without, and one that some users miss very badly – this vulture being one of them. It adds a working global menu bar to the GNOME top panel. We suspect this is something that will cause strongly contrasting opinions among many GNOME users: some will by puzzled why anyone would bother, while others may think "at last!" and rush to try it. There have been other attempts to do this before, and the Reg FOSS desk has tried several of them, but we never found one that worked with the majority of applications. Our fondness for this UI feature was visible in the two-part series we wrote in September on how to customize Xfce and then in part two how to get the global menu working with more apps. The problem is getting worse over time, as in recent versions (since GNOME 40 and Gtk4), the GNOME human-interface guidelines encourage smartphone-style hamburger menus, replacing the traditional horizontal menu bar. It is tricky to add global menu bar support to apps that lack a menu bar, but Orbit's developer "Unmade" found a rather labor-intensive solution. The menu bar applet contains maps of keyboard controls for 292 different apps, so it can show a menu all on its own and then send those apps simulated keystrokes to operate it. It's not the programs' full menu trees, just a subset of them, but it works. It's also not the most elegant solution, but it is a solution and it works. We tried it on Ubuntu 26.10 and every app in the full install worked to at least some extent. If you are willing and able to build and install a small additional connector, it lets the global-menu applet talk to lots more applications. The GNOME shell is unusual among open source desktop environments, to an extent that we have criticized before. GNOME Shell was designed with a distinctive look and feel of its own, unlike almost all other desktops. It has a minimalist, stripped-down layout that doesn't look or work quite like anything else, and it's intentionally not very customizable. To change how GNOME works means writing new Javascript code, then packaging it as an extension that users can install from the GNOME Extensions website. This requires both a browser extension and a "native host messaging" connector to be installed into the underlying OS – or a purpose-written app. By default, the desktop comes with neither. The end result is that GNOME lends a visual identity to the Linux desktop, one that is clear and distinct from either Windows or macOS. (Back in 2013, this vulture argued that when Microsoft threatened to sue multiple Linux vendors over infringing Windows UI patents, some 20 years ago, this UI fragmentation was just what the company wanted .) GNOME 2 was the Linux world's default desktop. GNOME Shell was controversial in its early days, and lost pole position, but it has since won it back. Today, GNOME is the default desktop on all the major distros: Ubuntu, Fedora and Red Hat Enterprise Linux and the RHELatives, as well as Debian and SUSE, all default to GNOME. GNOME does away with a lot of features that are significant functional parts of other graphical desktops. For instance, it has no desktop icons, no system tray or defined place for status indicators, and neither GNOME nor GNOME-compliant applications have menu bars, either inside windows (Microsoft style) or in the top panel (Apple macOS style). This is disorienting and confusing for those used to controlling software mainly using their menus – but now, that's mainly older hands. This design suits those who grew up on smartphones and tablets, or who feel more comfortable with their stripped-back keyboardless UI than a full desktop WIMP, which can be overwhelming to newbies and non-techies. If you've followed the evolution of graphical desktops for some 40 years, as this gray-plumed vulture has, some trends are very apparent that aren't so clear if you came in once evolution was underway. Apple introduced the first global menu bar in the Lisa, and improved on that in the Macintosh. DR GEM copied it very early on , but Apple sued and DR changed the PC version of GEM to be less Mac-like. Microsoft's Windows came along after this, and moved menu bars inside windows instead. When Apple acquired NeXT in 1996 , it moved NeXTstep's patent-avoidant vertical menus back to a global bar at the top, along with the clock and some status indicators. There they remain, 30 years later. In 2007, it launched the iPhone, containing a very cut-down OS based on OS X, replacing the Finder with a cut-down version of the Dashboard layer from OS X 10.4 . The panel remained, shorn of its menus, which were too fiddly for a small screen. As The Register mentioned in 2017 , in its preliminary releases, Android started out as a keypad-driven Java phone that looked and worked very much like BlackBerry. When the iPhone appeared, Google changed course . The new Android UI resembled iOS, complete with that top panel, still without menus. GNOME 3.0 was not far behind: in 2009 the team promised a revamp of the user experience, and in 2011, launched GNOME 3.0. It too has the fixed top panel — now huge on a laptop or desktop landscape screen – and mostly empty. Now that top panel regains its original 1983 function. We're rather impressed by the Orbit global menu. It does the job, and it even works with apps that don't have menu bars. It's not perfect: for instance, over-long menus have to scroll, and may fail to do so if new submenus appear. The GitHub repository has extensive instructions, including how to build and install the optional connector module that lets more apps export their real menus to the extension. It also tells you how to instruct some apps, notably Firefox, that there is a global menu for it to use. We are saddened to note that, as is so often the case, Wayland gets in the way here. It works rather well with some other extensions, too. With a menu bar, GNOME's strangely centered clock seems out of place, but several extensions, such as F rippery Move Clock , shove it over to the right where we still feel it belongs. If you prefer a lighter-colored panel and dock, it also plays nicely with Blur my Shell . ®

item.title: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – an adorable raccoon mends the world, one parcel at a time
item.description: Nintendo Switch/2, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/series X/S, PC; Denkiworks/Inpleron Limited This gentle game of fixing and fetching, in which you play as a furry post office worker on a BMX, has a slow, calming magic that delights in routine and restoration Arriving alongside November’s blue wave , Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a game of quiet restoration that feels perfectly suited to the current moment. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together. It sounds a bit like JL Carr’s compact but enchanting novel A Month in the Country , except instead of shell-shocked veterans of the first world war you’re left exploring the rich inner life of a Japanese racoon dog who can ride a BMX. Even so, the mixture of steady progress and general low stakes proves intoxicating. This is a short game, but it’s hard not to linger over it. Continue reading...

item.title: London hotel put admin login for booking website on whiteboard behind the front desk
item.description: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where all the victims are self-owned. This week, we welcome you to a London hotel where you could check out its admin credentials for a booking website just by walking past the front desk. Our story comes courtesy of Neycho Tepavicharov, co-founder of Flashcloud, a Delaware-based web hosting company. He was staying at a hotel in London when he noticed a shocking breach of basic security protocols by management, who were a little too hospitable with their credentials. As he was passing through the lobby, Tepavicharov noticed that the door behind the front desk was open and, inside that back room, there was a whiteboard. On the whiteboard, written in plain English, were the hotel’s Booking.com administrative username and password. Anyone near the desk could clearly see the login information, and if they didn’t have time to write it down, they could have snapped a picture for later use. As Tepavicharov explains, there’s plenty of mischief you could perform with these credentials. “With that login, someone could change or cancel reservations, see guests’ names and contact details, or message guests pretending to be the hotel,” he said. “Fake 'please confirm your payment' messages sent from compromised hotel accounts are a well-known scam.” An attacker could potentially exploit that access to disrupt hotel operations or target guests with convincing scams. Whether the exposed credentials alone would have been enough to access the account would depend on its security settings. Tepavicharov decided to play the role of good samaritan and warn the hotel’s manager that the business was endangering itself by showing everyone its password. “I asked to speak with the manager and showed him what I’d seen. He was mortified and very grateful,” Tepavicharov said. “Nobody on staff had thought of it as a risk. It was just the easiest way for the whole team to share one login.” After Tepavicharov talked to the manager, not only did the hotel change its ways, but it also moved its website to his hosting service, Flashcloud. Tepavicharov notes that there are plenty of takeaways from this incident. Most important: give each user dedicated credentials with their own separate login, and use multi-factor authentication. “The lesson is an old one, but it keeps happening,” he said. “Shared logins end up written somewhere convenient. Give each staff member their own login, turn on two-factor authentication, and keep passwords in a password manager, not on the wall.” ®

item.title: Data sovereignty takes more than keeping data close to home
item.description: Keeping sensitive data within national borders might satisfy a residency requirement. But does it mean your organization is genuinely in control? Not necessarily. Data could be stored locally while remaining subject to another jurisdiction's laws, dependent on overseas service providers or exposed to disruption beyond your control. For enterprise IT teams, that distinction is becoming harder to ignore. Geopolitical tensions, evolving regulations and the growing use of AI are forcing organizations to reconsider what data sovereignty means in practice. Yet translating those concerns into a workable strategy is another matter. And simply throwing more money at the problem won't necessarily solve it. In The Register's on-demand webinar, Data Sovereignty By Design, moderator Tim Phillips speaks with Patrick Smith, Field CTO for EMEA at Everpure, formerly Pure Storage, about moving beyond compliance checklists and taking a more strategic approach to data control. Drawing on findings from Everpure's research, Smith explores a curious disconnect: organizations are increasing their investment in sovereignty initiatives, yet many still lack a coordinated strategy. Some of the risks attracting the most attention aren't necessarily those receiving the greatest investment. The discussion examines why sovereignty shouldn't be treated as an IT-only responsibility. Decisions about which data needs protection, which services must remain operational and what level of risk is acceptable require input from business leaders, security, procurement and legal teams. There's also the question of priorities. Not every workload needs the same sovereign controls, and attempting to protect everything equally can make an already complicated challenge considerably harder. Smith explains the concept of the "minimum viable company," identifying the critical services, applications and data an organization needs to keep operating through disruption. He also considers why visibility into data access, supplier dependencies and potential exit strategies should influence technology decisions from the outset. For IT leaders trying to turn sovereignty from an abstract boardroom concern into something actionable, the conversation offers useful questions to take back to their organizations. Because knowing where your data sits is one thing. Knowing whether you can maintain control when circumstances change is quite another. Watch the full Data Sovereignty By Design webinar on demand Sponsored by Everpure

item.title: Kerrygold Engages Women in Business and Leadership at 25th WIMBIZ Annual Conference
item.description: Kerrygold strengthened its engagement with consumers and showcased its distinctive dairy offerings at the 25th Women in Management, Business and Public Service (WIMBIZ) Annual Conference, held on November 5 and 6, 2026, at Eko Hotel & Suites, Lagos. The participation provided an opportunity for the renowned Irish dairy brand to connect with an influential audience of women in business, leadership and public service. Through its sponsorship of the conference, Kerrygold aligned with a platform that brings together accomplished women from diverse sectors to share ideas, build networks and explore opportunities for growth. The 25th edition, which celebrated WIMBIZ’s 25-year contribution to women’s empowerment, was themed “ Rooted, Rising, Ready: Born in Africa, Built for the World,” with conversations centred on leadership, business growth and the evolving role of African women in shaping the future. A key highlight of Kerrygold’s participation was its exhibition stand, where attendees had the opportunity to explore the brand’s product range, learn more about its dairy offerings and enjoy product sampling. The stand also provided a welcoming space for direct interactions with guests, allowing them to experience Kerrygold more closely and discover what makes its products distinctive. Beyond showcasing its products, Kerrygold’s presence at the conference reflected its commitment to strengthening brand visibility, building relevance and fostering meaningful consumer relationships. By creating opportunities for attendees to interact with the brand and experience its offerings firsthand, Kerrygold brought its quality and distinctive taste closer to an audience with whom it sought to build lasting connections. As Kerrygold continues to grow its presence in Nigeria, engagements at relevant platforms such as WIMBIZ complement its efforts to introduce more consumers to the brand. Rooted in a rich Irish dairy heritage and celebrated for its distinctive rich, creamy taste, Kerrygold remains focused on creating opportunities for more people to discover and enjoy its quality dairy products. Sponsored Content The post Kerrygold Engages Women in Business and Leadership at 25th WIMBIZ Annual Conference appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Your AI agent is only as good as your endpoint data
item.description: Every so often a flaw comes along that shows how fast the ground can shift under IT and security teams. PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was one of them. Details leaked before the planned disclosure, frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and PHP shipped fixes the next day. For many teams, though, the patch was the easy part. So what does it take to respond at that speed, and where should teams begin? What does governed autonomous IT look like in practice? Picture a loop. Software finds where a risk lives and ranks what matters most. It proposes a fix, then, inside limits people define, carries it out and checks that it worked. Routine, low-risk actions can run on their own. Higher-impact ones wait for a person to approve. A few are never handed over at all. Each step leaves a record that someone can review and reverse. What challenges do IT and security teams face today? Three problems keep coming up. The first is visibility. PHP2Shell reportedly sat undetected for more than a decade. For these two flaws, the fix was a version upgrade. The hard part was finding every copy of PHP, including copies bundled inside other software or extracted by hand onto Windows machines that never registered as installed applications. Then teams had to work out which copies the internet could reach and check for signs of earlier attack. An inventory built from a periodic snapshot can't answer those questions on the day they matter. The second is tool-hopping. Answering "where does this run, and can the internet reach it?" often means pivoting across an asset inventory, a vulnerability scanner and an external attack surface tool, each with its own view. Every hop adds delay. Every console is another chance to disagree with the last. The third is pace. Several security firms reported exploitation attempts before PHP released its fixes, and Cloudflare reported early attacks hours ahead of the patch. Frontier AI models helped find PHP2Shell, and in April Anthropic said its Claude Mythos Preview model had found thousands of previously unknown flaws across every major operating system and browser. With models like these in the picture, the old rhythm of disclose, patch and verify assumes a gap that keeps shrinking. Put an AI agent on top of stale, fragmented data and these problems don't go away. They scale. Why does real-time endpoint data make autonomy trustworthy? Endpoints are where work happens and where many attacks end up, so they are the ground truth for any decision about the estate. Four qualities make that data a sound foundation for autonomous action: Accuracy: Live data from the endpoints themselves, not a snapshot that was true last week. Speed: A short path from question to action, with no hopping between tools to reconcile answers. Control: Approvals and an audit trail, plus the ability to roll back, so any automated action can be reviewed and reversed. item.dc:creator: Tanium
item.content:encoded: Every so often a flaw comes along that shows how fast the ground can shift under IT and security teams. PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was one of them. Details leaked before the planned disclosure, frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and PHP shipped fixes the next day. For many teams, though, the patch was the easy part. So what does it take to respond at that speed, and where should teams begin? What does governed autonomous IT look like in practice? Picture a loop. Software finds where a risk lives and ranks what matters most. It proposes a fix, then, inside limits people define, carries it out and checks that it worked. Routine, low-risk actions can run on their own. Higher-impact ones wait for a person to approve. A few are never handed over at all. Each step leaves a record that someone can review and reverse. What challenges do IT and security teams face today? Three problems keep coming up. The first is visibility. PHP2Shell reportedly sat undetected for more than a decade. For these two flaws, the fix was a version upgrade. The hard part was finding every copy of PHP, including copies bundled inside other software or extracted by hand onto Windows machines that never registered as installed applications. Then teams had to work out which copies the internet could reach and check for signs of earlier attack. An inventory built from a periodic snapshot can't answer those questions on the day they matter. The second is tool-hopping. Answering "where does this run, and can the internet reach it?" often means pivoting across an asset inventory, a vulnerability scanner and an external attack surface tool, each with its own view. Every hop adds delay. Every console is another chance to disagree with the last. The third is pace. Several security firms reported exploitation attempts before PHP released its fixes, and Cloudflare reported early attacks hours ahead of the patch. Frontier AI models helped find PHP2Shell, and in April Anthropic said its Claude Mythos Preview model had found thousands of previously unknown flaws across every major operating system and browser. With models like these in the picture, the old rhythm of disclose, patch and verify assumes a gap that keeps shrinking. Put an AI agent on top of stale, fragmented data and these problems don't go away. They scale. Why does real-time endpoint data make autonomy trustworthy? Endpoints are where work happens and where many attacks end up, so they are the ground truth for any decision about the estate. Four qualities make that data a sound foundation for autonomous action: Accuracy: Live data from the endpoints themselves, not a snapshot that was true last week. Speed: A short path from question to action, with no hopping between tools to reconcile answers. Control: Approvals and an audit trail, plus the ability to roll back, so any automated action can be reviewed and reversed. Shared truth: IT operations, security and the system of record working from one view, rather than arguing over whose data is right. Matt Psencik, a threat research engineer at Tanium, put the visibility problem bluntly when PHP2Shell broke: "The installations that worry me most are the ones a security team doesn't know it owns." How does AI fit in? AI sits on both sides of this. It helped researchers find the PHP2Shell flaws, and attackers can use it to build exploits too. For defenders, AI works best as the operator and the interface: it takes a plain-language question, works out what to ask of the data, and proposes or carries out the next step. But it is only as good as the data it is grounded in. A fluent answer built on outdated information is still wrong, just more confidently so. Keeping people in the loop where stakes are high is what makes automation safe to expand. What are the practical first steps? Teams don't need to hand over the keys all at once. Start here: Find every copy: Don't stop at the installed-applications list. PHP2Shell showed that software bundled inside other products can slip past it. Compare your CMDB against what is really on your network and record exact versions. Draw the lines: Rank systems by what the internet can reach, then decide which response actions run automatically, which need approval and which are never delegated. Write it down before an agent needs it. Pilot one low-risk workflow: Pick something contained, build approval into it, and read the audit trail before widening the scope. Teams can also shorten the pilot with a partner. World Wide Technology (WWT), a Tanium partner, works with many large organizations on technology rollouts and hosts a Tanium lab in its Advanced Technology Center, where customers can test an approach hands-on before moving it into production. That second problem, the hopping, is the one Tanium Atlas was built to close. Instead of moving between consoles, an operator asks a plain-language question, gets an answer from live endpoint data, and acts on it inside limits the team sets, with every action recorded. Want to see how it works in practice? Click here and set up time to see Tanium in action. Sponsored by Tanium.

item.title: Less drama, more listening, but is Kozo Tashima the candidate to topple Infantino?
item.description: Japan FA honorary president is hoping a calmer approach that makes fewer unwelcome headlines for Fifa will be welcomed by football Not many remember Japan’s bid for the 2022 World Cup, when the country finished the race with only two of the final 22 votes. Kozo Tashima was involved then, and now the honorary president of the Japan Football Association is going it alone in the hope of ousting Gianni Infantino. The 68-year-old Tashima is an unlikely insurgent and an unlikely challenger to Infantino. He is, however, a familiar and respected figure in Asian and global football politics, and ready to take the Fifa presidency out of the headlines into a quieter era. Continue reading...

item.title: AWS distills its cloud into a local emulator that runs on your PC
item.description: AWS has released an emulator that kind-of-almost lets you use its cloud on a PC. As explained in the GitHub repository for the prosaically named “AWS Emulator,” the tool “is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint.” The emulator doesn’t replicate the whole AWS cloud, instead offering its APIs. “You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI),” the repo explains. Because those tests never touch the AWS cloud, the tool is free to use. AWS wrote the emulator in Rust, a choice that senior specialist solutions architect Daniel Abib wrote helps to ensure the tool “stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop.” The emulator tool doesn’t replicate the entire AWS cloud. Abib said it supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub . The Register found over 1,300 items on that page. While the tool lets developers test APIs, it doesn’t replicate anywhere near all the features of the Amazonian cloud. “It doesn’t evaluate IAM [Identity and Access Management] policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior,” Abib wrote, adding “How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature.” AWS publishes “fidelity scores” that detail how closely the emulator works on different AWS services. Amazon tries to achieve full fidelity, so the emulator produces the same results as AWS for valid API calls, and the same errors for invalid ones. Coding agents can also drive the Emulator, an option The Register mentions because AWS advises the easiest way to check if a project will work with the tool is to use the aws-emulator skill for AI coding agents. “With the skill, your agent finds the AWS operations and resources that your project depends on. It checks them against the fidelity tests and fidelity scores for the emulator. It then tells you which parts of your project you can rely on the emulator for, and which ones might behave differently from AWS,” according to AWS documentation. AWS has made the emulator available as an RPM or Debian package. Mac and PC users will need to run Docker and an image of the Emulator. “You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint,” Abib instructed. “When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ . You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.” “From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment.” The cloud colossus’s intent appears, as ever, to encourage more use of its cloud – in this case by satisfying developers their code will run w

item.title: SpaceX launches 2nd mystery mission for US Space Force in 6-day span (video, photos)
item.description: null SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California tonight (Nov. 11), the second such flight for the company in a six-day span. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:36 p.m. EST (8:36 p.m. local California time; 0136 GMT on Nov. 12), kicking off a mission called USSF-627. Vandenberg hosted a similar liftoff less than a week ago: On Nov. 6, a Falcon 9 sent the USSF-432 mission skyward from the site, which lies on California's gorgeous but often foggy central coast. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches the USSF-627 mission for the U.S. Space Force from California on Nov. 11, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) We don't know much about USSF-627 or USSF-432; both are classified. Some experts have speculated , however, that each mission launched a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military branch track potential targets around the world. SpaceX didn't reveal details about either USSF-627 or USSF-432, and the company ended the webcast of both launches shortly after the first stages of their Falcon 9 rockets came back to Earth . In both cases, that touchdown occurred about 8.5 minutes after liftoff on the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange of Vandenberg in the Pacific Ocean. It was the seventh mission for USSF-627's Falcon 9 booster, which carries the designation 1103. A Falcon 9 first stage rests on a SpaceX drone ship shortly after launching the USSF-627 mission on Nov. 11, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) Previous Booster 1103 missions NROL-179 | SDA-T1TL-E | SDA-T1TL-A | 3 Starlink missions USSF-627 was the 120th Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the rocket's 15th national-security flight of the year to date. Eighty-five of the 120 flights have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink broadband constellation in low Earth orbit , which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites. The Falcon 9 is not on a record-breaking cadence this year. In 2025, the rocket flew a whopping 165 missions , and 122 of them were Starlink flights.

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 12 – Moon, Venus and Spica Meet
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 12 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Moon, Venus and Spica Meet Explanation: Not all those who wander are lost. A night sky example is that planets wander, and in fact the very word “planet” comes from “wandering star” in Greek. As planets shift relative to fixed stars , they may appear from our perspective to get closer to other astronomical objects. Such meetings are called conjunctions . They don’t happen by chance, but follow the precise laws of celestial mechanics . This peaceful image , captured in Poland , shows the crescent Moon above the Tatra Mountains , and bright Venus close by, a little lower in the horizon. The bright star to the left of Venus is Spica in the constellation of Virgo , the Maiden. Spica is one of the brightest stars in the sky, only about 250 light-years away. It was found in 1890 that Spica is a binary star: two massive blue stars orbiting each other every 4 days. But earlier this year it was reported that Spica, the current companion of wandering Venus, is actually a triple system . Tomorrow’s picture: what’s next? Date November 12, 2026 Credit & Copyright Włodzimierz Bubak Authors & editors: Cecilia Chirenti, Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Keighley Rockcliffe A service of: ASD at NASA / GSFC , NASA Science Activation & Michigan Tech. item.title: Olumide Oworu Declares House of Representatives Bid for Surulere Constituency 1 in 2027
item.description: Olumide Oworu has declared his candidacy for the Federal House of Representatives to represent Surulere Constituency 1 in 2027. Photo Credit: Olumide Oworu/Instagram Actor and media personality Olumide Oworu has declared his intention to contest for the Federal House of Representatives seat for Surulere Constituency 1 in the 2027 general elections. He will be running under the platform of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM). Olumide, who grew up in Surulere, Lagos, has a long-standing connection to the constituency. He began his acting career as a child, appearing in television productions such as Everyday People , before gaining wider recognition for his role in The Johnsons and other Nigerian film and television projects. This is his second attempt to enter legislative politics. In 2023, he declared his intention to contest for a seat in the Lagos State House of Assembly under the Labour Party. However, administrative challenges prevented his name from appearing on the final ballot. Olumide Oworu’s official campaign poster for the House of Representatives seat representing Surulere Constituency 1 under the Allied Peoples Movement. Photo Credit: Olumide Oworu/Instagram Reflecting on that experience in his candidacy announcement on Instagram, Olumide said the support he received from young people in Surulere had strengthened his belief in their readiness for more active participation in governance. “Despite the administrative hurdles that left our names off the final ballot, your resilience showed me that our vision was never a passing phase. Instead, it was the beginning of something much more significant,” he wrote. Explaining his decision to contest again, this time for a seat in the House of Representatives, he added: “We cannot afford to sit on the sidelines while our future is decided by a political class that won’t have to live with the consequences of today’s choices.” His campaign has highlighted issues including gaps in public services, community infrastructure and the participation of young Nigerians in policy decisions. Announcing his candidacy, he said he looked forward to continued support as he and his supporters worked towards what he described as a mission to “Reset Nigeria”. Olumide Oworu is contesting for a legislative seat in Surulere Constituency 1 under the APM platform. Photo Credit: Olumide Oworu/Instagram The post Olumide Oworu Declares House of Representatives Bid for Surulere Constituency 1 in 2027 appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: NASA kick-starts a fresh push to bring Mars samples home
item.description: null A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet. NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth. The PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG). Here's the PSRA strategy: Develop impartial recommendations for retrieving the Martian samples collected by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover and deliver them to Earth Assess proposed mission requirements Review prior lessons learned Evaluate current capabilities and acquisition options Morgan noted that there will be a PSRA strategy team kickoff in January 2027 with a final report due in winter 2027-2028. Pick-me-ups The backdrop to the PSRA activity is that there's one busy rover already on the Red Planet snagging and bagging samples. NASA's Perseverance Mars rover remains on the prowl within Jezero Crater following its touchdown in February 2021. That car-sized robot has been grabbing select specimens from across the area and gingerly dropping the sealed pick-me-ups on the surface of Mars , as well as stuffing them inside the rover itself. Those collectibles may well hold signs of past life on the enigmatic, dusty and foreboding Red Planet. NASA and the European Space Agency have for years been intently plotting out plans to send future spacecraft to Mars and haul those Perseverance-plucked bits, pieces, and sniffs of atmosphere to Earth for rigorous inspection here on Earth using state-of-the-art equipment. This photomontage shows each of the sample tubes deposited by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover at the Three Forks sample depot, as viewed by the WATSON camera on the end of the rover's robotic arm. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS) Sticker shock However, over the years, multiple reviews of a NASA Mars Sample Return (MSR) project by independent groups have reported sticker shock findings. Indeed, one last price tag came in at about $11 billion, with samples being returned to Earth in 2040. That finding was deemed by NASA itself as too costly and not doable within an acceptable time frame. Yet another appraisal group ended up finding it feasible to return Mars samples as early as 2035 for a less costly ship and shoot cost of some $8 billion. How the PSRA review deals with MSR cost and a multitude of other concerns is in the to-be-determined column. Why samples now? In the first place, why are samples from Mars delivered by robotic means? item.dc:creator: Leonard David
item.content:encoded: null A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet. NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth. The PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG). Here's the PSRA strategy: Develop impartial recommendations for retrieving the Martian samples collected by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover and deliver them to Earth Assess proposed mission requirements Review prior lessons learned Evaluate current capabilities and acquisition options Morgan noted that there will be a PSRA strategy team kickoff in January 2027 with a final report due in winter 2027-2028. Pick-me-ups The backdrop to the PSRA activity is that there's one busy rover already on the Red Planet snagging and bagging samples. NASA's Perseverance Mars rover remains on the prowl within Jezero Crater following its touchdown in February 2021. That car-sized robot has been grabbing select specimens from across the area and gingerly dropping the sealed pick-me-ups on the surface of Mars , as well as stuffing them inside the rover itself. Those collectibles may well hold signs of past life on the enigmatic, dusty and foreboding Red Planet. NASA and the European Space Agency have for years been intently plotting out plans to send future spacecraft to Mars and haul those Perseverance-plucked bits, pieces, and sniffs of atmosphere to Earth for rigorous inspection here on Earth using state-of-the-art equipment. This photomontage shows each of the sample tubes deposited by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover at the Three Forks sample depot, as viewed by the WATSON camera on the end of the rover's robotic arm. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS) Sticker shock However, over the years, multiple reviews of a NASA Mars Sample Return (MSR) project by independent groups have reported sticker shock findings. Indeed, one last price tag came in at about $11 billion, with samples being returned to Earth in 2040. That finding was deemed by NASA itself as too costly and not doable within an acceptable time frame. Yet another appraisal group ended up finding it feasible to return Mars samples as early as 2035 for a less costly ship and shoot cost of some $8 billion. How the PSRA review deals with MSR cost and a multitude of other concerns is in the to-be-determined column. Why samples now? In the first place, why are samples from Mars delivered by robotic means? Why not let a human expedition bring back the goods? Also speaking at MEPAG was Bruce Jakosky of the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder and Department of Earth and Space Sciences at the University of Washington. Jakosky called for an integrated approach to planning human missions to Mars. He highlighted recommendations stemming from a workshop in which he participated, held last May and organized by Explore Mars, Inc. That report focused on the impact of MSR on reducing risk for human missions, rather than focusing on the science, Jakosky told Space.com. "The purpose is to understand the risk to astronauts and to hardware. The risk includes that from compounds that are present in the soil that are hazardous to astronauts if breathed in," said Jakosky. "This includes perchlorates and chloromethanes that have been identified already, and detection of other species that might be present. It also includes dust that can be breathed in by astronauts and that can affect hardware wear and tear," he said. During the MEPAG gathering, Jakosky flagged the importance of returning samples prior to human missions to Mars, such as: Identify and characterize known hazardous chemicals to ensure astronaut safety (e.g., perchlorates and chloromethanes), and look for possible additional hazardous chemicals Characterize very fine dust particles that could cause respiratory issues in astronauts Characterize dust and regolith properties for spacesuit design and wear patterns Search in advance of the arrival of humans for evidence of extant life that could interact with terrestrial life Enhance astronaut effectiveness on the surface and science return from human missions by providing initial context and analysis Demonstrate successful round-trip to Mars Demonstrate successful round-trip travel, including entry, descent, landing and ascent from the surface of Mars. Demonstrate implementation of planetary protection protocols. While human missions would not use the same approaches, what we learn from doing these would make the approach for humans much easier to plan and implement. China's program Diagram of China's proposed Tianwen 3 Mars sample return mission. (Image credit: The University of Hong Kong/Zengqian Hou, et al.) Yet one more forcing factor for NASA in yet another relook at MSR is that China is making progress on its Tianwen-3 Mars Sample Return mission. According to the China National Space Administration, the country's Tianwen-3 probe will have a lander, an ascender, a service capsule, an orbiter, and an Earth reentry module. Tianwen-3 appears on track getting the trek underway around 2028 on two Long March-5 heavy-lift carrier rockets from the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China's southernmost island province of Hainan. China's Tianwen-3 mission is dedicated to bring back to Earth roughly 500 grams of Red Planet collectibles in 2031.

item.title: We can't see Fast Radio Bursts but we can now hear them thanks to a Finnish Cathedral
item.description:
Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston. 

Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound. Fast radio bursts, or FRBs , are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star. Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space. Catching one takes luck, as a telescope has to be pointed at the right patch of sky at the right moment. That changed with CHIME (the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) in British Columbia. With a very wide field of view and a supercomputer to process its data, CHIME more than quadrupled the number of known FRBs in its first year of operation alone. Between 2018 and 2023, CHIME recorded 4,539 bursts from 3,641 sources. As pulses of radio waves, our eyes haven't evolved to see FRBs, nor can we hear them as they aren't sound waves. The result is a range of tones, with distant FRBs humming, rumbling, popping, and whistling. The signals are old by any human measure. According to a description on Melchior's website , the youngest in the work are about 50 million years old, and the oldest are about 8 to 9 billion years old. Saxton, NRAO/AUI/NSF)) Physics also plays a role in what is heard. item.dc:creator: Sharmila Kuthunur
item.content:encoded:
Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston. 

Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound. Fast radio bursts, or FRBs , are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star. Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space. Catching one takes luck, as a telescope has to be pointed at the right patch of sky at the right moment. That changed with CHIME (the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) in British Columbia. With a very wide field of view and a supercomputer to process its data, CHIME more than quadrupled the number of known FRBs in its first year of operation alone. Between 2018 and 2023, CHIME recorded 4,539 bursts from 3,641 sources. As pulses of radio waves, our eyes haven't evolved to see FRBs, nor can we hear them as they aren't sound waves. Well, not until now. "Artist and composer Andrew Melchior turned all of the CHIME bursts into sound for "The Logos," an installation that has played daily at Oulu Cathedral in Finland since early April and is scheduled to run through the end of the year. Melchior and Kiyoshi Masui, an associate professor of physics at MIT, "sonified" the bursts, translating data into acoustics so that human ears can hear them. The structure of each real signal is mapped to varying musical pitches and played through 12 loudspeakers spread throughout the cathedral. The result is a range of tones, with distant FRBs humming, rumbling, popping, and whistling. The signals are old by any human measure. According to a description on Melchior's website , the youngest in the work are about 50 million years old, and the oldest are about 8 to 9 billion years old. An animation shows the random appearance of fast radio bursts (FRBs) across the sky (Image credit: NRAO Outreach/T. Jarrett (IPAC/Caltech); B. Saxton, NRAO/AUI/NSF)) Physics also plays a role in what is heard. Each burst arrives with its high frequencies first and sweeps downward, stretched by its journey through intergalactic gas, "and you can hear that dispersion as it falls from the dome," Melchior told Space.com by email. Since their discovery in 2007, the bursts are also still yielding discoveries. Last month, astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant FRB yet, one that went off when the universe was only about 3 billion years old. The galaxy, a small, young, star-forming dwarf, was far smaller than expected. That makes it harder to square with the theory that FRBs come from merging neutron stars, researchers say, which would take billions of years to occur. This fits better with a second theory, in which a young, highly magnetic neutron star called a magnetar produces the burst soon after a massive star explodes, according to NASA . An illustration of a magnetar launching a FRB (Image credit: Robert Lea (created with Canva)) Back on Earth, an upcoming event at Oulu Cathedral offers a more immediate encounter with the bursts. On Nov. 21, 30 singers will stand among the audience and "sing back to the sky in Finnish" while Melchior plays the bursts live from a keyboard, he told Space.com by email. "The fast flashes will echo as snare-like beats bouncing through the cathedral," Masui said in a previous MIT statement . "It should feel rich and layered, while also revealing something real about how these signals travel across billions of years of cosmic space before reaching Earth."

item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 11, 1966: NASA launches Gemini 12 mission with astronaut icons Buzz Aldrin and Jim Lovell aboard
item.description: null On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon. Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin . NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks. Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day. The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program . Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11 , and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13 . The Gemini 12 astronauts James Lovell and Edwin Aldrin lifted off aboard a Titan launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center on November 11, 1966, an hour and a half after their Agena target vehicle was orbited by an Atlas rocket. (Image credit: NASA/MSFC) Why it mattered Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon. It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11. "This approach became so successful, underwater training has become the primary spacewalk training method used by the United State, Russia and China," NASA officials said in a mission overview . "Today, NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston is large enough to include mockups of major sections of the International Space Station . As such, it is the largest indoor body of water in the world, with 6.2 million gallons of water." Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11. "This approach became so successful, underwater training has become the primary spacewalk training method used by the United State, Russia and China," NASA officials said in a mission overview . "Today, NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston is large enough to include mockups of major sections of the International Space Station . As such, it is the largest indoor body of water in the world, with 6.2 million gallons of water." Astronaut Buzz Aldrin practices spacewalking tasks for Gemini 12 in an underwater mockup of his spacecraft in 1966. NASA The Gemini 12 astronauts walk out to their launch pad with signs on their back denoting "THE END" of the Gemini program. NASA/MSFC NASA The Agena docking target for Gemini 12 launched into orbit just over 90 minutes ahead of Lovell (the mission commander) and Aldrin. Aldrin ended up using a sextant to help Lovell rendevous with the agena after they lost radar lock within 74 miles of the vehicle. During his spacewalks, Aldrin installed handrails, used foot restraints and other tools that have since become routine on spacewalks in orbit. They also tested tools and techniques that Aldrin and other moonwalks would use on the moon . Gemini 12 also tested a computer-controlled reentry technique when it returned to Earth on Nov. 15, landing Lovell and Aldrin just 3 miles from their target near their recovery ship the USS Wasp in the Atlantic Ocean, about 600 miles east of Cape Canaveral. item.title: Seven New Tracks From Rema? E-Mortal Boy (EMB) Is Coming Next Week
item.description: Rema announces his upcoming 7-track EP, E-Mortal Boy (EMB), scheduled for release on 20 November 2026. Photo Credit: Rema/Instagram Rema is getting ready to give fans a fresh body of music! The Nigerian singer has officially announced that his new seven-track EP, E-Mortal Boy ( EMB ), will be released next Friday, 20 November 2026. It’s been a little while since his last EP, so there’s plenty of reason for fans to be curious about what he has been working on. The 26-year-old Benin City star first introduced himself to listeners with his self-titled debut EP in 2019, released under Mavin Records and Jonzing World. Since then, he’s built an impressive catalogue, moving between different sounds while taking his music to audiences around the world. His 2022 debut album, Rave & Roses, marked a major turning point in his career, followed by the return to a more raw Afrobeats sound on the 2023 EP Ravage. In 2024, he switched things up again with HEIS , his high-intensity sophomore album, which earned him further international attention. Rema preparing for the release of his new EP E-Mortal Boy following his singles TEA and Oh No. Photo Credit: Rema/Instagram Now, Rema is opening another chapter with E-Mortal Boy (EMB). The project already has two singles to introduce its sound: “ Oh No ” and the fan-favourite “ TEA “. Both tracks give listeners an early taste of the music surrounding the new release, although Rema is keeping the rest of the project under wraps for now. The full tracklist and details of any featured artists have yet to be revealed. With seven tracks, E-Mortal Boy (EMB) will be Rema’s first EP since Ravage and his latest project following HEIS . The singer is set to release it on digital streaming platforms on 20 November, giving fans a new collection to get into as he continues to build on an already eventful musical journey. The post Seven New Tracks From Rema? E-Mortal Boy (EMB) Is Coming Next Week appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Awar Odhiang Named Model of the Year at The Fashion Awards 2026
item.description: Awar Odhiang featured in Vogue wearing a floral printed dress and sculpted oversized rose headpiece. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Remember the model who turned the finale of Matthieu Blazy ‘s first Chanel show into one of the most talked-about runway moments of 2025? That was Awar Odhiang, and she has another major reason to celebrate. The South Sudanese-Canadian model has been named Model of the Year at The Fashion Awards 2026. The 25-year-old will receive the honour at London’s Royal Albert Hall on 30 November. Born in a refugee camp in Ethiopia and raised in Canada, Awar’s journey to the international fashion scene has taken her from being discovered in Alberta to walking some of the world’s biggest runways. She is now represented by major modelling agencies across London, Milan, Paris and New York. Awar Odhiang walking the red carpet at the 2026 Met Gala in New York City. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Her runway résumé includes shows for Prada, Versace, Miu Miu, Saint Laurent and Jacquemus, but it was her appearance at Chanel’s Spring/Summer 2026 show in October 2025 that introduced her to an even wider audience. Closing Matthieu Blazy’s first collection for the fashion house, Awar wore the show’s bridal look, featuring an oversized white shirt and a voluminous, colourful feathered skirt. But it was what happened at the finale that captured everyone’s attention. As the models gathered for their final walk, Awar broke formation, smiling, clapping and twirling in her skirt. When Blazy appeared, she ran towards him and embraced him. The spontaneous moment quickly went viral, with fashion fans celebrating the joy she brought to the runway. It was also a historic appearance: Awar became only the third Black woman to close a Chanel show in the house’s 115-year history, after Alek Wek and Adut Akech. Model of the Year 2026 winner Awar Odhiang backstage at the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Since then, her career has continued to gather pace. Awar has appeared on eight international magazine covers this year and fronted campaigns for Chanel, Chloé, Louis Vuitton, Saint Laurent, Loro Piana and H&M. She has also used her growing platform to speak up for greater representation and inclusion of Black models in the luxury fashion industry. Awar Odhiang in Daniel Roseberry’s Schiaparelli Spring 2026 Haute Couture collection in Paris. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Her Model of the Year recognition celebrates a remarkable year of runway, editorial and campaign work, as well as the influence she continues to have beyond the catwalk. On 30 November, she’ll take that recognition to the Royal Albert Hall, adding another milestone to a career that is still unfolding. Awar Odhiang wearing a tailored blazer during international fashion week. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Awar Odhiang attending the 2026 Met Gala in custom Chanel by Matthieu Blazy. item.title: Andy Weir's 'Exoplanet' just landed on Audible, but what actually makes an exoplanet habitable?
item.description: null Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead. This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo . Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable? Learning from the stars An artist's concept illustrates a young, red dwarf star surrounded by three planets. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock. For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it. Using a technique called spectroscopy , astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance. Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere. A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise. Hostile stars Black holes are bad news for life, but living stars provide just as many problems. (Image credit: Audible) A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere . Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star. item.dc:creator: Alix Freckelton
item.content:encoded: null Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead. This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo . Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable? Learning from the stars An artist's concept illustrates a young, red dwarf star surrounded by three planets. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock. For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it. Using a technique called spectroscopy , astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance. Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere. A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise. Hostile stars Black holes are bad news for life, but living stars provide just as many problems. (Image credit: Audible) A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere . Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star. The age of a star matters too. Young stars tend to be more active, with radiation that could erode a planet’s atmosphere over time. Meanwhile, as stars age and evolve, their changing luminosities can drastically alter the conditions a planet experiences. For the stranded crew in “Exoplanet”, understanding the star overhead may therefore be as important as knowing the landscape beneath their feet. Is the air breathable? NASA illustration of Kepler-186f, the first Earth-size planet to be discovered in a habitable zone. (Image credit: NASA Ames/SETI Institute/JPL-CalTech via Wikimedia Commons) Even if a planet has survived all the complications we’ve just thrown at it, there’s still a rather important question: could we actually breathe the air? In "Exoplanet", one crew member discovers that the planet’s atmosphere contains enough oxygen for him to breathe without his spacesuit. On Earth, oxygen makes up around 21% of our atmosphere. However, finding a similar percentage on another planet wouldn’t automatically mean the air is safe to breathe. Atmospheric pressure matters just as much . At high altitudes on Earth, the oxygen percentage remains the same, but the lower pressure means less oxygen is available to our lungs. Oxygen isn’t the only concern, either. The fictional planet’s volcanic landscape releases gases such as sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide, both of which are hazardous at high concentrations. Even an oxygen-rich atmosphere could still be lethal. Searching for life An artist illustration of exoplanet K2-18b, an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. (Image credit: Hubble, M. Kornmesser via Wikimedia commons) But what if you don't just need to know if a planet is habitable? What if you need to know if something already lives there? Before the Wild Blue Yonder arrived at the planet, probes detected dimethyl sulfide, a molecule we associate with biological activity on Earth . This is a beautifully timely detail, as this very molecule has been at the heart of a scientific debate about one of the most intriguing exoplanets discovered so far. Astronomers have investigated possible signs of dimethyl sulfide in the atmosphere of K2-18 b , an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. However, both the detection itself and the biological interpretation remain heavily disputed . Astronomers can study the starlight that filters through exoplanet atmospheres, searching for signatures of molecules that may be signs of life. (Image credit: NASA, ESA and A. Feild (STScI)) The challenge is that detecting a single molecule isn’t definitive evidence of life. Its presence can be influenced by factors other than biology, like atmospheric chemistry and stellar radiation. Understanding whether such a molecule could actually indicate life means studying not just the planet’s atmosphere, but also the radiation it receives from its star. More than Earth Mark 2 (Image credit: Audible) Astronomers have discovered thousands of exoplanets. Understanding whether any could support life is, however, an extraordinary challenge. The distance between the planet and the star might give us a good clue, but its atmosphere, geology, and stellar environment are all interconnected in determining whether life could survive. For the unfortunate crew of the Wild Blue Yonder, those distinctions could mean the difference between survival and utter disaster. We might one day identify a planet with Earth-like temperatures, liquid water, and abundant oxygen. But even then, there’s still a huge gap dividing a potentially habitable planet from one where we could safely remove our helmets. "Exoplanet" is available now exclusively from Audible. It is free for members of its subscription tiers or available to purchase separately. One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary , The Martian ), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo.
