item.title: The Francophone African Music Industries Fair (SIMA) announces its 3rd Edition in Republic of Benin | November 12th – 13th
item.description: The Francophone African Music Industries Fair (SIMA) announces the third edition of the event, taking place on November 12–13, 2026, in Cotonou, Republic of Benin. Following its previous edition, which brought together more than 6,700 participants and over 3,000 industry professionals, this pan-African gathering dedicated to the cultural and creative industries returns with a clear ambition: African Music: From the Stage to Global Influence. SIMA 2026 is supported by major institutional and private-sector partners, including the Ministry of Culture, Arts and Heritage of Benin,the Ministry of Tourism and Foreign Trade of Benin,the Embassy of France in Côte d’Ivoire,the BOAD Foundation, as well as SACEM, Sony Music and Warner Music Africa. These partnerships reflect the growing interest in the development and structuring of Africa’s cultural and creative industries. For the second consecutive year, Benin will host SIMA, in line with the country’s broader efforts to strengthen the role of the cultural and creative industries in the structural transformation of its economy and to enhance its cultural influence at both regional and international levels. Co-founded in 2022 by cultural entrepreneur Mamby Diomandé and artist and producer Pit Baccardi , SIMA has established itself as a platform dedicated to structuring, connecting and developing Africa’s creative ecosystems. By placing music at the heart of a broader reflection on the transformation of culture and the creative industries, SIMA also seeks to address the technological shifts reshaping the sector—from artificial intelligence to new ways of creating, distributing and consuming content. Co-founded in 2022 by cultural entrepreneur Mamby Diomandé and artist and producer Pit Baccardi , SIMA has established itself as a platform dedicated to structuring, connecting and developing Africa’s creative ecosystems. By placing music at the heart of a broader reflection on the transformation of culture and the creative industries, SIMA also seeks to address the technological shifts reshaping the sector—from artificial intelligence to new ways of creating, distributing and consuming content. Our challenge now is to transform this influence into sustainable economic power. SIMA aims to build connections between creators, investors, institutions and markets so that the international visibility of our talents translates into measurable data, content monetization, economic opportunities, jobs and value creation for the continent.” Mamby Diomandé , Co-Founder of SIMA Three Priorities for Turning Creativity into Economic Power To address the challenges of a rapidly evolving global market, SIMA 2026 will structure its programme around three key priorities. The first focuses on competitiveness and internationalization, with the aim of strengthening the economic performance of industry stakeholders and facilitating the international export of African talent. The second emphasizes cross-sector collaboration, bringing music closer to fashion, film, tourism, sports and other creative industries in order to unlock new revenue opportunities. The third focuses on public policy, intellectual property and regulatory frameworks, with the ambition of developing concrete recommendations and strengthening the mechanisms that will enable the sector to better capture the value it generates. Beyond discussions and professional exchanges, SIMA aims to make creativity a genuine driver of connection across the ecosystem. Through its artist residency, live sessions and immersive formats, the event encourages collaboration between artists, producers, industry professionals and international stakeholders, while creating bridges between African markets and the international creative economy. A Week at the Crossroads of Creativity, Business and Influence From November 7–11, 2026, SIMA Lab. Music will bring together artists and beatmakers from across the continent for an artistic residency designed to produce a collaborative EP, with distribution by an international major label under consideration. On November 12–13, 2026, the professional days and panels will bring together key players from the music ecosystem to explore major issues shaping the future of the industry, including artificial intelligence, copyright, mobility, financing and emerging market opportunities. At the intersection of the cultural and sports industries, a dedicated session will also explore the convergence between football and music, two powerful drivers of influence across the continent, with the participation of sports executives and opinion leaders. As part of this dynamic, Makaya, SIMA’s showcase platform dedicated to discovering new talent, will spotlight emerging artists from Togo, Kenya, Madagascar and other African countries, providing a new stage for the next generation of talent. The programme will also feature the presentation of the Hamed Bakayoko Award, an honorary distinction recognizing the commitment of a patron to the development of Africa’s cultural and creative industries. On November 14, 2026, SIMA will extend the experience through a tourism circuit organized in collaboration with Benin Tourism, inviting artists, professionals and international guests to discover the heritage and iconic sites of Benin. This immersive experience will give participants an opportunity to gain a deeper understanding of the host country’s cultural, historical and tourism assets, while extending networking and exchanges beyond the professional framework of the event. As a true platform for connecting the cultural and creative industries, SIMA provides ecosystem stakeholders with a space to create, learn, share, connect and foster new collaborations, while contributing to discussions on the cultural, economic and technological issues shaping Africa’s creative industries and their international reach. item.title: Ayra Starr Joins Coachella 2027 Lineup Alongside SZA, Dua Lipa & More
item.description: Ayra Starr returns with her third studio album, Starrgirl. Ayra Starr is taking her global run to another big stage! The Nigerian singer has been named among the performers at Coachella 2027, adding another major festival appearance to her growing list of international milestones. The Beninese-born singer, who rose to prominence as one of Afrobeats’ leading voices after joining Mavin Records, is set to perform on both weekends of the festival, Sunday, April 11, and Sunday, April 18, 2027. Coachella will take place at the Empire Polo Club in Indio, California. It’s been a big year for Ayra, with her third studio album, Starrgirl, adding to an already exciting run. Fans heading to the festival can look forward to hearing songs from the project, including “ Tornado ” and “ Midnight in New York “, as well as her collaboration “ Gimme Dat “. There’s also room for crowd favourites such as “ Rush “, “ Commas ” and “ Heaven Baby “. Ayra shares the Sunday bill with headliner SZA , alongside Victoria Monét , Jorja Smith , Becky G and Don Toliver . The wider festival, running from April 9 to 11 and April 16 to 18, will also feature headliners Dua Lipa and Tame Impala , with Madonna set for a special appearance in the dance tent. Her Coachella booking follows another major moment in London, where she performed at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium as part of the NFL International Games halftime show, becoming the first African artist to headline the show. And there’s even more for fans to look forward to. Ayra has announced her 20-city Starrgirl World Tour , which will take her across Europe and North America in early 2027 before she heads to the California desert for Coachella. What a year ahead for the Starr girl. The official Coachella 2027 lineup featuring Nigerian singer Ayra Starr alongside headliners Dua Lipa, Tame Impala, and SZA at the Empire Polo Club in Indio, California. item.title: Did comets bring building blocks of life to Earth? Scientists aren't so sure anymore
item.description: The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet. Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth . Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space? New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth. "Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement . Stripping the romance from the Earth's turbulent past Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system ’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets. For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely. Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves. In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS . An artist’s impression of a comet crashing into the early Earth (Image credit: Scarlett White) The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second). Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. Even on the rare occasions that the complex organic molecules survived, they were usually not in great enough abundance to provide any meaningful prebiotic chemistry. item.dc:creator: Keith Cooper
item.content:encoded: The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet. Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth . Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space? New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth. "Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement . Stripping the romance from the Earth's turbulent past Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system ’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets. For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely. Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves. In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS . An artist’s impression of a comet crashing into the early Earth (Image credit: Scarlett White) The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second). Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. Even on the rare occasions that the complex organic molecules survived, they were usually not in great enough abundance to provide any meaningful prebiotic chemistry. "It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way, but it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke." Maybe life on Earth is a fluke It is not yet known if the origin of life on Earth was a fluke, or whether life is plentiful in the universe, so a fluke occurrence could still have been a trigger for life on our planet. However, researchers are coming around to alternatives, either that all the pre-biotic chemistry that resulted in life took place on Earth without requiring material from space, or asteroids instead brought those important molecules to Earth. Scientists have found asteroids to be rich in those molecules – for example, the sample of material brought back by the OSIRIS-REx mission from the near-Earth asteroid Bennu contained all the building blocks of RNA. However, other planets could have plausibly benefitted from comet impacts. The simulations showed that complex organic molecules in comets would stand a slightly better chance of surviving impacts on Mars , because of the Red Planet’s thinner atmosphere and lower gravity. "This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but it suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative is that it didn’t happen on either planet." The 7 planets circling the star TRAPPIST-1, 3 of which might be able to keep liquid water on its surface. (Image credit: R. Hurt/T. Pyle/NASA) More intriguing are the possibilities on exoplanets, specifically the peas-in-a-pod multi-planet systems around red dwarf stars such as TRAPPIST-1 , where all the planets are bunched up close. In 2023 Anslow wrote a research paper describing how comets could gravitationally bounce from one planet to the next, losing velocity in the process so that when they crash into one of the planets, they impact is not so severe and complex organic molecules might have a chance to survive. The team's research was published on 28 October in Scientific Reports .

item.title: 'There's tremendous demand': Rocket Lab raises price of Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million
item.description: null The coming launch bottleneck has ramped up demand for a rocket that has yet to leave the ground. Rocket Lab announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that it recently raised the price of a Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million — an increase of more than 25%, for a ride on a rocket that's set to debut in 2027. "Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said on Monday during the company's third-quarter earnings call. "We saw a pent-up launch market on the horizon, and rather than provide early discounted launches, we set out to deliver a rocket into an environment with extreme demand at full price or higher." Rocket Lab is best known for Electron , a workhorse small-satellite launcher that debuted in 2017 and now has 90 orbital missions under its belt. The 59-foot-tall (18 meters) expendable rocket and can haul 660 pounds (300 kilograms) to low Earth orbit (LEO). Neutron is the company's entry into the medium-lift market. It features a reusable first stage, stands 141 feet (43 m) tall and can carry 14.3 tons (13 metric tons) of payload to LEO. Rocket Lab announced Neutron back in 2021 and first targeted a 2024 debut for the vehicle. But various problems have cropped up over the years, pushing things back. Last month, for example, Rocket Lab announced that it was delaying the first Neutron flight from late 2026 into 2027 due to a manufacturing issue (which it says is now under control). Such setbacks have not dampened demand for Neutron's services, however. During Monday's call, Beck revealed that Rocket Lab booked eight Neutron launches during the third quarter of 2026, which ran from July 1 through Sept. 30. The contracts for those eight flights are worth "a total of roughly 515 million, including multiple missions on a new escalated base price of $70 million," Beck said. Neutron's first 16 launches are now sold out, he added, and bookings from here on will be for flights in the 2030s. "The demand is a function of both a tightening global launch supply and our customers' confidence that Rocket Lab is the right partner to break the world's launch bottleneck," Beck said. Artist's illustration of Neutron's first stage coming down for a landing on a ship at sea. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) That bottleneck is coming in 2028 or so, when SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 rocket . For some perspective, and comparison with Neutron: SpaceX currently charges $74 million for each Falcon 9 launch. The rocket has a reusable first stage and can carry about 25 tons (22.7 metric tons) to LEO. The medium lifter has been the world's most prolific rocket for the past few years. In 2025, for example, it flew 165 times — roughly the same number of orbital missions as all other launchers in the world combined. And all 165 of those flights were successful. item.dc:creator: Mike Wall
item.content:encoded: null The coming launch bottleneck has ramped up demand for a rocket that has yet to leave the ground. Rocket Lab announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that it recently raised the price of a Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million — an increase of more than 25%, for a ride on a rocket that's set to debut in 2027. "We saw a pent-up launch market on the horizon, and rather than provide early discounted launches, we set out to deliver a rocket into an environment with extreme demand at full price or higher." Rocket Lab is best known for Electron , a workhorse small-satellite launcher that debuted in 2017 and now has 90 orbital missions under its belt. The 59-foot-tall (18 meters) expendable rocket and can haul 660 pounds (300 kilograms) to low Earth orbit (LEO). Neutron is the company's entry into the medium-lift market. It features a reusable first stage, stands 141 feet (43 m) tall and can carry 14.3 tons (13 metric tons) of payload to LEO. Rocket Lab announced Neutron back in 2021 and first targeted a 2024 debut for the vehicle. But various problems have cropped up over the years, pushing things back. Last month, for example, Rocket Lab announced that it was delaying the first Neutron flight from late 2026 into 2027 due to a manufacturing issue (which it says is now under control). Such setbacks have not dampened demand for Neutron's services, however. During Monday's call, Beck revealed that Rocket Lab booked eight Neutron launches during the third quarter of 2026, which ran from July 1 through Sept. 30. The contracts for those eight flights are worth "a total of roughly 515 million, including multiple missions on a new escalated base price of $70 million," Beck said. Neutron's first 16 launches are now sold out, he added, and bookings from here on will be for flights in the 2030s. "The demand is a function of both a tightening global launch supply and our customers' confidence that Rocket Lab is the right partner to break the world's launch bottleneck," Beck said. Artist's illustration of Neutron's first stage coming down for a landing on a ship at sea. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) That bottleneck is coming in 2028 or so, when SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 rocket . For some perspective, and comparison with Neutron: SpaceX currently charges $74 million for each Falcon 9 launch. The rocket has a reusable first stage and can carry about 25 tons (22.7 metric tons) to LEO. The medium lifter has been the world's most prolific rocket for the past few years. In 2025, for example, it flew 165 times — roughly the same number of orbital missions as all other launchers in the world combined. And all 165 of those flights were successful. But SpaceX is phasing out the Falcon 9 — and its heavy-lift cousin, the Falcon Heavy — nonetheless, shifting all launch work over to its fully reusable Starship megarocket, which can haul more than 100 tons to LEO. There's a real worry among folks in the space community that this massive payload capacity won't be available to them for a while. SpaceX has made it pretty clear that early Starship operations will be geared toward internal priorities — specifically, the buildout of SpaceX's Starlink V3 broadband network and its Starmind AI data-center constellation. These will be very big jobs, even for the most powerful rocket ever built. For example, the Starlink V3 megaconstellation will consist of about 100,000 satellites , according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk . Starship can carry about 60 of these spacecraft to LEO per launch, so just building out the constellation will require about 1,700 liftoffs. The numbers for Starmind will be even more mind-boggling, for SpaceX wants that constellation to eventually harbor a million satellites . The coming launch bottleneck should increase demand for Electron as well as Neutron, Beck said during Monday's call. After all, many small-satellite operators have launched with SpaceX over the years, booking spots on Falcon 9 "rideshare" flights . And those opportunities are now drying up. "The next logical alternative is of course an Electron, so we see tremendous traction there," Beck said.

item.title: Omotunde’s 5 Days in South Korea: Exploring LG’s World of Innovation & Discovering the Best of Korean Culture
item.description: Hello BNers, Omotunde here. From exploring futuristic smart homes and AI-powered manufacturing facilities to tasting Korean street food, discovering Seoul, and experiencing the country’s rich culture, my 5-day South Korea adventure with LG Electronics was unforgettable. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) Some trips leave you with beautiful photographs, others with unforgettable memories, and some leave you with a whole new perspective. My experience in South Korea with LG Electronics was a combination of all three. South Korea had been on my travel wish list for a while, so finally getting the opportunity to visit was exciting in itself. But this was more than just a trip to a new destination. It was an opportunity to explore the world of LG Electronics, understand its journey, experience its innovations firsthand and discover how technology continues to shape the way we live. Over five days, we explored different locations, met incredible people, exchanged ideas, experienced some of Korea’s most exciting innovations and, of course, made time to enjoy the country’s food, culture and lifestyle. From Seoul to Changwon , every day brought something new. Here’s a look at how the experience unfolded. PART ONE: THE LG INNOVATION TOUR Our LG experience began with an introduction to the company’s vision, its Home Appliance Solutions business, and its ambition to become a Smart Life Solution Company. While many of us know LG for its home appliances, televisions, and consumer electronics, the tour offered a much broader understanding of the brand and the thinking behind its innovations. item.dc:creator: Omotunde Ibironke
item.content:encoded: Hello BNers, Omotunde here. From exploring futuristic smart homes and AI-powered manufacturing facilities to tasting Korean street food, discovering Seoul, and experiencing the country’s rich culture, my 5-day South Korea adventure with LG Electronics was unforgettable. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) Some trips leave you with beautiful photographs, others with unforgettable memories, and some leave you with a whole new perspective. My experience in South Korea with LG Electronics was a combination of all three. South Korea had been on my travel wish list for a while, so finally getting the opportunity to visit was exciting in itself. But this was more than just a trip to a new destination. It was an opportunity to explore the world of LG Electronics, understand its journey, experience its innovations firsthand and discover how technology continues to shape the way we live. Over five days, we explored different locations, met incredible people, exchanged ideas, experienced some of Korea’s most exciting innovations and, of course, made time to enjoy the country’s food, culture and lifestyle. From Seoul to Changwon , every day brought something new. Here’s a look at how the experience unfolded. PART ONE: THE LG INNOVATION TOUR Our LG experience began with an introduction to the company’s vision, its Home Appliance Solutions business, and its ambition to become a Smart Life Solution Company. While many of us know LG for its home appliances, televisions, and consumer electronics, the tour offered a much broader understanding of the brand and the thinking behind its innovations. At the LG Twin Towers, we were introduced to different aspects of the company’s business and got to explore some of its products and technologies, including the LG WashTower, InstaView refrigerator, Heat Pump Washer Dryer Combo, SolarDOM, and SKS premium appliances. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) What stood out to me was how much attention is being given to making everyday living smarter, more convenient, and more connected. It was interesting to see how products that perform familiar household functions are evolving through technology to offer entirely new experiences. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) It was a great introduction to what would become five days of learning and discovery. Changwon Smart Park: Where AI, Robotics and Manufacturing Meet One of the most insightful experiences of the tour was visiting LG Smart Park in Changwon. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) Before this visit, my idea of a manufacturing facility was largely shaped by traditional production lines and machinery. However, what I encountered at Changwon offered a completely different perspective. From the Heritage Lounge , where we got an introduction to LG’s manufacturing journey, to the Lighthouse Factory experience, there was so much to learn about how the company is integrating artificial intelligence, robotics, data and automation into its manufacturing processes. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) Recognised by the World Economic Forum as a Lighthouse Factory, LG Smart Park demonstrates how advanced technologies can transform manufacturing and improve efficiency. Seeing how robots, intelligent systems and people work together was particularly fascinating. It also got me thinking about the ongoing conversations around artificial intelligence and the future of work. Rather than simply viewing AI as a technology that replaces human effort, I got to see how it can support people, take on repetitive tasks and improve the way complex processes are managed. It was one of those visits that makes you appreciate just how much goes on behind the products we use every day. LG Science Park: A Glimpse Into the Future Our next stop was LG Science Park in Magok, Seoul, one of the company’s major research and development hubs. This was another opportunity to see how LG is thinking about the future of technology and everyday living. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) We explored the LG AI Home experience, ThinQ Real Home, the Innovation Showroom and the D5 flagship experience. The demonstrations offered a glimpse into what connected living could look like, with smart technologies and appliances working together to create a more seamless home experience. Imagine a home where your appliances communicate with one another, respond intelligently to your needs and make everyday routines easier. That was the kind of future these experiences brought to life. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) It was fascinating seeing how research, technology and innovation are being translated into solutions that could eventually become part of our everyday lives. And just when I thought there was already so much to take in, I got to meet CLOiD ! View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) Meeting CLOiD: When the Future Becomes Real Meeting a live robot called CLOiD was definitely one of those surreal moments of the trip. We have seen robots in movies and watched countless videos of artificial intelligence and robotics, but seeing one up close and experiencing it in person is something else entirely. It was fascinating to see how far robotics has come and how these technologies are moving beyond futuristic concepts into real-world applications. Experiences like this make you pause and think about how different our everyday lives could look in the years ahead. From Goldstar to LG: Understanding the Evolution of a Global Brand Another interesting part of the tour was learning more about LG’s history and evolution. The company’s story dates back to 1947, when it began as Lak Hui Chemical. In 1958, Goldstar was established, marking its entry into the electronics industry. The company eventually adopted the LG identity in 1995. Getting to see this journey represented through its history, milestones and innovations gave me a deeper appreciation of how the brand has evolved over the decades. It was particularly interesting learning about some of LG’s early milestones, including its first electric fan in 1960, refrigerator in 1965, air conditioner in 1968 and washing machine in 1969. From those early innovations to the smart appliances and technologies we explored during the tour, it was a remarkable reminder of how far the company has come. It also reinforced something I took away from the experience: innovation is not a one-time achievement. It requires continuous learning, improvement and the willingness to imagine what is possible beyond the present. The LG Flagship Store: Experiencing Innovation in One Space Our visit to the LG Flagship Store was a lovely way to bring different aspects of the tour together. Having spent the preceding days learning about LG’s history, exploring its manufacturing facilities and experiencing its smart home technologies, visiting the flagship store offered another opportunity to interact with the brand’s innovations in one space. One of my favourite experiences there was the Vision Hall. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) Stepping into the space felt like stepping into another world. The colours, visuals and immersive displays created such a beautiful cinematic experience. It was almost otherworldly, and I found myself completely immersed in the moment. Beyond the visual experience, it made me appreciate how far technology has come and the possibilities that innovation continues to create. item.title: How years of research built Grand Theft Auto VI’s obsessively detailed world
item.description: The developers behind its virtual Florida share how they built their most ambitious world so far • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.” I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? Did locals know what they were doing? This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.” Continue reading...

item.title: Hubble Space Telescope reveals glittering stars with mysterious origins | Space photo of the day for Nov. 11, 2026
item.description: null The Hubble Space Telescope has captured a breathtaking view of thousands of stars glittering like cosmic jewels in a dazzling display of blue, gold and orange. But this spectacular scene is far more than just a pretty picture. Some of these stars are almost as old as the universe itself and could hold clues to how our Milky Way formed. M30 is a globular star cluster located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth. (Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini) What is it? The exquisite image released by ESA on Nov. 5 shows Messier 30 (M30), a densely packed collection of stars located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth in the constellation Capricornus. M30 is a globular cluster, a roughly spherical collection of tens of thousands to millions of stars held together by gravity . Our Milky Way is home to at least 150 of these ancient stellar gatherings, some of which are estimated to be between 11.5 billion and 13.5 billion years old. For comparison, the universe itself is approximately 13.8 billion years old! Why is it amazing Besides looking like a vast cosmic treasure trove glittering across the universe, M30 also has a fascinating story to tell. Globular clusters are essentially cosmic time capsules. Their ancient stars preserve chemical clues about the conditions that existed when they formed, helping astronomers piece together the Milky Way's early history. Astronomers have also discovered that M30, along with several other globular clusters, traverses the Milky Way in the opposite direction to the galaxy's rotation. This unusual motion raises the intriguing possibility that M30 may not have formed in our galaxy at all. It could have simply been captured by the Milky Way billions of years ago.

item.title: Why I recommend the Seestar S30 Plus smart telescope for beginners — full review
item.description: null I’ve used several smart telescopes over the last few years, but I'd recommend the ZWO Seestar S30 Plus to almost anyone wanting to get started in astrophotography. At $499/€499, it’s a complete imaging system that can photograph galaxies, nebulae and star clusters automatically, even from a light-polluted city. Better still, it’s so small that it can live on a bookshelf. The Pleiades (M45), photographed in mosaic mode with the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter The Dumbbell Nebula (M27) photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter I recently captured images of the Dumbbell Nebula (M27), the North America Nebula (NGC 7000), the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) and the Pleiades (M45) with the S30 Plus. All were remarkably easy to capture, and none of the images accompanying this review required external processing. It’s basically point-and-shoot astrophotography — if you live under light-polluted skies, that’s a game-changer. Star trails photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus’s dedicated Star Trail mode. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter) I also think the S30 Plus makes an ideal companion to a conventional optical telescope. I can set it to photograph a nebula I have no hope of seeing under light pollution while I try to find brighter objects through the eyepiece of another telescope. It will then get on with collecting photons while I enjoy observing. For anyone who already owns a telescope but doesn’t want the expense and complexity of conventional astrophotography, that’s a compelling proposition. I photographed nebulas despite light pollution The S30 Plus is Seestar’s new entry-level smart telescope. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter) One problem with buying a cheap optical telescope is that deep-sky objects rarely resemble the colorful photographs you see online. The moon, planets and bright star clusters can look wonderful through an eyepiece, but faint galaxies and nebulas are much harder to appreciate, particularly from a town or city. Like all smart telescopes, the S30 Plus gets around that problem by photographing objects rather than showing them directly. Its camera takes repeated exposures, which the telescope automatically stacks to reduce noise and gradually reveal faint detail. The longer you leave it working, the better the resulting image tends to become. Being able to photograph colorful nebulas without traveling to a remote observing site is one of the biggest attractions of the S30 Plus. For beginners living in cities, it could transform their experience of astronomy. It’s the perfect companion to my optical telescope The North America Nebula (NGC 7000) photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus. item.dc:creator: Jamie Carter
item.content:encoded: null I’ve used several smart telescopes over the last few years, but I'd recommend the ZWO Seestar S30 Plus to almost anyone wanting to get started in astrophotography. At $499/€499, it’s a complete imaging system that can photograph galaxies, nebulae and star clusters automatically, even from a light-polluted city. Better still, it’s so small that it can live on a bookshelf. The Pleiades (M45), photographed in mosaic mode with the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter The Dumbbell Nebula (M27) photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter I recently captured images of the Dumbbell Nebula (M27), the North America Nebula (NGC 7000), the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) and the Pleiades (M45) with the S30 Plus. All were remarkably easy to capture, and none of the images accompanying this review required external processing. It’s basically point-and-shoot astrophotography — if you live under light-polluted skies, that’s a game-changer. Star trails photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus’s dedicated Star Trail mode. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter) I also think the S30 Plus makes an ideal companion to a conventional optical telescope. I can set it to photograph a nebula I have no hope of seeing under light pollution while I try to find brighter objects through the eyepiece of another telescope. It will then get on with collecting photons while I enjoy observing. For anyone who already owns a telescope but doesn’t want the expense and complexity of conventional astrophotography, that’s a compelling proposition. I photographed nebulas despite light pollution The S30 Plus is Seestar’s new entry-level smart telescope. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter) One problem with buying a cheap optical telescope is that deep-sky objects rarely resemble the colorful photographs you see online. The moon, planets and bright star clusters can look wonderful through an eyepiece, but faint galaxies and nebulas are much harder to appreciate, particularly from a town or city. Like all smart telescopes, the S30 Plus gets around that problem by photographing objects rather than showing them directly. Its camera takes repeated exposures, which the telescope automatically stacks to reduce noise and gradually reveal faint detail. The longer you leave it working, the better the resulting image tends to become. Being able to photograph colorful nebulas without traveling to a remote observing site is one of the biggest attractions of the S30 Plus. For beginners living in cities, it could transform their experience of astronomy. It’s the perfect companion to my optical telescope The North America Nebula (NGC 7000) photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter) I’ve always preferred spending my nights looking at the sky rather than fiddling with equipment, which is one reason I enjoy smart telescopes. Traditional astrophotography can involve a camera, tracking mount, adapters, cables, alignment, a laptop and considerable patience before the first useful exposure begins. The S30 Plus removes almost all of that. The Seestar S30 Plus has two 3.7MP cameras — almost 80% more pixels than the original S30. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter) I can put it outside, connect the Seestar app and choose a target from its built-in sky atlas. The telescope then moves to the correct position, identifies the star field, centers the object, focuses and begins imaging. Within minutes, a photograph starts appearing on my smartphone. That leaves me free to use an optical telescope alongside it — or stay inside and do something else. The moon on a cloudy night, photographed with the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter) The sun photographed with a Seestar S30 Plus fitted with its supplied magnetic solar filter. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter The Seestar S30 Plus is small enough to fit in any backpack. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter Its 3/8-inch tripod thread can be annoying if you’re used to 3/4-inch threads. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter The longer I leave it alone, the better the images get The Seestar S30 Plus has built-in filters to reduce light pollution. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Using the S30 Plus’s built-in UV/IR cut filter — which blocks ultraviolet and infrared light — I captured the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), a popular deep-sky object. As the hours went by, the dust lanes on its outskirts appeared in ever more detail. That’s how smart telescopes work — they collect and combine dozens or hundreds of short exposures, gradually revealing fainter structure while reducing noise. So impressive is the image after only about five or six exposures that it’s tempting to stop after a few minutes — but patience makes an enormous difference. Fortunately, you don’t have to stand beside the S30 Plus. You can leave it collecting light — even overnight, thanks to its scheduling option (though it’s not waterproof, so check the weather forecast!). Using the dual-band anti-light pollution filter, the Pleiades open cluster (M45) provided another interesting test. The S30 Plus has a mosaic mode that photographs overlapping sections of sky to create a larger image than its main camera can capture in a single frame. It’s ideal for expansive targets such as the Pleiades and Andromeda, although gathering enough exposures takes time. The app shows how much of the mosaic has been completed, and if needs be, you can continue collecting data on subsequent nights. I also photographed the Double Cluster in Perseus (NGC 869 and NGC 884) and the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules (M13), both relatively swift targets, but as anyone who’s used a smart telescope knows, it’s the faint nebulas that are the real prize. For those, dark skies mean better data — and that’s exactly why a smart telescope needs to be portable. It’s small enough to fit in my camera bag There are new post-processing features in the Seestar app. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter) The S30 Plus weighs just 3.64 lbs (1.65 kg) and measures 8.25 x 5.5 x 3.15 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm) when switched off. That’s small enough to fit into a camera bag in place of another lens or camera body, which is a major advantage because I travel to remote locations quite frequently. That fact that it sits on such a tiny tripod is also a boon. I’ve recently used the much larger Seestar S50 Pro , which weighs 6.17 lbs (2.8 kg). It’s a more capable imaging instrument with a 50mm aperture and a larger 8.3-megapixel sensor, but its heavier, bulkier chassis is harder to get into carry-on luggage. The S30 Plus and the higher-spec S30 Pro also differ from the S50 Pro in that they come with a padded carry case. This has a useful carrying handle, although there’s no shoulder strap or dedicated storage for the tripod and magnetic solar filter. It’s also worth taking along a portable battery and USB-C cable to recharge its built-in 6,000mAh battery during long sessions, though it lasts about six hours, which will suit most observing sessions. It’s much more advanced than the original S30 Switch off the S30 Plus, and it locks into the closed position. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter) The original, now-discontinued S30 was already impressive, but the S30 Plus is a substantial upgrade. It has improved four-element apochromatic optics with ED glass and two 3.7-megapixel cameras, each producing 1,440x2,560-pixel images. That’s almost 80% more pixels than the original S30’s main camera. The main camera’s field of view has increased slightly to about three degrees, while the wide-angle camera now covers 43.5 degrees of sky. The latter can be used for sta

item.title: NASA's new UVEX space telescope will peer deep into the universe's most violent events
item.description: null A new NASA space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility. The Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission, developed by NASA in conjunction with the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), will be the first mission to create deep all-sky maps in ultraviolet light. Thus, when it launches in 2031, UVEX will join new sky-mapping surveys like NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer), which scans the cosmos in infrared, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which does the same over the southern hemisphere in visible light, in creating deep-sky maps across a broad swathe of the electromagnetic spectrum. UVEX's ultraviolet views will reveal explosive events such as the collisions between ultra-dense stellar corpses called neutron stars and the supernova explosions that mark the deaths of massive stars and the births of neutron stars and black holes. Additionally, the NASA ultraviolet telescope should be able to detect a multitude of low-mass galaxies much closer to the Milky Way than similar galaxies that are currently being observed millions and even billions of light-years away by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) . The $590 million UVEX mission will "advance fundamental frontiers in astrophysics, from understanding the smallest galaxies to diagnosing the aftermath of neutron-star mergers and other cosmic explosions," the mission's principal investigator, Caltech physics professor Fiona Harrison, said in an Oct. 27 statement . "The first major ultraviolet space mission in two decades, UVEX is a bold leap forward in our exploration of the ultraviolet universe," Caltech President Ray Jayawardhana said in the same statement. UVEX will paint a picture of cosmic life, death and afterlife UVEX will benefit from a major leap forward in UV sensitivity thanks to its Caltech-built sensors, which are based on complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) imaging technology. This will help the spacecraft tap into what Harrison described as "the untapped opportunity in the UV." UVEX will be uniquely poised to spot millions of nearby, small, and faint galaxies that are teeming with infant stars that emit bright UV light. "In optical light, it's very hard to distinguish these nearby galaxies from faraway ones that look similar," Harrison said. "UV light will make them easier to find." UVEX won't just be investigating the infancy of stars , however. It will also examine the deaths of ancient stars in the form of supernovas. The supernova relic Pa 30, as seen by the Gemini north telescope. "The first major ultraviolet space mission in two decades, UVEX is a bold leap forward in our exploration of the ultraviolet universe," Caltech President Ray Jayawardhana said in the same statement. UVEX will paint a picture of cosmic life, death and afterlife UVEX will benefit from a major leap forward in UV sensitivity thanks to its Caltech-built sensors, which are based on complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) imaging technology. This will help the spacecraft tap into what Harrison described as "the untapped opportunity in the UV." UVEX will be uniquely poised to spot millions of nearby, small, and faint galaxies that are teeming with infant stars that emit bright UV light. "In optical light, it's very hard to distinguish these nearby galaxies from faraway ones that look similar," Harrison said. "UV light will make them easier to find." UVEX won't just be investigating the infancy of stars , however. It will also examine the deaths of ancient stars in the form of supernovas. The supernova relic Pa 30, as seen by the Gemini north telescope. (Image credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA) Supernovas occur when a massive star runs out of fuel for nuclear fusion and can no longer support itself against the inward push of its own gravity. As the core of the star collapses, its outer layers are blasted outward in cosmic explosions we call supernovas. This is a process that scientists are keen to understand, as these explosions fling the heavy elements forged during the stars' lifetimes into surrounding galaxies. This material becomes the building blocks of the next generation of stars, planets, and possibly even life. UVEX will also investigate what happens to the end products of some supernovas, neutron stars, when they meet and merge. An illustration shows two neutron stars colliding and merging. (Image credit: Robert Lea (created with Canva)) Neutron stars contain between one and two times the mass of the sun crammed into a width of around 12 miles (20 kilometers). That means they are composed of matter so dense that, if a teaspoon of it were brought to Earth, it would weigh over 1 billion tons. That's equivalent to stacking around 9 million adult blue whales on a spoon. So, when neutron stars in binary systems spiral together and merge, they create an environment so violent that it's the only place in the universe where scientists are sure that elements heavier than lead, like gold, silver, and platinum, are able to be forged. Currently, neutron star mergers are detected via ripples in spacetime called gravitational waves . Scientists can then follow up on the aftermath of the mergers by observing them in electromagnetic light, from high-energy gamma rays to low-energy radio waves. Thus, UVEX will add another aspect to the investigation of neutron star collisions and our understanding of where heavy elements originate. The new space telescope's maneuverability will allow it to observe these explosive events very shortly after they happen, giving it an advantage over other instruments, including NASA's long-serving Hubble Space Telescope. "With UVEX, we will now be able to follow up on gravitational-wave events in ultraviolet light," UVEX team member and Caltech scientist Mansi Kasliwal said in the same statement. "I can count on two hands how many spectra we have of transient events in their infancy phase with the Hubble Space Telescope. Hubble is, of course, amazing and does have some ultraviolet capabilities, but it cannot rapidly pivot to observe real-time events." An illustration of a stripped blue star (Image credit: Robert Lea) UVEX will also be revolutionary in the study of blue stars that have had their outer layers of hydrogen stripped away by companion stars. These stars offer researchers a unique opportunity to study the interior of stars, which is usually obscured by their outer layers. "We will be able to see what's inside the stars," Kareem El-Badry, an associate professor of astronomy at Caltech and a member of the UVEX team, said in the same statement. "We only know of a small number of stripped stars of this type now. UVEX will find hundreds." All of the above elements discussed are the expected discoveries and investigations that UVEX will be involved with. Perhaps even more exciting, however, are the unexpected elements of the universe it will uncover. "Every time you look at the skies in a new wavelength, you learn something new and unexpected," El-Badry said.

item.title: Meagan Good & Jonathan Majors Look Picture-Perfect at AFRIFF in Lagos
item.description: Meagan Good and Jonathan Majors coordinating in neutral tones and a red cap accent for AFRIFF. Who knew an ivory mini dress and a classic black suit could make such an interesting pairing? During their time in Lagos for AFRIFF, Meagan Good and Jonathan Majors posed for a studio portrait in two looks that took very different approaches to dressing up. Meagan’s dress brought together colourful beadwork, a fitted silhouette and a floor-length train, while Jonathan opted for black tailoring, an open-neck white shirt and a red cap. And while his outfit keeps things relatively simple, there’s nothing ordinary about the details of hers. Let’s start with Meagan’s dress, because there is quite a lot happening here. At first glance, the ivory mini might seem relatively simple, but look a little closer and the details begin to unfold. The fitted halter-neck bodice is covered in rows of turquoise, bronze and dark green beads, arranged horizontally to follow the shape of her waist. Then there’s the skirt, which takes a more unexpected turn with clusters of dark beaded embellishments scattered across the fabric. And just when you think you’ve taken it all in, an extended panel falls from the side of the mini skirt, creating a long, floor-sweeping train. It’s a fun combination of short and dramatic, with the beadwork giving the dress plenty to say without needing much else. Meagan Good styled in a sculpted halter-neck corset dress featuring multi-coloured beaded detailing and a side train. Meagan kept the rest of her styling fairly simple. Black ankle-strap heels and a textured black clutch were her accessories of choice, while her voluminous curls were left loose around her shoulders. Her bronze-toned makeup and glossy nude lip tied everything together without competing with the dress. Jonathan went in a completely different direction, keeping things classic with a black jacket and matching trousers over a white shirt, worn open at the neck. A grey patterned scarf added another detail around the collar, while his light-framed sunglasses and black patent shoes completed the outfit. But it’s the red cap that really changes the look. Against all that black and white, it gives the outfit a welcome hit of colour and makes the styling feel more personal. Meagan Good and Jonathan Majors showcasing intricate beaded dress embroidery and red cap styling. It’s an interesting pairing: Meagan’s dress has all the beadwork, colour and movement, while Jonathan’s outfit is built around simple tailoring and a few well-chosen accessories. There’s plenty to appreciate in both, wouldn’t you agree? Meagan Good displaying horizontal beadwork in turquoise and bronze paired with bronze-toned makeup. *** Photo Credit: Amplify Africa/Instagram The post Meagan Good & Jonathan Majors Look Picture-Perfect at AFRIFF in Lagos appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: What Are The Effective Ways of Using AI?
item.description: Two people engaging with technology in a contemporary hotel lobby work setting. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing how people learn, work, communicate and solve problems. In today’s world, if you’re not on board with AI, it could be said you’re being resistant to the fastest-growing technological innovation in the world. From students researching academic subjects to professionals developing business ideas, AI tools have become companions in everyday activities for people. They can help save time, explore new ideas, understand difficult concepts and approach tasks differently. However, as more people embrace these AI tools, it is important to understand that using AI effectively goes beyond knowing what prompts to enter. It requires knowing when to use it, how to question its responses and, most importantly, when to rely on your own knowledge and judgement. AI could make us better at what we do, not make us dependent on it. Here are ways we think you use AI effectively: Use AI as a Research Assistant One of the most effective ways to use AI is for research and information gathering. Whether you are writing an article, preparing a presentation or exploring an unfamiliar subject, AI can help you identify relevant topics, explain complex ideas and suggest areas worth investigating. You can ask it to break down unfamiliar concepts, identify key questions, or suggest research directions. However, do not treat every response as fact. Verify important information using credible sources, published research, books and reliable websites. AI can help you find information, but you are responsible for establishing what is true. Use AI to Brainstorm and Explore Ideas Like knowledge gathering, AI can brainstorm ideas with you. Sometimes, the hardest part of starting a project is knowing where to begin. AI can help you overcome this challenge by suggesting ideas, exploring different approaches and presenting perspectives you may not have considered. For writers, entrepreneurs, researchers and creatives, it can be a useful brainstorming partner. You can share an idea, ask questions about its strengths and weaknesses, and explore ways to develop it. However, brainstorming should not become an excuse to surrender your imagination. Let AI expand your thinking, not replace it. Use AI to Improve Your Work, Not Replace Your Skills This is becoming more important. AI can help you identify grammatical errors, improve sentence construction, organise information, summarise lengthy documents and make your communication clearer. It can reduce the time spent on repetitive tasks and create more room for important responsibilities. The important thing is that you should remain actively involved. Read what AI produces, question its suggestions and make the final decisions yourself. Your skills improve when you practise them, not when you consistently hand them over to a machine. item.dc:creator: BellaNaija Features
item.content:encoded: Two people engaging with technology in a contemporary hotel lobby work setting. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing how people learn, work, communicate and solve problems. In today’s world, if you’re not on board with AI, it could be said you’re being resistant to the fastest-growing technological innovation in the world. From students researching academic subjects to professionals developing business ideas, AI tools have become companions in everyday activities for people. They can help save time, explore new ideas, understand difficult concepts and approach tasks differently. However, as more people embrace these AI tools, it is important to understand that using AI effectively goes beyond knowing what prompts to enter. It requires knowing when to use it, how to question its responses and, most importantly, when to rely on your own knowledge and judgement. AI could make us better at what we do, not make us dependent on it. Here are ways we think you use AI effectively: Use AI as a Research Assistant One of the most effective ways to use AI is for research and information gathering. Whether you are writing an article, preparing a presentation or exploring an unfamiliar subject, AI can help you identify relevant topics, explain complex ideas and suggest areas worth investigating. You can ask it to break down unfamiliar concepts, identify key questions, or suggest research directions. However, do not treat every response as fact. Verify important information using credible sources, published research, books and reliable websites. AI can help you find information, but you are responsible for establishing what is true. Use AI to Brainstorm and Explore Ideas Like knowledge gathering, AI can brainstorm ideas with you. Sometimes, the hardest part of starting a project is knowing where to begin. AI can help you overcome this challenge by suggesting ideas, exploring different approaches and presenting perspectives you may not have considered. For writers, entrepreneurs, researchers and creatives, it can be a useful brainstorming partner. You can share an idea, ask questions about its strengths and weaknesses, and explore ways to develop it. However, brainstorming should not become an excuse to surrender your imagination. Let AI expand your thinking, not replace it. Use AI to Improve Your Work, Not Replace Your Skills This is becoming more important. AI can help you identify grammatical errors, improve sentence construction, organise information, summarise lengthy documents and make your communication clearer. It can reduce the time spent on repetitive tasks and create more room for important responsibilities. The important thing is that you should remain actively involved. Read what AI produces, question its suggestions and make the final decisions yourself. Your skills improve when you practise them, not when you consistently hand them over to a machine. For students, AI can explain difficult topics and provide feedback on your work. Protect Your Creativity and Intellectual Independence It is not advised to outsource your knowledge, original thinking or creativity to AI and then present its output as entirely your own. When students submit assignments generated by AI without engaging in the intellectual effort themselves, they undermine the true purpose of education. When writers publish AI-generated ideas as if they are personal experiences or original thoughts, they misrepresent their contributions to creativity. When professionals rely entirely on AI to perform tasks that they are expected to understand, they compromise the integrity of their work. There is nothing inherently wrong with seeking assistance. The ethical problem is when assistance becomes substitution, particularly when you claim credit for work, knowledge or experiences that are not yours. Your ideas, experiences, perspective and ability to think independently are valuable. Do not surrender them for convenience. AI could be considered not the enemy of human intelligence, creativity or productivity. Well, it did not create itself. If used responsibly, it can help learn faster, work smarter, explore opportunities and achieve things that might otherwise take considerably more time. But the goal should not be to become someone who cannot work without AI. Let AI assist your thinking, not do all your thinking. Let it improve your work, not become the source of all your work. Use it to research and learn. Whatever it is you’re learning – coding, digital marketing, photography, data analysis or another language – you can use AI to structure your learning journey. It can create a beginner-friendly curriculum, recommend practical exercises and assess your progress. But never allow the convenience of artificial intelligence to make you neglect the value of your own intelligence. item.title: From Lagos to Cotonou! BN’s Osas is Taking You Inside SIMA 2026
item.description: One thing you can always bet on, as far as BellaNaija is concerned, is our alignment with African culture, creativity, and the people shaping the continent’s stories. “For where our treasure is, our heart will be”. And this time around, our heart is in Cotonou! Oh, and so are we! Hey BNers! Osas Okonyon here, and I’m heading to the Republic of Benin for the third edition of the Salon des Industries Musicales d’Afrique Francophone (SIMA), where I’ll be over the next few days. SIMA is bringing together artists, music executives, producers, creatives, investors and other key players in the African music industry for conversations about the future of our sound, the business behind it, and how African music can continue to make its mark on the world. This year’s theme, “African Music: From the Stage to Global Influence,” is particularly exciting. Beyond the music we love and the artists we celebrate, there’s so much to explore about the business, opportunities, collaborations and structures that help African creativity thrive. From conversations around music financing, artificial intelligence and intellectual property to the intersections of music, fashion, film, tourism and sports, SIMA promises a fascinating look into the evolving creative landscape. So, whether you’re a music lover, a creative, an industry enthusiast or simply someone who loves experiencing Africa through its people and culture, come along with me. I’ll be bringing you the conversations, the discoveries, the behind-the-scenes moments and, of course, all the good vibes from Cotonou. Put on your seatbelts, BNers. We’re about to get into the sound and influence of African music! Follow along on Instagram via @bellanaija using any of these hashtags: #BNTravel #SIMA2026 #BNinCotonou #MusiqueAfricaine The post From Lagos to Cotonou! BN’s Osas is Taking You Inside SIMA 2026 appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: What time will SpaceX launch Starship Flight 15, its 1st double landing test, today? (Full mission timeline)
item.description:
Tariq is the Editor-in-Chief of Space.com based out of our New York City office and joined the team in 2001, first as an intern and staff writer, and later as an editor. He covers human spaceflight, exploration and space science, as well as skywatching and entertainment. He became Space.com's Managing Editor in 2009 and Editor-in-Chief in 2019. In October 2022, Tariq received the Harry Kolcum Award for excellence in space reporting from the National Space Club Florida Committee. In June 2025, the National Space Society awarded him the Space Pioneer Award for Excellence in Mass Media at the International Space Development Conference in Orlando, Florida.

Hailing from Stockton, California (where he attended the same high school as NASA astronaut Jose Hernandez), Tariq studied print journalism and astronomy at the University of Southern California in Los Angeles, earning a bachelor's degree in journalism in 1999 along with a minor in astronomy. He then served as a staff reporter for The Los Angeles Times covering education and city beats in La Habra and Fullerton in Orange County for the Our Times sections.

In 2000, Tariq became the city reporter for the Huntington Beach Independent, a weekly publication of the Los Angeles Times, covering local politics and events, crime, business and environmental issues. He left the Los Angeles Times in 2001 to study science journalism at New York University, where he earned a master's degree in 2002 from NYU's Science and Environmental Reporting Program (now the Science, Health and Environmental Reporting Program) under the direction of space reporter William Burrows.

Tariq first joined Space.com as an intern in September 2001 while also serving as a research assistant for nutrition writer Gary Taubes and writing freelance projects, where his work appeared in The Scientist and Laboratory Equipment Magazine. He became a full-time reporter covering spaceflight in 2004, with this first launch being NASA's STS-114 Return to Flight mission in July 2005.

Tariq is also an Eagle Scout (yes, he has the Space Exploration merit badge) and went to Space Camp four times as a kid and a fifth time as an adult. When not writing about space, you can find Tariq watching the latest Star Trek TV series, sci-fi movies and reading about hippos, his favorite animal. You can find Tariq at Space.com and as the co-host to the This Week In Space podcast with space historian Rod Pyle on the TWiT network. To see his latest project, you can follow Tariq on Twitter @tariqjmalik.

Update for 6:25 p.m. ET: SpaceX has launched the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing. See launch video and our full Starship Flight 15 liftoff wrap . SpaceX is counting down to what might be its most ambitious test flight yet of the company's massive Starship megarocket, the largest launch vehicle ever built. Today (Nov. 13), SpaceX will launch its next Starship test flight on a mission that, if successful, will return both its Super Heavy first-stage booster and Ship upper stage to Earth for back-to-back landings at their launch pad. It will be the first full recovery of an orbital rocket in history. And if you want to watch it live, you'll need to know what time and where to tune in. In our guide below, we'll explain exactly when and how to watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission . It is the 15th test flight of the giant stainless-steel reusable rocket, which SpaceX wants to use for everything from Starlink internet satellite launches to landing NASA Artemis astronauts on the moon in 2028, and even for a crewed flight to Mars. But first, SpaceX has to successfully recover and refly both stages, something it's never done before — and that's where Flight 15 comes in. It's the first time the company will try to land an entire Starship rocket. Here's when to tune in. What time is SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch (and landing)? The Starship Flight 15 test mission is currently scheduled to launch no earlier than Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT) , from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. But there is a chance of a later liftoff time. SpaceX has said it has a 75-minute window in which to launch Starship Flight 15 to add some flexibility into its preflight countdown. That means the launch could take place anytime between 5:45 p.m. and 7 p.m. EST (2245-0000 Nov. 14) . The local time for the launch window will be 4:45 p.m. to 6 p.m. CST . SpaceX has not formally announced if it has backup days for the launch, but if the company does have those options, liftoff would likely occur at the same time, based on past Starship missions that saw delays. One thing that separates Starship Flight 15 from past Starship test flights is its length. The mission, if it runs its full duration, will last just over 22.5 hours until Ship lands back at Starbase. That landing would occur on Saturday, Nov. 14, at 4:17 p.m. EST (2117 GMT) . If SpaceX launches at the end of its window on Friday, at 7 p.m. EST, the Ship landing would occur on Saturday at 5:32 p.m. EST (2232 GMT) . Meanwhile, the Super Heavy, known as Booster 22, will land about 6.5 minutes after liftoff . Related: Read our SpaceX Starship and Super Heavy guide for a detailed look at the megarocket. Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon . Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g. View Deal Can I watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch? Yes, you'll be able to watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch online, and you have many ways to do so. Space.com will host a livestream simulcast of Starship Flight 15 on this page, as well as on our homepage and our YouTube channel VideoFromSpace. That webcast will begin about 30 minutes before liftoff, at 5:15 p.m. EST (2215 GMT) . However, it may start earlier at 4:58 p.m. EST (2158 GMT) , based on a new start time on SpaceX's X account. SpaceX, of course, will offer its own Starship Flight 15 livestream on its Flight 15 mission page , as well as on its X account . That livestream will also begin 30 minutes before launch, at 5:15 p.m. EST (it's the same one as on Space.com). A prelaunch show If you need your Starship launch preparations fix before the Nov. 13 launch, good news: You can see SpaceX's prep work live online. NASASpaceflight's YouTube channel offers live views of SpaceX's Starship pads at Starbase 24 hours a day, seven days a week. On Wednesday (Nov. 11), the channel will stream live views of the Starship Flight 15 rocket stacking, starting at 3 p.m. EDT (1900 GMT) . The NASASpaceflight Flight 15 launch webcast will begin on Nov. 13 at 11:45 a.m. EDT (1645 GMT) , about six hours before launch. NASASpaceflight typically offers live commentary and constantly changing views of the Starship launch pad via remote cameras positioned around Starbase. In-person launch options If there was ever a SpaceX Starship test flight to see in person, this just might be it. In addition to watching the world's largest rocket launch into space, Starship Flight 15 offers the chance to see both parts of that megarocket return to Earth and be caught in mid-air, 22.5 hours apart. If you've read our past Starship launch viewing guides, you'll know that SpaceX doesn't have an official viewing site for Starship launches. But you can see the spectacle from several public beaches (as well as private campgrounds). Cameron County Amphitheater at Isla Blanca Park on South Padre Island is always my first recommendation ( I watched the first Starship launch from there in April 2023). The pa

item.title: Inside Delphino Drunch: How The Lagos Event Merged Business, Music & Premium Hospitality
item.description: Lagos had a date with good food, music and conversation on 1 November as Delphino Drunch brought together entrepreneurs, corporate executives and creatives for an afternoon out. Powered by The Glenlivet, the gathering gave guests a chance to enjoy a leisurely lunch, try specially prepared whisky cocktails and catch up with familiar faces while meeting new ones. There was plenty to enjoy beyond the dining table. Guests were treated to a multi-course menu, with cocktails made using The Glenlivet’s single malt Scotch whisky served alongside the food. The afternoon’s music also had its own progression, beginning with relaxed background sounds over lunch before making way for DJ sets as the gathering continued into the early evening. The guest list brought together people from different corners of Lagos’ business and creative communities, and the setting gave them room to connect away from the usual work meetings and formal events. There was also plenty to take in fashion-wise, with guests arriving in tailored co-ords, polished separates and contemporary daywear. From the food and drinks to the music and conversations, Delphino Drunch offered a lovely way to spend a November afternoon in Lagos. See photos: The post Inside Delphino Drunch: How The Lagos Event Merged Business, Music & Premium Hospitality appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Forget the Usual Black Suit, Priscilla Ojo Is Making a Case for Chocolate Brown
item.description: Priscilla Ojo wearing an embellished chocolate brown suit co-ord paired with pointed-toe camel pumps Who says a business launch calls for the usual power suit? Priscilla Ojo had a different idea when she stepped out to introduce her latest venture, PalmPriy. The content creator, entrepreneur and style tastemaker chose a rich chocolate brown two-piece, but this was no ordinary office suit. With bronze and amber beaded fringe running across the jacket, her look brought a little extra personality to corporate dressing. The suit makes a case for giving brown tailoring a place in your wardrobe. Its single-breasted blazer features sharp shoulders and a defined waist, while the floor-length wide-leg trousers give the outfit a relaxed, fluid finish. Then come the embellishments: heavy bronze and amber beads tracing the lapels, hemline and cuffs. They add movement and texture to the jacket, making it the piece that draws the eye without overwhelming the overall look. Priscilla Ojo styled in a custom beaded chocolate brown suit for the official launch of her business, PalmPriy. Priscilla also got the proportions right with her footwear. She paired the wide-leg trousers with pointed-toe camel pumps, allowing just a glimpse of the shoes beneath the long hems. The rest of her accessories stayed simple, with subtle drop earrings and delicate rings leaving the embellished suit plenty of room to speak for itself. A detailed view of Priscilla Ojo’s chocolate brown blazer featuring hand-sewn pearls and beaded fringe. Her beauty look followed the warm colour palette. She wore her hair in long, cascading waves with copper highlights, parted down the middle, and completed the look with bronze-toned soft glam and a glossy nude lip. For anyone looking to take their tailoring beyond the familiar black or grey suit, Priscilla’s PalmPriy launch outfit offers a lovely starting point. Chocolate brown, wide-leg trousers and a little embellishment make for a combination worth considering, whether you’re dressing for a business event or looking to give your workwear a new direction. Priscilla Ojo posing in her PalmPriy launch look, featuring structured shoulder tailoring and beaded tassel cuffs *** Photo Credit: Priscilla Ojo/Instagram The post Forget the Usual Black Suit, Priscilla Ojo Is Making a Case for Chocolate Brown appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world.
